properties.notes: The valley between the Capitoline and the Palatine has been the centre of Roman public life for eight hundred years, and by 117 CE it is built up to its edges. The Senate meets in the Curia at the north end. Magistrates speak from the Rostra, its platform studded with the bronze rams of captured warships. Temples of Saturn, of Concord, of Castor and Pollux and of the deified Caesar ring the open ground, and the state treasury sits in the vaults under Saturn's podium. Two basilicas take the law courts and the bankers indoors. Triumphs end here and funerals pass through.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum from Palatine Hill · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Varro
ancient_sources.note: Walks the Forum naming its parts and arguing where each name came from — the Comitium, the Rostra, the Lacus Curtius, the streets running off it.

ancient_sources.author: Dionysius of Halicarnassus
ancient_sources.note: Credits Tarquin with draining the valley into the Cloaca Maxima and laying out the Forum as the city's meeting place.

properties.notes: Third permanent Senate House on this site, begun by Julius Caesar in 44 BCE to replace the Curia Cornelia/Hostilia, completed and dedicated by Augustus in 29 BCE; rebuilt again after a fire under Domitian c. 94 CE. Standing and in use as the meeting hall of the Senate in 117 CE. Survives today largely intact because it was converted into the church of Sant'Adriano in 630 CE.
properties.image_credit: Curia Julia, Roman Forum · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Records Augustus dedicating the Curia Julia in 29 BCE, with the altar and statue of Victory set inside it.

properties.notes: Civil law-court basilica on the south side of the Forum, begun by Caesar in 54 BCE, dedicated unfinished in 46 BCE, completed by Augustus and rededicated in 12 CE to Gaius and Lucius Caesar after a fire. Housed the centumviral court; standing in 117 CE (it burned again only in 283 CE under Carinus).

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Names the basilica between the temples of Castor and Saturn as Caesar's foundation, finished by Augustus, burned down and rebuilt on a larger plan.

properties.notes: North side of the Forum, opposite the Basilica Julia; first built by the censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior in 179 BCE, rebuilt after fires under Augustus (14 BCE) and again after a fire in 22 CE under Tiberius, with continuing Julio-Claudian era repairs. Pliny (NH 36.24) counted it among the most beautiful buildings in the world; standing in 117 CE (it was finally destroyed by the Visigothic sack of 410 CE).

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Ranks it among the three most beautiful buildings the world has ever seen, alongside the Forum of Augustus and the Temple of Peace.

properties.notes: One of the oldest temples in the Forum, dedicated 497 BCE at the foot of the Capitoline; rebuilt by L. Munatius Plancus c. 42 BCE. Doubled as the state treasury (Aerarium Populi Romani), standing and functioning as such in 117 CE (the surviving columned facade dates from a later, post-283 CE, rebuild).
properties.image_credit: Temple of Saturn, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Livy
ancient_sources.note: Dates the temple's dedication to the early Republic and notes the Saturnalia was instituted with it.

properties.notes: A small round temple with a conical roof and a vent for smoke, holding no statue of the goddess — only the fire. Six priestesses keep it burning, and it is relit each year on the first of March by rubbing wood rather than by carrying a flame from anywhere else. Behind the hearth is a storeroom no man may enter, said to hold the tokens of Rome's survival carried out of Troy. In June the temple opens to the women of the city, who come barefoot with offerings. If the fire goes out, the Vestal on watch is beaten. In 117 CE the building standing here is the Augustan rebuild.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Vesta, Roman Forum · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Ovid
ancient_sources.note: Explains the round shape as an image of the earth, and that the temple holds no statue of the goddess — only the fire, which is her.

properties.notes: Six women live here, in a colonnaded house of two storeys built around a long courtyard of pools, wedged between the Forum and the Palatine slope. They are the Vestals: taken as children, bound to thirty years of service and to chastity, and answerable to the chief priest of Rome. Their work is to keep the hearth fire of the state alight, and letting it go out is treated as a public emergency. Romans also lodge wills and treaties with them, on the reasoning that nobody would dare rob this house. In 117 CE the building is newly rebuilt, and grander than the one it replaced.

The Dioscuri were said to have appeared on the Roman side at the battle of Lake Regillus, then to have watered their horses at the spring here while bringing news of the victory to the city ahead of any messenger. The temple was vowed on that promise and dedicated in 484 BCE. Tiberius rebuilt it after a fire and rededicated it in 6 CE in his own name and his dead brother's. Its high podium doubles as a speaker's platform, the office of weights and measures works out of the vaults beneath, and bankers keep strongrooms there. In 117 CE it is one of the busiest buildings in the Forum, and not only for worship.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Castor and Pollux · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Livy
ancient_sources.note: The temple is vowed on the field at Lake Regillus when the Dioscuri are seen fighting for Rome, and dedicated by the vower's son fifteen years later.

properties.notes: Caesar's body was burned in the Forum by a crowd that would not wait for the funeral to finish, and this temple stands on the spot. Augustus dedicated it on 18 August 29 BCE, the first temple in Rome raised to a Roman who had been made a god. Its front platform is a second speaker's rostra, faced with the beaks of ships taken at Actium, so anyone addressing the Forum from it stands on the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra. A round altar in a recess below marks the pyre. In 117 CE the cult of the deified emperors begins here, with the founder of the line.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Divus Julius · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Describes the crowd burning Caesar's body in the Forum itself, and the column later raised on the spot where the pyre stood.

properties.notes: Original temple vowed 367 BCE, rebuilt 121 BCE by L. Opimius; completely rebuilt on a larger scale by the future emperor Tiberius between 7 BCE and 10 CE and rededicated as the Aedes Concordiae Augustae on 16 January 10 CE. This Tiberian-era temple was standing at the west end of the Forum in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Concord · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Ovid
ancient_sources.note: Marks 16 January as the dedication day of the temple Tiberius rebuilt from German spoils, and calls Concord the goddess of the imperial house.

properties.notes: Traditionally the residence of the kings of Rome, later the official headquarters of the Pontifex Maximus and seat of the pontifical archives; rebuilt in stone/marble after a fire in 36 BCE by Cn. Domitius Calvinus. Standing and functioning as the pontifical office in 117 CE (in this period the emperor himself held the office of Pontifex Maximus).

ancient_sources.author: Ovid
ancient_sources.note: Ovid names the Regia directly, describing the small space now holding Vesta's atrium as once having been the great palace (regia) of long-haired King Numa.

properties.notes: Public oratory platform at the northwest end of the Forum square, decorated with captured ships' prows (rostra); rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BCE as a curved 'hemicycle' and extended by Augustus with a rectangular marble-faced platform c. 24 m wide. In active use for public speeches in 117 CE. Coordinates are approximate (no precisely surveyed findspot published for the platform's exact footprint independent of later Severan-era rebuilding).

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: After Cicero's proscription in 43 BCE, his severed head and right hand were displayed on the Rostra in the Forum, the platform from which he had delivered his speeches.

properties.modern_location: Rome, Italy, Via Sacra, Roman Forum
properties.notes: A single marble archway at the highest point of the Sacred Way, put up by Domitian for his dead brother and inscribed to the deified Titus. Inside the passage two relief panels face each other. On one, soldiers carry the loot of the Jerusalem temple in triumph — a seven-branched lampstand held high, the show-bread table, silver trumpets, placards naming the captured towns. On the other, Titus rides a four-horse chariot with Victory reaching over his shoulder to crown him. In the vault above, an eagle carries him up to the gods. In 117 CE the war it commemorates is still within living memory.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Titus, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the triumph of 71 CE and the spoils carried through Rome — the golden table, the lampstand, the Law — the same objects carved on the arch's inner panel.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VI 945
ancient_sources.quote: Senatus populusque Romanus divo Tito divi Vespasiani f. Vespasiano Augusto
ancient_sources.note: The attic text: the Senate and People of Rome dedicate the arch to the deified Titus, son of the deified Vespasian — cut after his death.

properties.notes: Chief state temple of Rome atop the Capitoline, originally dedicated 509 BCE; destroyed and rebuilt three times (83 BCE fire, Vitellian-era fire 69 CE, Titus-era fire 80 CE), with the final Domitianic reconstruction in gleaming Pentelic marble dedicated c. 82 CE. This was the temple standing in 117 CE, the terminus of every triumphal procession.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction by Léon Vaudoyer, 1830 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Capitol burning in the fighting of 69 CE and calls it the worst disgrace to befall the Roman state, the temple having stood since the kings.

ancient_sources.author: Livy
ancient_sources.note: The foundation story: the human head found in the footings, read as a sign that this hill would be the head of the empire.

properties.notes: Rome's public records are kept in a massive building wedged into the Capitoline slope, closing the west end of the Forum like a retaining wall with a face on it. An arcade of eleven arches framed by engaged Doric columns runs along its front, looking down over the whole valley. Inside are the bronze tablets on which laws, treaties and decrees of the Senate are cut — the memory of the state, in metal, in one fireproof room of stone. It was finished in 78 BCE by a consul rebuilding after fire had swept the Capitol. In 117 CE it still works, and its arcade frames every view of the Forum from the west.

ancient_sources.author: CIL I² 736
ancient_sources.quote: Q. Lutatius Q. f. Q. n. Catulus co(n)s(ul) substructionem et tabularium de s(enatus) s(ententia) faciund(um) coeravit eidemque probavit
ancient_sources.note: Cut on the record-office's doorposts: the consul Quintus Lutatius Catulus had the substructure and archive built and approved it, by decree of the Senate.

properties.notes: Private residential wing of Domitian's vast Flavian imperial palace on the Palatine, completed 92 CE by his architect Rabirius; from this point the main imperial residence of Rome through the 2nd century. In use as the emperor's palace in 117 CE (Trajan died in Cilicia, but Rome's imperial household still resided here).

ancient_sources.author: Statius
ancient_sources.note: A guest's account of dining in Domitian's new palace: a hall so high the eye tires before it reaches the ceiling, and columns that could hold up the sky.

properties.notes: The public half of the emperor's house on the Palatine, finished in 92 CE, is built to make an audience feel small. Its throne hall is roofed in a single unsupported span nearly thirty metres across and lined with coloured marble columns and niches of statuary. Next door a basilica gives the emperor a courtroom; on the other side a banqueting hall opens through wide windows onto sunken fountain courts, so guests eat looking at moving water. Between them a peristyle garden holds a maze-shaped pool around an island. In 117 CE Trajan's household works here, and after August, Hadrian's.

Rome's great chariot-racing stadium in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine, traditionally founded under the kings; rebuilt in stone/monumentalized under Julius Caesar and Augustus, and rebuilt again by Trajan after a fire under Domitian, with Trajan's reconstruction completed c. 103 CE. This Trajanic-era Circus, capable of holding well over 150,000 spectators, was in full use in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Circus Maximus, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Dionysius of Halicarnassus
ancient_sources.note: Gives the circus its dimensions and describes the tiers of seating, the shops and porticoes beneath, and the euripus running down the middle.

properties.notes: Vespasian drained the ornamental lake of Nero's palace and gave the ground back to the people as an amphitheatre; the politics of the gesture were the point of it. Titus opened the building in 80 CE with a hundred days of games, and Domitian added the top storey and the two-level basement of cells, cages and lifts beneath the arena floor. Around fifty thousand people come in through eighty numbered arches on tokens that match their seats, sorted by rank from senators at the arena rail to women and the poor at the top. Sailors work an awning on ropes above the crowd. In 117 CE it is thirty-seven years old.
properties.image_credit: Colosseum, Rome · Diliff, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Vespasian begins an amphitheatre in the middle of the city, on ground Augustus had wanted to use for one.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Titus's inaugural games: a hundred days of hunts, gladiators and a flooded arena staging a sea battle.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VI 40454a
ancient_sources.note: Reconstructed from the nail-holes on a reused seating block: the amphitheatre was built from the spoils of war — originally credited to Vespasian, the text amended after his death to insert Titus's name.

properties.notes: Last and largest of the Imperial Fora, built with the spoils of the Dacian Wars, designed by Apollodorus of Damascus, construction begun c. 105-107 CE and formally dedicated 112 CE; the Basilica Ulpia, twin libraries, and Column followed by 113 CE. Newly completed and the showpiece of the city in 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
ancient_sources.note: Constantius II, shown Rome in 357, stops dead in Trajan's Forum — a structure, Ammianus says, unique under heaven and beyond description.

properties.notes: Built into the cut face of the Quirinal beside Trajan's Forum, this is six storeys of brick-faced concrete holding roughly a hundred and fifty rooms, linked by stairs, ramps and a paved street that runs across the slope halfway up. A vaulted hall at its centre is roofed by concrete groin vaults springing from piers — a way of covering a wide space without filling it with columns. The rooms were long read as shops; more likely they are offices for the staff who administered the grain dole and the city's supply. In 117 CE the complex is barely finished, and the mortar is still curing.
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Market, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: 38 m (with pedestal) freestanding marble victory column between the Basilica Ulpia and the twin libraries, its shaft wrapped in a continuous helical relief depicting the Dacian Wars; dedicated 12 May 113 CE. Newly erected and gleaming in 117 CE; Trajan's ashes were interred in its base after his death in August 117.
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Column, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: The column is set up in the forum both to mark how high the ground stood before the hill was cut away, and as the emperor's tomb.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VI 960
ancient_sources.note: The pedestal records that the Senate and People of Rome set the column up to Trajan, and — famously — to show how high the ground and hill stood before the works for his Forum cut them away.

properties.notes: Twin library halls (one Latin, one Greek), each holding an estimated 20,000 scrolls, flanking Trajan's Column within the Forum of Trajan; founded by Trajan c. 114 CE. One of the great libraries of the ancient world, newly opened and functioning in 117 CE. Coordinates approximate the space between the Basilica Ulpia and the Temple of the Deified Trajan.

The first of Rome's monumental 'imperial' bath complexes, built on the Oppian Hill over part of the buried Domus Aurea; designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and formally inaugurated on 22 June (Kalends of July) 109 CE. Covering roughly 330 x 340 m, it was operating at full scale in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Baths of Trajan · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: names the baths among the works Apollodorus of Damascus built for Trajan in Rome, in the anecdote explaining Hadrian's later grudge against the architect

properties.notes: Public bath complex built quickly by Titus and dedicated in 80 or 81 CE alongside the newly opened Colosseum, incorporating part of Nero's former Domus Aurea. One of the earliest 'imperial thermae' establishing the symmetrical plan later copied at the Baths of Trajan next door; still in operation in 117 CE, though already overshadowed by Trajan's larger complex.

ancient_sources.author: Martial
ancient_sources.note: Set beside the new amphitheatre as proof that ground Nero had taken for himself was being handed back to the people.

properties.notes: Public baths in the Campus Martius near the Pantheon and Saepta, built by Nero c. 62-64 CE (the earliest of Rome's grand imperial thermae, predating even Titus's); listed among the notable buildings of the city by Martial and later authors. Still standing and in use in 117 CE under its original name (it was only enlarged and renamed Thermae Alexandrinae after Severus Alexander's restoration in the 3rd century).

ancient_sources.author: Martial
ancient_sources.note: Martial jokes that nothing was worse than Nero, yet nothing better than his baths, holding up the Baths of Nero as the standard of luxury against a rival's new bathhouse.

properties.notes: The Pantheon everyone pictures was not finished in Trajan's lifetime. Agrippa built a rectangular temple on this ground in 27 BCE; it burned in the great fire of 80 CE, was rebuilt, and burned again around 110 CE after a lightning strike. Work on the replacement — the domed rotunda — began under Trajan in the years after that fire, with brick stamps showing material arriving on site from about 114 CE. In August 117 CE this is a building site: the drum is rising, the dome is not yet closed, and dedication is more than a decade away. Hadrian, who becomes emperor that month, takes the credit for it.
sources: Lise Hetland, 'Dating the Pantheon', Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007), summarized at https://erenow.org/ancient/the-pantheon-from-antiquity-to-the-present/3.php
properties.image_credit: Pantheon, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL VI 896
ancient_sources.ref: M AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIVM FECIT
ancient_sources.note: The Pantheon's porch frieze names Marcus Agrippa, consul for the third time, as builder - the inscription Hadrian kept from Agrippa's original temple when he rebuilt the Pantheon around it.

properties.notes: Augustus finished the theatre his adoptive father had begun and put on it the name of a nephew who had died at nineteen. The curved outer wall is travertine, three storeys of arcades with engaged Doric columns below and Ionic above — the arrangement every later Roman theatre and amphitheatre copies, the Colosseum included. Somewhere between eleven and twenty thousand people can be seated, depending how tightly you count them in. It stands by the river at the foot of the Capitoline, next to the vegetable market and its old temples. In 117 CE it is the principal stone theatre of Rome and in constant use.

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Lists the theatre among the works Augustus built in another's name, dedicating it to his dead nephew Marcellus.

properties.notes: Open consecrated ground in the southern Campus Martius, laid out by censor Gaius Flaminius in 221 BCE; unlike the Circus Maximus it was never a fully enclosed monumental racetrack, functioning more as a public square used for games, assemblies, and triumphal musters, surrounded over time by temples and porticoes (e.g. Porticus Octaviae). Still an active open space in 117 CE. Its exact perimeter is not archaeologically fixed, so the point is an approximate centroid.

Vast circular tomb (90 m diameter, c. 42 m tall) built by Augustus in 28 BCE in the northern Campus Martius as the dynastic tomb for himself and the Julio-Claudian family, planted with cypresses and topped by his statue. Standing and receiving imperial burials (it remained the resting place of the Julio-Claudians and was still an active monument, though Trajan himself was interred instead at the base of his own Column) in 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: A great mound on a high white marble base by the river, planted to the top with evergreens, a bronze Augustus on the summit and the burial chambers below.

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Records that Augustus built it between the Via Flaminia and the Tiber bank in his sixth consulship, and opened the surrounding groves to the public.

properties.modern_location: Rome, Italy, right bank of the Tiber
properties.notes: In August 117 CE this is open ground on the right bank of the Tiber, across the river from the Campus Martius, and nothing has been built on it. The tomb that will stand here is Hadrian's, and he becomes emperor in the same month this map is set — acclaimed within days of Trajan's death on 8 August. Brick stamps put the start of building no earlier than 123 CE, and the drum was finished and the mausoleum dedicated only in 139, a year after Hadrian himself died. It is marked here because the reign it belongs to begins at the snapshot.

Marble altar within a sculpted precinct wall commemorating the Pax Romana established by Augustus, commissioned by the Senate in 13 BCE and consecrated 30 January 9 BCE, sited on the west side of the Via Flaminia in the Campus Martius. Standing and in cult use in 117 CE. Coordinates mark the approximate ancient findspot beneath the later Palazzo Fiano-Almagia (excavated 1937-38); the monument was moved and reassembled at its current Richard Meier museum site near Augustus's Mausoleum only in the 20th century.

ancient_sources.author: Augustus
ancient_sources.note: Augustus records that on his return from Spain and Gaul the Senate voted to consecrate an altar of Augustan Peace in the Campus Martius, with magistrates, priests, and Vestals to sacrifice there yearly.

properties.notes: NOT extant as a functioning palace in 117 CE - kept on the map for context because it directly underlies two extant POIs. Nero's sprawling post-fire palace complex (64 CE) was disowned by the Flavians: its lake was drained for the Colosseum, and its Esquiline wing was deliberately buried under earthen fill to serve as the foundation for the Baths of Titus (80 CE) and then the much larger Baths of Trajan (104-109 CE). By 117 CE the site was entirely subsumed beneath Trajan's bathing complex; the buried frescoed halls survived underground and were not rediscovered until the Renaissance.

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Suetonius reports Nero's only comment on dedicating his finished palace: that he could at last begin to live like a human being.

properties.name_latin: Aquae Claudia et Anio Novus (ad Portam Maiorem)
properties.name_english: Aqua Claudia / Anio Novus crossing at Porta Maggiore
properties.notes: Monumental double-arched travertine structure built by Claudius in 52 CE to carry the Aqua Claudia and (stacked above it) the Anio Novus aqueduct channels across the Via Praenestina and Via Labicana as they entered the city; restored under Vespasian and Titus. This arched aqueduct crossing was fully functional in 117 CE, supplying two of Rome's principal aqueducts (it was only incorporated as a city gate, Porta Maggiore, into the Aurelian Walls in the 270s CE, after our snapshot).

ancient_sources.author: Frontinus
ancient_sources.note: Claudius's two aqueducts, the Aqua Claudia from the Caerulean and Curtian springs and the Anio Novus, brought in on the same arches and finished in 52 CE.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VI 1256
ancient_sources.note: Claudius's inscription on the aqueduct crossing itself records that he brought in the Aqua Claudia and the Anio Novus at his own expense; Vespasian's and Titus's repair texts run below it on the same stones.

properties.name_english: Aqua Virgo terminus (later site of the Trevi Fountain)
properties.notes: Aqueduct completed by Agrippa in 19 BCE, running c. 20.5 km mostly underground from springs east of Rome, built specifically to feed Agrippa's Baths and the pools/canal (Euripus) of the Campus Martius. Fully operational and delivering water into central Rome in 117 CE; its terminal distribution point in antiquity lay near where the Baroque Trevi Fountain now stands (the fountain itself is an 18th-century addition, included here only to mark the ancient terminus location).

Rome's first purpose-built imperial harbor at the Tiber mouth, begun by Claudius in 42 CE to supplement the silting river-mouth port at Ostia; two long curving moles enclosed roughly 200 ha of open water, with an artificial mole-top island carrying the Pharos at the seaward entrance. Nero completed associated works and issued sestertii celebrating the harbor's operation at its ceremonial opening in 64 CE. Exposed to open-sea swell and prone to storm damage (part of the reason Trajan later built the sheltered hexagonal basin inland of it), but the basin itself, its moles, and surrounding quays were still functioning port infrastructure in 117 CE, working alongside Trajan's newer basin. Coordinates mark the approximate center of the basin as reconstructed from excavation/LIDAR plans (Keay et al., Portus Project); exact mole outlines are better attested than this single representative point, so treat coordinates as approximate (±300 m).
sources: Simon Keay, Martin Millett, Kristian Strutt, Portus: An Archaeological Survey of the Port of Imperial Rome (British School at Rome, 2005)

properties.notes: Trajan's inland hexagonal harbor basin, roughly 32 ha in area and about 716 m across, dug inland (southeast) of the exposed Claudian basin and connected to it and to the Tiber by canals, giving ships a sheltered anchorage safe from the open-sea storms that had damaged Portus Claudii. Construction ran c. 100-112 CE; the basin and its surrounding warehouse quays were functional and in full operation well before Trajan's death, squarely extant and in active use at the 117 CE snapshot. Together with the older Claudian basin it formed 'Portus Augusti et Traiani Felicis.' Coordinates from Pleiades' place record for the Trajanic harbor.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. on Portus

ancient_sources.author: Juvenal
ancient_sources.note: A ship works its way into the inner basin past the harbour arms and the tower — water calmer, the poet says, than any lake.

properties.notes: Monumental lighthouse modeled on the Pharos of Alexandria, built on an artificial mole-top island at the seaward mouth of the Claudian basin as part of Claudius's harbor project; functioning and celebrated on Nero's sestertii minted for the harbor's 64 CE dedication (obverse/reverse harbor scene showing the lighthouse between the two curving moles). A functioning aid to navigation still in active use in 117 CE, guiding shipping into both the Claudian and the newer Trajanic basin. Later depicted again on coinage under Trajan and subsequent emperors. Exact structure position is reconstructed from excavation on the mole between the two basins; treat this point as approximate (±200-300 m) pending direct access to Portus Project survey plans.

properties.modern_location: Fiumicino, Italy, between Portus and Ostia
properties.notes: Artificial canal (c. 90 m wide) linking the Portus basins to the Tiber and the sea, cutting off the wedge of land between it and the river's main channel to create the Isola Sacra. Sources disagree on strict attribution: despite the name 'Fossa Traiana,' the canal's origin is tied to Claudius's flood-relief/harbor-access works of the 40s CE (an inscription of 46 CE mentions it), though tradition and its surviving name credit Trajan, whose hexagonal-basin project of c. 100-112 CE certainly reused, enlarged, and depended on it as the link to the Tiber and sea. Whichever emperor's work is emphasized, the canal was long-since dug and functioning by 117 CE. Medieval Fiumicino ('little river') preserves its name. Coordinates are an approximate midpoint of the canal's course between Portus and the river; low positional precision.

A three-story administrative and residential complex on the east side of Portus's hexagonal harbor basin, built for imperial visits and the officials who ran Rome's grain supply. Brick stamps date construction to 112–120 CE, so building was still underway across the site's roughly two hectares when Trajan died in August 117. Renovations continued into Hadrian's reign and beyond.

properties.modern_location: Fiumicino, Italy, on the artificial island between Ostia and Portus
properties.notes: Port-workers' cemetery strung for roughly 1.5 km along the road linking Ostia and Portus, on the 'sacred island' created by the Fossa Traiana canal. Burials began in the later 1st century CE and the necropolis was in continuous, active use through the 2nd-4th centuries; predominantly freedmen, merchants, sailors, and craftsmen tied to the port economy, with a documented shift from cremation to inhumation over the period. Squarely in active use at 117 CE, though its best-known monumental tomb facades and the bulk of excavated structures date to the 2nd-early 3rd century expansion (Hadrianic-Severan), i.e. after this snapshot -- included here as an active, populated burial ground already established by 117, not for its later, more famous phase.

The civic and religious center of Ostia, at the crossing of the Decumanus Maximus and Cardo, in use since the late Republic and continuously monumentalized under the early Empire (Tiberius built the Temple of Rome and Augustus here; a Republican-era predecessor temple to the Capitoline triad also stood at the forum's north end). By 117 CE the forum was a fully developed civic square, though its most famous surviving monument -- the great brick Capitolium -- was still a few years from completion under Hadrian (see separate entry). Point marks the forum's approximate center.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 4-5

properties.name_english: Capitolium of Ostia (Temple of Jupiter, Juno, Minerva)
properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, north side of the Forum
properties.notes: Ostia's grandest temple, a brick-built, marble-clad Capitolium raised on a tall podium at the north end of the Forum and dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva. Hadrian's builders finished it around 120 CE, a few years after Trajan's death. An older cult building to the same three gods had stood on the same spot since the 1st century BCE, so Ostia's Capitoline triad already had a home here in 117 — just not yet this one.

properties.name_english: Temple of Rome and Augustus, Ostia
properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, south end of the Forum
properties.notes: Podium temple (c. 24.4 x 13.7 m) closing the south end of the Forum, built early in Tiberius's reign, shortly after Augustus's death and deification in 14 CE, as part of Tiberius's broader building program at Ostia (which also gave the town its first fully monumental forum). Only the opus-reticulatum substructure survives today, but the temple was a standing, functioning cult building at 117 CE, over a century old by the snapshot date.

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, behind the Theatre
properties.notes: Large colonnaded square behind Ostia's theatre, designed together with the theatre in the Augustan period; its double-row Doric portico was added under Claudius (mid-1st century CE), giving it the form -- rows of small rooms (stationes) opening off the colonnade, used as offices by roughly 40 shipping and trade guilds (navicularii, negotiantes) -- that was substantially in place by 117 CE. The black-and-white mosaics identifying individual guilds by trade/origin (grain shippers, Sardinian and North African traders, ropemakers, etc.) that make the site famous today were laid in overlapping phases from the later 1st into the 2nd century CE, so some of the surviving mosaic pavement likely postdates 117; the square, portico, and guild-office function were established well before then. A small central temple (deity uncertain -- Ceres, Annona, and the deified emperors have all been proposed) was added around the end of the 1st century CE, also pre-117.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 6

properties.notes: Ostia's theatre went up at the end of the 1st century BCE, built by Augustus's son-in-law Agrippa and originally seating around 3,000 people. This Augustan-era building was still the one standing in 117 CE. Emperor Commodus began enlarging it to roughly 4,000 seats decades later, and the brick-faced theatre visitors see today wasn't dedicated until 196 CE under Septimius Severus.

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, near the Decumanus Maximus
properties.notes: Ostia's most famous bath complex, its floors covered in black-and-white mosaics of Neptune's chariot, tritons and sea nymphs. Hadrian funded the project himself, but construction ran from about 117 to 138 CE and wasn't dedicated until 139, under Antoninus Pius. In 117 this block still held an older Domitianic bathhouse, whose cistern survives beneath the later palaestra.

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, near the Forum
properties.notes: Ostia's largest and most important grain warehouse, with storage capacity for an estimated 6,000 metric tons of grain (about a year's dole for 16,000 people). Original construction begun under Claudius (reign 41-54 CE) -- identifiable by the characteristic rough-faced opus rusticum tufa-block east and west walls -- with expansion under Nero. That Julio-Claudian building, central to Rome's grain-supply chain (annona), was standing and in active use at 117 CE. It was substantially rebuilt in brick with an added first floor and extra storage cells in a later phase spanning the late 2nd-early 3rd centuries CE (Commodan/Severan), which postdates this snapshot and is not what's being marked extant here.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 15

properties.notes: One of Ostia's oldest surviving warehouses, its tufa-columned courtyard ringed with storage cellae for grain and goods passing through the port. Tradition names it for Lucius Hortensius, a fleet prefect at Misenum, and its brickwork points to construction somewhere in the late Republic or early 1st century CE. Either way it had been serving Ostia's harbor trade for generations by 117.

Ostia's main east-west street, running from the Porta Romana through the Forum to the Porta Marina near the ancient shoreline, and continuing beyond the walls toward Rome as the Via Ostiensis. Its line goes back to the original castrum (fortified settlement, traditionally 4th century BCE, precise founding date disputed) and it remained the town's principal commercial and processional axis throughout antiquity, lined by shops, baths, and civic buildings by 117 CE. Point marks a representative location on the street near its crossing with the Cardo Maximus at the Forum, not the whole route (a single Point cannot represent a linear street; treat this as an anchor/label point only).
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 2

properties.notes: Northeastern gate of Ostia's Republican-era city walls, opening onto the Via Ostiensis toward Rome, at the start (from Rome's direction) of the Decumanus Maximus. The larger walled circuit that replaced Ostia's original small castrum is generally dated to the late 2nd-early 1st century BCE (often attributed to Sulla's era, c. 87-82 BCE, though scholars note the Sullan attribution itself lacks hard proof); a statue of Minerva excavated at the site is associated with the gate's decoration. Definitely standing and in use as the city's principal landward entrance at 117 CE.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 2

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, southwest circuit, near the ancient shoreline
properties.notes: Southwestern gate of Ostia's Republican walls, where the Decumanus Maximus left the walled town toward the ancient coastline (the sea has since retreated several km from this point due to Tiber siltation). Belonged to the Republican-era wall circuit, usually dated to around the middle of the 1st century BCE; its remains lie at a lower level than the present Decumanus surface. In use as the city's seaward gate at 117 CE, before the Hadrianic-Antonine bath and residential district later built up outside it (Terme di Porta Marina, synagogue vicinity) reached its later monumental form.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 2

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, outside Porta Marina, near the ancient shoreline
properties.notes: One of the oldest synagogue sites in the Jewish diaspora, serving Ostia's port-town Jewish community from as early as the reign of Claudius in the mid-1st century CE. Its excavator identified a purpose-built prayer hall from this period, complete with a later aedicula for the Torah shrine. Ostia's Jewish community was worshipping on this spot well before 117 CE, whatever form the building itself had taken by then.
sources: L. Michael White, 'Synagogue and Society in Imperial Ostia: Archaeological and Epigraphic Evidence', Harvard Theological Review 90 (1997)
M. Floriani Squarciapino, excavation reports on the Ostia synagogue (1961-64)

properties.name_english: Baths of the Marine Gate (Terme di Porta Marina)
properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, just outside Porta Marina
properties.notes: A large bath complex just outside Ostia's Porta Marina gate, built to catch sea breezes on the road out toward the beach. Trajan broke ground around 110 CE, but construction dragged on through Hadrian's whole reign and wasn't dedicated until 138 or 139. It was still an active building site when Trajan died in 117.

At roughly 167 meters long, Londinium's second forum-basilica was the largest Roman building north of the Alps, replacing a smaller Flavian predecessor torn down around 100 CE. Excavations at Leadenhall Market date its construction across 100–125 CE, with several accounts tying its completion to Hadrian's visit to Britain in 122. In 117 it was still a building site, not yet the finished civic hall Londinium would come to know.

A large official residence and administrative complex on the north bank of the Thames, built c. 80-100 CE, with offices, reception halls, private quarters and an ornamental pool; identified with the site now under Cannon Street station. Plausibly the residence/office of the governor of Britannia. Definitely standing and in continuous official use by 117 CE.

A stone-walled 'playing-card' fort in Londinium's northwest corner, roughly 220 by 215 meters, garrisoning about 1,000 troops including the governor's ceremonial guard. Archaeologists date the stone fort to around 120 CE, likely tied to Hadrian's 122 visit to the province. In 117 Londinium had no fort at all on this site — still an undefended civilian town.

The original Roman timber bridge across the Thames, close to today's London Bridge, around which Londinium's settlement first grew around 47–50 CE. Roman engineers rebuilt the timber structure periodically throughout the occupation, but a bridge stood continuously at this crossing from the mid-1st century CE onward. It carried traffic straight into the heart of the growing port town.

One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World; construction begun under Ptolemy I Soter, completed under Ptolemy II Philadelphus (traditionally dated 247/246 BCE), on the island of Pharos at the harbor mouth. Described in detail by Pliny (who gives its architect, Sostratus of Cnidus) and Strabo. Still standing and functioning as an active lighthouse throughout the Roman imperial period at the 117 CE snapshot; it survived until a series of medieval earthquakes felled it between the 11th and 14th centuries CE (long after our snapshot). Point is the traditional site, now occupied by the 15th-century Qaitbay Citadel.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: A white marble tower of many storeys on the island's tip, given by Sostratus of Cnidus for the safety of sailors on a coast with no landmarks and dangerous shoals.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Puts the cost at 800 talents and worries that a fire burning steadily at sea can be mistaken for a star.

properties.notes: Founded under the early Ptolemies as the research wing of Alexandria's royal Mouseion, once the ancient world's greatest center of scholarship. A purge of scholars in 145 BCE and a fire during Caesar's siege in 48 BCE had each cost it dearly, but writers of the 2nd century CE still describe active scholarship in the city. Alexandria itself was rocked by the Kitos War in 115–117 CE, suppressed by Trajan's general Marcius Turbo the same month Trajan died — the Mouseion's exact condition at that moment isn't recorded, but the institution itself endured.

Great Greco-Egyptian temple to Serapis built under Ptolemy III Euergetes (r. 246-222 BCE), housing a 'daughter library' subordinate to the main Mouseion collection. Sited on Alexandria's only natural hill, in the Rhakotis quarter. Standing and functioning at 117 CE; it was later destroyed by a Christian mob in 391 CE under Theophilus of Alexandria -- well after this snapshot.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction of the Serapeum of Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
ancient_sources.note: Ranks the Serapeum second in the world only to the Capitol at Rome, for its colonnades, its statues and its halls.

properties.notes: A roughly seven-stadia (c. 1,300m) mole/causeway built under Ptolemy I connecting the mainland to Pharos island, dividing Alexandria's harbor into the Great Harbor and the harbor of Eunostos. Functioned as both a dam and a road; still in use in 117 CE. Later silted up and built over, forming the base of the modern city's Ras el-Tin peninsula neighborhood, so its exact ancient course is only approximately reconstructable -- point marks the traditional midpoint. Used 'road' as the closest existing category rather than adding a new one for a single feature.

Originally cut into the west slope of Panayır Dağ (Mt Pion) in the Hellenistic period (c. 200 BCE), the theatre was progressively enlarged in the Roman period: the stage building (scaenae frons) was completed under Nero (by 66 CE), the north analemma wall added under Domitian (92 CE), and the south analemma completed under Trajan (102-114 CE) -- meaning the theatre reached essentially its final, largest form (142m diameter, capacity c. 24,000) only shortly before the 117 CE snapshot. Definitely standing and in active use at Trajan's death.

ancient_sources.author: Acts of the Apostles
ancient_sources.note: The silversmiths' protest against Paul: the crowd sweeps into the theatre and shouts for two hours before the town clerk gets them out.

properties.notes: A grand funerary library on Ephesus's Curetes Street, built by Tiberius Julius Aquila to honor his father, the former proconsul of Asia Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, whose sarcophagus lies beneath the building. Construction began around 110 CE, but Aquila died before it was finished and his heirs completed it, with the facade's full sculptural program not finished until around 135 CE under Hadrian. In 117 it was still an active building site.

One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The temple burned in 356 BCE (in a fire ancient writers synchronized with Alexander the Great's birth) and was rebuilt on an even grander scale over the following century, with the reconstruction generally dated complete by the mid-3rd century BCE. That Hellenistic-era structure -- described in detail by Pliny -- remained standing and was a major pilgrimage/cult site throughout the Roman period, including at 117 CE; it was eventually destroyed by a Gothic raid in 268 CE, well after this snapshot. Coordinates match the point already present in this repo's places_medium.geojson gazetteer for consistency.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction of the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: A hundred and twenty years in the building, 127 columns each the gift of a king, raised on marshy ground deliberately chosen to hold against earthquakes.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The successive temples on the site, the man who burned the last one down, and the right of asylum its precinct carried.

properties.notes: A small, richly decorated temple on Ephesus's Curetes Street, dedicated to the emperor Hadrian. Hadrian only became emperor with his accession on 11 August 117 — the same event that closes this map's snapshot — so a temple built in his honor couldn't yet have existed on that date. It went up sometime after, and is one of the best-known monuments in Ephesus today.

Archaic Doric temple built c. 560 BCE, one of the oldest stone temples in mainland Greece; seven of its original 38 monolithic limestone columns still stand. It survived the Roman sack of Corinth under Mummius in 146 BCE and remained a landmark when Julius Caesar refounded the city as Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis in 44 BCE, still dominating the Roman forum in 117 CE. Pausanias (writing mid-2nd century CE, i.e. shortly after this snapshot) describes it standing over the marketplace.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo at Corinth · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Passed on the way up from the market place: a temple of Apollo with a bronze statue of the god in front of it.

properties.notes: A monumental spring-fed fountain house at the heart of Roman Corinth, just north of the speaker's platform, drawing on a source linked in myth to the winged horse Pegasus since the Archaic period. The elaborate two-story marble facade often credited to Herodes Atticus dates from the 150s CE, well after this snapshot. In 117 CE a simpler Hellenistic-era fountain house still stood on the same spot, already centuries old.

Roman civic basilica at the east end of the Corinthian forum/agora, dedicated to the Julio-Claudian imperial family and generally dated to the late 1st century BCE/early 1st century CE building phase of the refounded Roman colony. Standing and in use by 117 CE as part of the forum's administrative complex.

Panhellenic sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus east of Corinth, seat of the biennial Isthmian Games (one of the four Panhellenic 'crown' games), administered by Corinth throughout the Roman period. The Archaic temple (c. 690 BCE) burned in 470 BCE and was rebuilt; the sanctuary remained active and the games continued to be celebrated under Roman rule, including at 117 CE. Coordinates reuse the 'Isthmia' point already present in this repo's places_medium.geojson gazetteer for consistency.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The pine grove, the sanctuary of Poseidon with its team of gilded horses, and the Isthmian games held in the god's honour.

properties.notes: Built at the foot of the Croix-Rousse hill at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône, funded around 19 CE by the imperial-cult priest Gaius Julius Rufus, per his own surviving dedication (CIL XIII 1698). It hosted the annual Council of the Three Gauls, the federal assembly of Gaul's provinces. Two added galleries later raised its capacity to roughly 20,000, but the original amphitheatre was already in full use by 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The temple to Augustus at the meeting of the rivers, put up jointly by all the Gauls, with its altar and the names of sixty tribes carved on it.

properties.notes: Built into the slope of the Fourvière hill (site of the original Roman colonia founded 43 BCE) under Augustus, c. 15 BCE, with a capacity of roughly 10,000; enlarged under Hadrian later in the 2nd century. Definitely standing and in use as of 117 CE, prior to the Hadrianic enlargement.

properties.name_english: Federal Altar / Sanctuary of the Three Gauls
properties.notes: Altar to the cult of Roma and Augustus dedicated in 12 BCE at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône, the ritual and political center of the Concilium Galliarum -- the annual gathering of representatives from the 60 civitates of the Three Gauls to elect the high priest of the imperial cult (the first was Gaius Julius Vercondaridubnus, an Aeduan) and celebrate games. Continuously in use throughout the early Empire, including 117 CE. Located adjacent to (and administratively linked with) the Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls built nearby a generation later; exact footprint of the altar precinct itself is only approximately reconstructed archaeologically, hence medium rather than high confidence on the point location.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction, Sanctuary of the Three Gauls · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The longest of Lugdunum's four aqueducts, running roughly 86 kilometers from the Gier valley and crossing the Beaunant and Chaponost valleys on dramatic inverted-siphon bridges. A 2018 tree-ring study dated the Beaunant siphon's timber foundations to 110 CE, putting the engineering work under Trajan. By 117 it had been carrying water into Lugdunum for years.

Cut into the slope of the Concepción hill so that the audience climbs to its seats, the theatre of Carthago Nova holds about six thousand and was paid for as an act of imperial flattery: inscriptions on its altars name Gaius and Lucius Caesar, the grandsons Augustus meant to succeed him. Marble for the stage front came in by sea. The colony below it lives on silver from the hills behind and on the esparto grass that ropes the fleet. In 117 CE it is a working theatre in a working port; later building buried it so completely that it was found again only in 1988.

ancient_sources.author: Theatre dedication
ancient_sources.note: Marble altars and a large lintel from the entrances honour Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Augustus's grandsons — the same imperial heirs named on the Maison Carrée.

properties.notes: Part temple, part college for the imperial cult, built as part of Augustus's extensive redesign of Carthago Nova alongside its new forum, streets and theatre; sits within the Molinete hill archaeological park in the heart of the old town. Exact construction date within the Augustan period and full identification of the structure's function are still debated in the Spanish excavation literature, hence medium confidence, but the building's Augustan-era existence and continuity into the 2nd century CE are not in dispute.
properties.image_credit: Augusteum, Cartagena · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The civic centre of the colony sits on the low Molinete hill above the harbour: a paved square with a hall for the town council along one side and a temple raised on a podium at the head of it. A bath building and a banqueting hall stand just downhill, their walls painted with garlands, theatrical masks and imitation marble panelling. All of it belongs to the rebuilding that followed the refoundation of the city under Augustus, the same programme that produced the theatre a few streets away. In 117 CE Carthago Nova is past its silver-mining peak but still one of the great ports of Hispania.

The vast silver-and-lead mining district in the hills east of Carthago Nova, worked since Hannibal drew on its silver in the 220s BCE and massively expanded under Rome. The geographer Strabo counted roughly 40,000 workers, most of them enslaved, laboring across the district around the turn of the era. Its output made Carthago Nova one of the wealthiest cities in Hispania Tarraconensis for two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons — Cabezo Rajao mine workings in the Sierra Minera de Cartagena-La Unión, exploited for silver and lead since Roman times

properties.notes: One of the largest circuses in the Roman world, over 490 meters long with room for up to 80,000 spectators, modeled on Rome's Circus Maximus. Cassius Dio records that Trajan himself took shelter here during Antioch's catastrophic earthquake of 13 December 115 CE, escaping through a window as aftershocks shook the city for days. Antioch — one of the empire's four largest cities — was still rebuilding from that quake when Trajan died less than two years later.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Describes how Trajan, present in Antioch during the catastrophic earthquake of December 115 CE, escaped his lodgings and then lived out of doors in the city's hippodrome (circus) for several days as aftershocks continued.

properties.notes: A theatre built into the rocks of Mount Silpius above Antioch, begun during Julius Caesar's visits to the city in the mid-1st century BCE and enlarged by later emperors. Antioch was still recovering from a devastating earthquake on 13 December 115 CE when Trajan died less than two years later, and the theatre's exact condition at that moment isn't recorded. No evidence suggests it had stopped standing.

Famous oracular sanctuary and sacred grove of Apollo and Artemis at Daphne, a suburb roughly 8km southwest of Antioch, established alongside the city's founding tradition under Seleucus I (c. 300 BCE) and described by Strabo as one of the most celebrated sanctuaries of the ancient world. A major pilgrimage and recreational site throughout the Roman period, including 117 CE. Point uses the same Harbiye/Daphne location already present in this repo's places_medium.geojson gazetteer for consistency.
properties.image_credit: Ruins at Daphne · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The residence and administrative seat of the governor of Germania Inferior, its remains — including a sewer system and a 1st-century staircase found in recent excavations — lie beneath Cologne's city hall. Built originally as army headquarters for the Lower Rhine command, it became the governor's palace once Germania Inferior was formally organized as a province in 83 or 84 CE. It was still the seat of provincial government in 117 CE.

A stone fortification circuit roughly 4 kilometers around, with at least nine gates and nineteen round towers, enclosing the colonia Rome founded in 50 CE. Builders raised it around 89–91 CE, late in the 1st century. By 117 CE it defined the full built-up extent of the city.

The oldest known stone structure in Cologne: a tuff-stone tower roughly 9 meters square and originally about 12 meters tall, marking the entrance to the Rhine harbor of the pre-Roman Ubian settlement. Tree-ring dating puts its oak-pile foundations in the winter of 4–5 CE. The later city wall, built around 90 CE, cut into the tower, so only a reduced stump of the original structure was still standing by 117.

A prosperous Campanian town of ~11,000-12,000 people at the mouth of the Sarno river, buried under ~4-6 m of pumice and ash in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius on 24-25 August 79 CE and never reoccupied. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's 117 CE snapshot — included as a general wayfinding/city-center pin so the site reads on the map even though nothing here was standing at Trajan's death; individual landmark pins carry the architectural detail. Point marks a representative centroid near the Forum.
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16 and 6.20 (to Tacitus, eyewitness account of the eruption)

ancient_sources.author: Seneca the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Reports the earthquake of 62 CE that wrecked Pompeii and damaged the towns around it, and notes the town was still being rebuilt.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: The eruption of 79 seen from across the bay, written twenty-five years later for Tacitus: the cloud shaped like an umbrella pine, ash falling hotter and thicker as the ships close in.

properties.notes: The rectangular civic, religious, and commercial heart of Pompeii, laid out by the 2nd century BCE and ringed by the Capitolium, Basilica, macellum, comitium, and temples of Apollo and the Genius of Augustus. Buried by the 79 CE eruption. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

Built c. 70 BCE at private expense by local magistrates Gaius Quinctius Valgus and Marcus Porcius shortly after Pompeii became a Roman colony (80 BCE); it is the oldest known permanent stone amphitheatre in the Roman world, predating the Colosseum by roughly 150 years, and held about 20,000 spectators. Buried by the eruption of 79 CE. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.
sources: Tacitus, Annales 14.17 (the 59 CE riot between Pompeian and Nucerian spectators at this amphitheatre)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: A gladiatorial show in 59 CE turns into a riot between Pompeians and Nucerians; the Senate bans public gatherings at Pompeii for ten years.

properties.notes: Founded in the second half of the 2nd century BCE, originally dedicated to Jupiter alone; after Pompeii became a Roman colony in 80 BCE it was reconsecrated as a Capitolium to the triad Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, closing the north end of the Forum. Badly damaged in the earthquake of 62 CE and still unrepaired when the 79 CE eruption buried it. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.
sources: Seneca, Naturales Quaestiones 6.1 (on the 62 CE earthquake damage to Pompeii's public buildings)

properties.notes: Pompeii's oldest and most important religious sanctuary, with cult origins reaching back to the 6th century BCE under Greek/Etruscan influence; the present colonnaded form dates to a 2nd-century BCE rebuild, with further repairs under way after the 62 CE earthquake, still incomplete in 79 CE. Bronze statues of Apollo and Diana found here are now in the Naples Archaeological Museum. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 787
ancient_sources.note: The magistrates Marcus Holconius Rufus and Gaius Egnatius Postumus paid 3,000 sesterces for precinct works, by decree of the council; the text names the town 'Colonia Veneria Cornelia'.

properties.notes: Built c. 130-120 BCE, this is among the oldest surviving basilicas anywhere in the Roman world, predating the amphitheatre by several decades. It served as Pompeii's law court and a covered meeting hall for business, with a raised two-story tribunal at its western end. Buried in 79 CE. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

The oldest and largest of Pompeii's public bath complexes, with an original core going back to the 2nd century BCE (some scholars trace earlier phases to the 4th century BCE); enlarged repeatedly, it only received piped aqueduct water around the turn of the 1st century CE, having previously relied on a well and roof-catchment reservoir. Buried by the 79 CE eruption. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 829
ancient_sources.note: Records that two magistrates rebuilt the sweat-room, scraping-room, porticoes and palaestra out of fine-money, by decree of the town council.

properties.notes: A stone theatre cut into a natural hillside slope in the Samnite/Hellenistic tradition, with an original phase as early as the 3rd century BCE and a major 2nd-century BCE rebuild; seated roughly 5,000. Renovated again under Augustus at the private expense of the Holconius brothers. Buried by the 79 CE eruption. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

One of the largest and best-preserved private houses in Pompeii, c. 1,100 sq m, originally built in the 2nd century BCE and lavishly redecorated in the elaborate Fourth Style after the 62 CE earthquake for its owners, the freedmen brothers Aulus Vettius Restitutus and Aulus Vettius Conviva. Sealed under ash in 79 CE with its frescoes almost intact, making it one of the most-studied domus in the Roman world. New category "house" introduced for this feature (domus) since none of the existing categories fit a private residence; logged per shift convention of introducing categories freely. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy, c. 400 m northwest of the walls near the Herculaneum Gate
properties.notes: A suburban villa just outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate, built in the 1st century BCE and famous for the near-life-size Dionysiac frieze (c. 60 BCE) painted around its triclinium (Room 5), thought to depict a woman's initiation into a mystery cult of Dionysus/Bacchus. Because it lay outside the town walls it took relatively light structural damage in 79 CE, which is why its frescoes survive so completely. New category "villa" introduced (distinct from in-town "house") for this and the Villa of the Papyri entry, following the shift log's precedent of adding categories freely. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

One of Pompeii's seven city gates, on the western wall near the ancient shoreline, connecting the town to its harbor and the Bay of Naples; its double-arched, barrel-vaulted form (a wide arch for animals/carts, a narrow one for pedestrians) is largely a Sullan-colony-era (post-80 BCE) rebuild of an older opening in the Samnite walls. Buried in 79 CE and not fully excavated until 1861 under Giuseppe Fiorelli. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

A smaller, wealthier seaside town of perhaps 4,000-5,000 people on a coastal spur of Vesuvius, about 8 km southeast of Neapolis. Spared the initial ash-fall that struck Pompeii (giving most residents time to flee toward the shore) but destroyed the following night and morning by a series of pyroclastic surges and flows that buried the town up to 20 m deep, carbonizing (rather than burning away) organic material — wood, food, papyrus, even some human tissue — far more completely than at Pompeii. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as a general wayfinding/city-center pin, same reasoning as the Pompeii city pin.
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16 and 6.20 (to Tacitus)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-32623-3 (Scientific Reports, 2023, on the pyroclastic surge sequence at Herculaneum)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the town on its headland above the sea, held in turn by Oscans, Etruscans and Samnites, with air the writer thought unusually healthy.

properties.notes: Meeting hall and shrine of the Augustales, a civic college mostly of wealthy freedmen tasked with maintaining the imperial cult of Augustus (the priesthood was formalized under Tiberius in 14 CE, though this building's core dates slightly earlier, funded by patrons A. Lucius Proculus and A. Lucius Iulianus). Decorated with Fourth-Style frescoes of the labors of Hercules, the city's mythic founder. Rediscovered in 1740 by early Bourbon tunnel excavations. New category "collegium" introduced since this is a civic/cult association's meeting hall rather than a standalone temple; logged per shift convention. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

Built in the early 1st century CE as a gift to the town by its greatest benefactor, Marcus Nonius Balbus (ex-tribune, ex-consul, ex-proconsul of Crete), who split the complex off from his own adjoining residence; damaged in the 62 CE earthquake and subsequently expanded with an open-air pool and nymphaeum. Widely regarded as the best-preserved Roman bath building anywhere, buried by the 79 CE pyroclastic flows and only fully excavated/opened in the 20th-21st centuries. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.name_english: House of the Deer (Casa dei Cervi)
properties.notes: The grandest excavated house in Herculaneum, a two-story waterfront residence built/rebuilt under Claudius (41-54 CE) and expanded by absorbing a neighboring property; named for two marble sculptures of deer attacked by hounds found in its garden, and noted for well-preserved still-life frescoes. Street-facing rooms were converted to shops after the 62 CE earthquake. Fully uncovered by Amedeo Maiuri's open-air excavations of 1929-1932. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Ercolano, Campania, Italy, northwest of the main excavated town, mostly still unexcavated/underground
properties.notes: A vast luxury villa on the coast northwest of the town center, plausibly linked (unconfirmed) to Julius Caesar's father-in-law L. Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus; famous for its library of over 1,800 carbonized papyrus scrolls, discovered by Bourbon tunneling from 1750, mostly Epicurean philosophical texts including many works of Philodemus of Gadara. COORDINATE/EXTENT CAUTION: only a fraction of the villa has ever been excavated (much still lies under modern Ercolano and below the water table), so its full footprint and this point's precision are both genuinely uncertain — the coordinates mark the excavated atrium/peristyle area reached by 18th-century tunnels and 20th-century open-air digs, not a confirmed full-villa centroid. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

Legio I Adiutrix was raised from marines of the Ravenna fleet in the civil war year of 68 CE, and moved to Brigetio on the Danube bend under Domitian, where it stayed for the next three centuries. In August 117 CE the fortress is its home but the legion is not in it: I Adiutrix went east with Trajan for the Parthian war and returns to Pannonia only under Hadrian, in 118. The garrison holding Brigetio at the moment of this snapshot is Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix, which took the place over in 105 and hands it back when I Adiutrix marches home.
sources: https://www.livius.org/articles/legion/legio-i-adiutrix/ (cross-referenced via search synthesis, direct fetch blocked)

properties.notes: Legio I Minervia was levied by Domitian in 82-83 CE for the Chattian War and based at Bonna (Bonn) from its founding; it remained the legion's home fortress for the rest of its existence (with a brief detachment fighting for Trajan in the Dacian Wars). The legion's legate c. 101-106 CE was the future emperor Hadrian. By 117 CE the legion had long since returned to and was firmly garrisoned at Bonna.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Tacitus describes Bonna as a legionary camp fought over during the Batavian revolt of 69-70 CE, recounting the clash there between Civilis's forces and Roman troops.

properties.notes: Legio I Italica, raised by Nero in 66-67 CE from Italian recruits, was posted to Novae on the lower Danube by Vespasian in 69-70 CE and remained there for the rest of its long service (into the 5th century). Its timber-and-earth camp was rebuilt in stone during the Trajanic period (98-117 CE), so by the 117 CE snapshot the legion occupied a substantially stone fortress. Detachments served in Trajan's Dacian and Parthian campaigns, but the main base stayed at Novae throughout.

ancient_sources.author: Procopius
ancient_sources.note: Procopius lists Novae among the Danube-line fortresses in Moesia that Justinian's engineers repaired and strengthened.

properties.notes: Legio II Adiutrix, like I Adiutrix raised from fleet marines (68-70 CE), fought in Trajan's Dacian Wars based temporarily at Singidunum, then was permanently transferred to Aquincum in 106 CE once the new province of Pannonia Inferior was organized, becoming that province's senior garrison and the anchor of what grew into Aquincum's civilian town (later Pannonia Inferior's capital). Its earlier wood-and-earth camp was under stone reconstruction during Hadrian's reign, begun essentially at the 117 CE snapshot.

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's gazetteer of Pannonia Inferior lists Aquincum among the province's towns with coordinates — a bare place-name entry rather than a narrative description.

properties.notes: Legio II Augusta, one of Claudius's original invasion legions of 43 CE, moved to a new purpose-built fortress at Isca Silurum (Caerleon) in South Wales c. 74-75 CE under governor Sextus Julius Frontinus, replacing timber defenses in stone c. 99-100 CE per a Trajanic building inscription. The legion was still garrisoned there in 117 CE and would remain for roughly two more centuries.

ancient_sources.author: Antonine Itinerary
ancient_sources.note: Records Isca (Legio II Augusta's fortress at Caerleon) as a station on several road routes through Roman Britain, under the name Isca Leg. II Aug.

properties.name_english: Camp of Legio II Traiana Fortis (Judaea)
properties.modern_location: Kefar 'Otnay / Legio junction, near Megiddo, Israel
properties.notes: Legio II Traiana Fortis was raised by Trajan c. 101-105 CE for the Dacian Wars and fought in his Parthian campaign (114-117). Multiple sources place it 'in Iudaea, to ensure peace' specifically in 117 CE, immediately after the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt (115-117) — i.e. present in the same province, and very plausibly the same Jezreel Valley camp at Caparcotna/Legio, as VI Ferrata (see that entry) during this transitional year. GENUINE UNCERTAINTY: the legion's permanent post-117 home was Nicopolis near Alexandria, Egypt, but sources disagree on whether it arrived there by c. 119-120 or only by 125 CE. Pinned here at the Judaean camp for the 117 CE snapshot specifically, distinct from its later Egyptian base (not shown, since it postdates 117).

Legio III Augusta is the only legion in Africa, and by 117 CE it is at Lambaesis in the northern foothills of the Aurès. It had moved up from Ammaedara to Theveste under Vespasian and on to Lambaesis around 100 CE, each step pushing the garrison closer to the mountain and desert country of the Musulamii, whose seasonal movements Rome wanted watched and taxed. The camp at this date is earth and timber. The great stone fortress, and the parade ground where Hadrian addressed the assembled troops in a speech they cut into a pillar, come later, in the 120s.

Legio III Cyrenaica moved from Egypt to garrison the newly annexed province of Arabia (106 CE) after Trajan's peaceful annexation of the Nabataean kingdom, founding a fortress at Bostra, the new provincial capital. GENUINE UNCERTAINTY FOR THE 117 CE SNAPSHOT: sources indicate the legion (or a large detachment) was pulled back to Egypt around 116-117 CE to help suppress the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt, is attested together with XXII Deiotariana in Egypt in 119 CE, and only clearly returned to Bostra c. 120-127 CE. It is therefore genuinely unclear whether the legion's main body was physically at Bostra or in Egypt at the exact moment of Trajan's death in August 117. Pinned at Bostra as its official provincial post (both immediately before and after this disruption).

Legio III Gallica, an old Caesarian-era legion long stationed in Syria, was based at Raphanaea (modern Rafniye) in the Orontes valley through the late Republic and into the imperial period, continuing under Trajan and Hadrian. The site is only lightly excavated (limited visible remains, walled-enclosure traces from 1930s aerial survey), so the coordinate is a settlement-level approximation rather than an excavated principia point.

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio IV Flavia Felix (Singidunum)
properties.notes: Legio IV Flavia Felix was raised by Vespasian in 70 CE from the cadre of the disbanded IV Macedonica, and was moved to Singidunum (modern Belgrade) by Domitian in 86 CE to shore up the Danube frontier after the Dacian invasion that destroyed V Alaudae. It remained Singidunum's garrison through 117 CE and for centuries after (into the 5th century).

ancient_sources.author: Priscus of Panium
ancient_sources.ref: fragment on the 441 CE Hunnic invasion
ancient_sources.note: Priscus, a 5th-century Byzantine historian, names Singidunum among the Danube cities sacked by Attila's Huns in 441 CE, alongside Viminacium and Margus — a genuine literary description, though written centuries after 117 CE.

properties.notes: Legio IV Scythica was stationed at Zeugma, guarding the strategic Euphrates crossing on the Syria-Parthia frontier, from 66 CE onward for roughly a century, including through Trajan's Parthian War (114-117), in which the legion took part. Recent excavation (Zeugma archaeological project) places the actual legionary camp on the plateau west of the town proper (the 'Meydani' sector), rather than directly on the riverbank city site itself; the point given here marks the town/site as commonly plotted, with that camp-vs-town nuance noted.

Legio V Macedonica, veteran of Trajan's Dacian Wars, was transferred to Troesmis on the lower Danube in 107 CE to guard against the Roxolani Sarmatians and the Black Sea Greek cities' hinterland. It remained based there through 117 CE and until the 160s, though a vexillation was sent east for Trajan's Parthian campaign (115-117).

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's gazetteer of Moesia Inferior lists Troesmis among the region's towns with coordinates — a bare place-name entry.

properties.notes: Legio VI Ferrata was brought into Judaea as its second permanent legion (alongside X Fretensis at Jerusalem) in the aftermath of the Kitos War, founding a camp on a hill above the Jezreel Valley near Kefar 'Otnay/Caparcotna (which gave the later settlement its name, 'Legio', and eventually modern Lajjun/Megiddo). Sources consistently cite 117 CE for this establishment, though the user's brief flags — and archaeological/epigraphic work (Tel Aviv University/Jezreel Valley Regional Project excavations) leaves open — that the stone fortress construction and full garrison strength may date slightly later, c. 117-120 CE, into Hadrian's reign. May have briefly overlapped in the area with II Traiana Fortis (see separate entry) during this same transitional year before that legion moved on toward Egypt.

Legio VI Victrix came up from Novaesium to the single-legion fortress at Vetera on the lower Rhine around the turn of the century, and it is still there in 117 CE. With Legio X Gemina downriver it holds this stretch of the frontier, quiet enough by now that the veterans' colony beside it is the busier place. In 122 Hadrian takes the legion to Britain to build the wall that carries his name, and Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix moves into the empty fortress behind it — five years after the date of this map.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Tacitus gives an extended narrative of the siege of the legionary camp at Vetera during the Batavian revolt, covering Civilis's blockade, the failed relief efforts, and the garrison's eventual surrender.

properties.notes: Legio VII Claudia had been in the Moesian theatre since the mid-1st century and became the fixed garrison and namesake military anchor of Viminacium once Domitian split Moesia into two provinces in 86 CE, with Viminacium as Moesia Superior's capital and governor's seat. The legion was still there in 117 CE (Viminacium was elevated toward municipium status right around Hadrian's accession) and remained for centuries.

ancient_sources.author: Priscus of Panium
ancient_sources.ref: fragment on the 441 CE Hunnic invasion
ancient_sources.note: Priscus describes the Huns under Attila destroying Viminacium in 441 CE, naming the city directly among the Danube settlements sacked — written centuries after 117 CE.

properties.notes: Legio VIII Augusta was permanently stationed at Argentorate (Strasbourg), guarding a key Rhine crossing, from c. 90 CE and remained there for over three centuries. By 117 CE the fortress's defenses were being reinforced as part of Hadrian's broader consolidation of the German limes.

ancient_sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
ancient_sources.note: Ammianus gives a detailed narrative of the 357 CE Battle of Argentoratum (Strasbourg) between Julian's Roman army and the Alamanni, fought at this fortress site.

properties.notes: Legio IX Hispana founded the legionary fortress at Eboracum (York) in 71 CE and was recorded rebuilding it in stone in 107-108 CE. It was still based there in 117 CE; a later, much-debated tradition (going back to Mommsen) has the legion wiped out fighting a Brigantian/Caledonian uprising around 117-120 CE, but this is now widely doubted — inscriptions from Nijmegen suggest elements of IX Hispana were redeployed to the Rhine by c. 120 CE rather than destroyed, with the legion's actual disappearance from the record more plausibly explained by later events (a Rhine posting, or loss during the Parthian War of Lucius Verus or the Bar Kokhba Revolt). FLAGGED PER BRIEF: this entry reflects only the well-attested 117 CE status (still garrisoned at York); its subsequent fate is a genuine, unresolved scholarly dispute, not a 117 CE fact.

Legio X Fretensis garrisoned the ruins of Jerusalem continuously from the city's destruction in 70 CE, encamped on the southwestern hill (the former Herodian Upper City), incorporating the Phasael/Hippicus/Mariamne towers of Herod's palace into its camp wall.
