It was still Jerusalem's sole legionary garrison in 117 CE; the refoundation of the city as the colony Aelia Capitolina is usually dated c. 130 CE under Hadrian (one late source, Epiphanius, gives 117, but mainstream scholarship treats that as a chronological error), so at the 117 CE snapshot this is still a legionary camp on Jerusalem's ruins, not yet the colonia.

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Titus levels the city but leaves the towers and part of the west wall standing, to quarter the Tenth Legion behind and to show what had been taken.

properties.notes: Legio X Gemina, long stationed at Noviomagus (Nijmegen) in Germania Inferior (71-103 CE), was transferred east to Aquincum in 103 CE and then to a new permanent fortress at Vindobona (Vienna) in 114 CE, where it remained the garrison through 117 CE and for centuries afterward, anchoring the Danube frontier opposite the Marcomanni and Quadi.

ancient_sources.author: Aurelius Victor
ancient_sources.note: Aurelius Victor states that Marcus Aurelius died at Vindobona in 180 CE — though other ancient authors instead give Sirmium, so the site of his death is itself disputed among ancient sources.

properties.notes: Legio XI Claudia carries its title from the revolt of 42 CE, when it stayed loyal to Claudius. It transferred from Brigetio to Durostorum on the lower Danube sometime between 104 and 114, and in 117 CE it garrisons the fortress there, watching the river crossings against the Getae and the Roxolani beyond. It will still be at Durostorum three centuries later. A civilian town has grown along the road outside the walls, and the legion's veterans settle in it rather than going home.

ancient_sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
ancient_sources.note: Ammianus names Durostorum in his geographic survey of the lower Danube/Black Sea region; Ptolemy's Geography also lists the town among Moesia Inferior's settlements.

properties.notes: Legio XII Fulminata was posted to Melitene on the upper Euphrates after the First Jewish-Roman War (from 71-72 CE), guarding the crossing into Armenia and the end of the road east from Caesarea. It took part in Trajan's Armenian campaign (114) and remained based at Melitene through 117 CE and for centuries after (attested there in the Notitia Dignitatum).

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Tacitus describes Corbulo massing allied cavalry, infantry, and legionary detachments at Melitene before crossing the Euphrates into Armenia during the Parthian War of the early 60s CE.

properties.notes: Legio XIII Gemina stayed behind in the newly conquered province after Trajan's Second Dacian War, founding its fortress at Apulum (modern Alba Iulia) in 106-108 CE and becoming the senior garrison of the new province. It remained Dacia's principal legion through 117 CE, even as sub-units were pulled for Trajan's simultaneous Parthian campaign (115-117).

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's gazetteer of Dacia lists Apulum among the province's towns with coordinates — a bare place-name entry.

properties.notes: Legio XIV Gemina was sent to Pannonia in 92 CE to replace the destroyed XXI Rapax, initially camping at Vindobona, then relocated to Carnuntum after Trajan's Dacian Wars. Sources vary on the precise year of the Carnuntum move (given variously as 106, 114, or 117-118), but agree the legion was there by, or essentially at, the 117 CE snapshot and remained for the next three centuries as the provincial capital's garrison and headquarters of the Pannonian fleet.

Legio XV Apollinaris fought in Trajan's Parthian War (114-117) and was in Egypt in the war's immediate aftermath; scholarship on its movements (Speidel) dates its departure for its new permanent post at Satala, on the Cappadocian-Armenian frontier, to around August 117 CE (i.e., essentially at Trajan's death/Hadrian's accession), arriving and establishing its castrum stativum there by summer 118. At the exact 117 CE snapshot the legion was thus most likely already marching toward, or just arriving at, Satala rather than fully garrisoned in its permanent stone fortress — flagged accordingly.

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio XX Valeria Victrix (Chester)
properties.notes: Deva was first built by Legio II Adiutrix c. 70 CE, but II Adiutrix left Britain in the mid-80s and Legio XX Valeria Victrix took over the fortress c. 88 CE, rebuilding it in stone. XX Valeria Victrix remained Deva's garrison through 117 CE and for the following two centuries.

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's Geography lists Deva among the towns of the Cornovii and explicitly identifies it as the camp of Legio XX Victrix.

properties.modern_location: Sidi Gaber area, east Alexandria, Egypt
properties.notes: Legio XXII Deiotariana (descended from client-king Deiotarus of Galatia's forces, absorbed by Augustus) was one of Egypt's two permanent legions, based with III Cyrenaica at the double-legion fortress of Nicopolis just east of Alexandria. Elements were used to suppress the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt in Egypt and Cyrenaica (115-117), so the legion (or most of it) was in the immediate Alexandria area through 117 CE; it is attested there again with III Cyrenaica in 119. It was later destroyed or disbanded during the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132-136 CE), long after this map's snapshot. No visible remains of the fortress survive and its precise footprint is unexcavated, so the point is a settlement-level approximation.

Legio XXII Primigenia, raised by Caligula in 39 CE, was stationed at Mogontiacum (Mainz) from 92 CE onward (having shared earlier Rhine postings with other legions), guarding the Rhine and the Mainz bridge. It remained Mainz's garrison through 117 CE and for the following two centuries; the future emperor Hadrian served as one of its military tribunes in 97-98 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Cassius Dio recounts the revolt of Lucius Antonius Saturninus, governor of Germania Superior, who rose against Domitian at Mogontiacum in 89 CE with the two legions stationed there.

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix (Brigetio)
properties.notes: Trajan raised Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix for the Dacian wars — the thirtieth legion, hence the number, and Ulpia for his own family name. When Legio XI Claudia left Brigetio for Durostorum on the lower Danube, XXX Ulpia Victrix took the vacated Pannonian fortress in 105 CE, and it holds the place through the whole of 117. It moves on only in 122, to Vetera on the Rhine, as part of a three-way shuffle: Hadrian sends Vetera's Legio VI Victrix across to Britain to build his wall, and Legio I Adiutrix comes back from the East to reclaim Brigetio.

Misenum was home to the classis Misenensis, the senior fleet of the Roman navy, founded by Augustus in 27 BCE to command the western Mediterranean. Up to 10,000 sailors and marines were based on the peninsula, drawing fresh water from the vast vaulted cistern known as the Piscina Mirabilis. Pliny the Elder commanded the fleet from here in 79 CE and sailed from this harbor to his death during the eruption of Vesuvius. In 2023 archaeologists uncovered a monumental harborside villa believed to belong to the fleet's prefect.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Sets out the standing fleets of the empire — one at Misenum for the western sea, one at Ravenna for the Adriatic.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: His uncle is in command of the fleet at Misenum when Vesuvius erupts, and orders the ships out towards the shore to take people off.

properties.notes: Classe was the harbor of the classis Ravennas, the second of Augustus's two main Italian fleets, guarding the Adriatic. The base held up to 250 ships and 10,000 marines, linked to Ravenna itself and to the Po by the Fossa Augusta canal, with naval yards and docks stretching some 22 kilometers along the waterway. Silting has since pushed the coastline nine kilometers east of the ancient shoreline.

Forum Iulii's stone harbor, nicknamed Claustra Maris or Sea Bolt, was built by Octavian after Actium as a third great naval base alongside Misenum and Ravenna, guarding the northwest Mediterranean. Its fleet, the classis Gallica, stayed active through the Julio-Claudian era but lost its standing amid the civil wars of 69 CE, after which its ships were reassigned toward Misenum and the Adriatic. The hexagonal harbor basin, once ringed by warehouses and now landlocked more than a kilometer from the sea, still survives as the Lanterne d'Auguste monument marking its ancient entrance.

The classis Alexandrina was established after Actium to guard Rome's most vital grain route, escorting the Alexandrian corn fleet across the Mediterranean and patrolling the Nile. Its ships moored in the Great Harbor below the royal quarter on the Lochias peninsula, close by the Pharos lighthouse that already marked the port for the ancient world.

Seleucia Pieria served as the seaport of Antioch and home of the classis Syriaca, the Roman navy's main eastern fleet. Vespasian rebuilt the harbor around 70 CE with an inner and outer basin fed by a canal cut partly through solid rock, a feat of engineering still visible today as the Titus Tunnel, designed to flush silt from the port entrance.

Gesoriacum was the Channel headquarters of the classis Britannica, the fleet Claudius built to launch and then supply the conquest of Britain from 43 CE onward. The fortified port sat on the cliff above the Liane estuary, doubling as the customs post for cross-Channel trade and the usual embarkation point for emperors and officials bound for Britannia.

The Alteburg fort on a low bluff south of Cologne was the headquarters of the classis Germanica, the Rhine fleet and the largest of Rome's provincial navies. More than a thousand marines were garrisoned here to patrol the river from the Rhine-Meuse delta up past the legionary fortresses, keeping the frontier's supply lines and communications running.

Taurunum stood at the meeting of the Sava and Danube rivers and served as the main base of the classis Flavia Pannonica, the fleet that patrolled the upper and middle Danube from Regensburg down to Belgrade. Flotillas based here ferried troops and supplies to the string of forts along the river frontier.

Noviodunum guarded the last narrow crossing of the Danube before the river fans into its delta and the Black Sea beyond. It headquartered the classis Flavia Moesica, the fleet that policed the lower Danube from the Iron Gates to Crimea, and gained extra importance as a logistics hub during Trajan's Dacian campaigns.

Pike Hill stood on high ground overlooking the Stanegate road, one of a chain of signal towers built in the early second century to watch the frontier before Hadrian's Wall existed. Its foundations run unusually deep for a 6-meter-square tower, suggesting real height, and the site kept turning up soldiers' gear into the fourth century. When the Wall was built two decades later, its line was bent slightly off-axis just to incorporate this older tower.

Set on the northern edge of Barcombe Hill above Vindolanda, this signal post gave the Stanegate garrison a clear line of sight across the valley toward the fort below and toward the next tower down the frontier road. Excavations here in 1939 and 1950 uncovered the tower's stone footings inside an earlier Iron Age enclosure.

Mains Rigg's watch tower sat roughly halfway between the Stanegate forts at Nether Denton and Throp, its turf-covered stone footings tracing a tower about six and a half meters square with walls a meter thick. It formed part of the relay of signal posts that let messages travel the length of the frontier road faster than any horse could ride it.

Watchtower 4/49 stood on the Wetterau stretch of the Limes Germanicus, part of a chain of roughly nine hundred wooden lookout posts spaced under a kilometer apart along the cleared frontier road between the Rhine and the Danube. Its original timber tower predates Hadrian's later wooden palisade by two decades; a full-scale reconstruction now stands on the excavated stone footings near Giessen.

properties.modern_location: Chesterholm, near Bardon Mill, Northumberland, England
properties.notes: Vindolanda anchored the Stanegate frontier decades before Hadrian's Wall was built alongside it. Its timber-and-turf forts were rebuilt at least nine times, and the waterlogged ground beneath preserved hundreds of ink writing tablets from around 100 CE, including a soldier's letter recording the oldest known handwritten Latin by a woman, Claudia Severa's birthday invitation to a friend.

ancient_sources.author: Claudia Severa
ancient_sources.note: A birthday invitation from the wife of a nearby commander, written on wood in the 90s CE — the earliest known writing in a woman's hand in Latin.

properties.notes: Corbridge guarded the point where the Stanegate road crossed the River Tyne, on the main route north into Scotland. A Trajanic coin sealed beneath its rampart dates this second fort on the site to 103 CE or later, built just as Trajan was pulling troops out of Britain for his second Dacian campaign. The fort later grew into one of the best-supplied garrison towns on the whole northern frontier.

ancient_sources.author: Antonine Itinerary
ancient_sources.note: Lists the station Corstopitum (Corbridge) on the road route through northern Britain, situated between Vindomora and Bremenium.

properties.notes: This small fortlet guarded the crossing where the Stanegate road forded Haltwhistle Burn, holding a single century of about eighty men behind an earth rampart with a stone face. It was one of the first fortlets built anywhere in Roman Britain, part of a new tactic of splitting garrisons into small posts to watch the frontier road closely.

Throp's fortlet sat on a spur above the Poltross Burn, its square turf-and-stone ramparts enclosing barely a quarter of a hectare. Like its sister post at Haltwhistle Burn, its whole purpose was watching a single river crossing on the Stanegate road, decades before Hadrian's Wall's own milecastles took over the job a few hundred meters to the north.

Newbrough's fortlet sat on the Stanegate road between Corbridge and Vindolanda, roughly equidistant from both, holding a small garrison of around 160 men. St Peter's church now occupies the site of its later stone-built successor in the village churchyard, though the original earthwork fortlet predates the church by centuries.

Boothby's fortlet overlooked the River Irthing from the north, built in the late first or early second century when the river itself still marked the edge of Roman control in this sector. A single ditch and clay rampart enclosed just under half a hectare, big enough for a small detachment watching the crossing below.

properties.modern_location: Bad Homburg vor der Hohe, Germany
properties.notes: The Saalburg guarded a key pass through the Taunus hills on the Limes Germanicus, built up from earlier Domitianic earthworks into a timber-and-earth numerus fort around 90 CE. It housed roughly 160 auxiliary troops through Trajan's reign. Hadrian rebuilt it in stone as a full cohort fort a generation later, and it stands today as the most completely reconstructed Roman fort anywhere on the former frontier.

Zugmantel sat on the western Taunus stretch of the limes, built under the Flavians around 90 CE and rebuilt through four distinct phases over the century and a half it stayed garrisoned. It anchored one end of a dense chain of wooden watchtowers running through the forest toward Saalburg.

Arnsburg held the northernmost bend of the limes as it curved through the Wetterau plain, built under Domitian before 90 CE to anchor the frontier's most exposed salient. A cohort of auxiliary infantry was based here for the better part of two centuries, watching the open farmland beyond the frontier line.

Echzell was one of the largest auxiliary forts on the Wetterau limes, its earth-and-timber defenses enclosing more than five hectares on the edge of the modern village that still bears its name. Troops here watched the open frontier plain that Domitian's campaigns against the Chatti had brought under Roman control a decade earlier.

Markobel held the southeastern end of the Wetterau limes near where it met the Main valley. Pottery finds and brick stamps from Legio XIIII Gemina, withdrawn from Mainz to the Danube around 97 CE, point to an early foundation date under Domitian or Trajan, making it one of the first forts built along this stretch of frontier.

Ruckingen held the southeastern corner of the Wetterau limes where it met the River Kinzig. Archaeological dating places its construction somewhere between 110 and 125 CE, a window that straddles Trajan's death on 11 August 117 CE. Since the fort cannot be confirmed complete by that exact date, it is marked absent from this snapshot rather than assumed finished.

Kapersburg sheltered a mounted scout unit on the Taunus limes, in front of a hill the locals called the Sow's Head. While a Roman military presence in this sector goes back to the first century, the numerus fort whose stone walls are visible today belongs to the limes reinforcement of the later second century, after Trajan's death, so it is excluded from this 117 CE snapshot pending firmer dating of an earlier phase.

Munningen was part of the Alblimes, the chain of forts Domitian pushed north of the Danube into the Nordlingen Ries basin after his Chattian campaigns. Excavations date its founding to around 90 CE, making it one of the earliest Roman military footholds in this stretch of Raetia.

Biriciana was raised in timber around 90 CE to hold the ground Domitian had newly won north of the Danube, garrisoning roughly three hectares behind earth ramparts. The fort was rebuilt in stone in the mid-second century, well after the 117 CE snapshot, and its museum today displays one of the best-preserved collections of Roman cavalry parade armor ever found.

Mediana was among the oldest forts on the Raetian limes, raised in wood and earth under Domitian in the late first century. A military diploma confirms a cavalry cohort, the Cohors V Bracaraugustanorum, garrisoned here by 107 CE. Its stone rebuild, dated by inscription to 144 CE, came decades after the 117 CE snapshot.

Gerulata held a bend of the Danube just downstream from Carnuntum, its earth-and-timber fort raised under Domitian in the late first century. During Trajan's reign the cavalry unit Ala I Cannanefatium took over the garrison, part of the general strengthening of the Danube frontier during the Dacian Wars.

Solva watched a strategic bend of the Danube on the Pannonian frontier, garrisoned by the thousand-strong Cohors I Ulpia Pannoniorum. The settlement grew enough around its military camp that Hadrian granted it town status in 121 CE, a step that presumes a well-established fort already standing here by the 117 CE snapshot.

Ad Maiores was built in 104 or 105 CE on the orders of Minicius Natalis, legate of the Third Augustan Legion, to anchor the desert edge of Numidia's frontier southeast of the Aures mountains. It marks the Trajanic-era origin of the fortified line that would later be extended and consolidated as the Fossatum Africae.

Gemellae was the best-studied strongpoint of the Fossatum Africae, its ditch and rampart mapped in detail by aerial photography on the edge of the Sahara. It was established around 126 CE under Hadrian, roughly a decade after Trajan's death, so it falls outside this snapshot even though it anchors the frontier system the Trajanic sections fed into.

Buridava was raised soon after Trajan's First Dacian War, part of the new chain of forts strung along the east bank of the Olt river to hold the freshly won province. Three successive auxiliary cohorts garrisoned it over the following decades, and it briefly served as headquarters for the governor of Moesia Inferior's forces during the Dacian campaigns.

Castra Traiana takes its name directly from its builder: an earthwork fort with double ditches raised between 102 and 105 CE during Trajan's Dacian Wars, part of the Limes Alutanus running up the Olt river valley. Brick stamps from the Cohors Hispanorum mark its first garrison.

Pons Aluti controlled a crossing of the Olt river on the new Dacian frontier road, its name meaning simply Bridge over the Aluta. An inscription dated to 102 CE names it as a customs post, making it one of the earliest firmly dated points on the entire Limes Alutanus.

Pons Vetus sat on the left bank of the Olt at the mountain gateway into Dacia, recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana and by the geographer of Ravenna as a customs station. An inscription of 102 CE naming it a statio vamalis places it firmly in the opening years of Trajan's Dacian frontier.

Rusidava held the southern stretch of the Limes Alutanus where the Olt valley opens onto the Wallachian plain, part of the same wave of fort-building that followed Trajan's conquest of Dacia. Its precise foundation year is not pinned down as tightly as its neighbors up the valley, but it belongs to the same early Trajanic chain along the river.

Praetorium reinforced the Limes Alutanus roughly midway up the Olt valley, garrisoned by a unit of couriers and border guards known as the numerus Burgariorum et Veredariorum. Construction is dated to 138 CE, two decades after Trajan's death, so it postdates this snapshot even though it filled a gap in the same Trajanic-era frontier line.

Arutela stood where the Olt river valley narrows into the Carpathian foothills, a strongpoint on the Limes Alutanus later famous for its attached bath complex. It was founded in 138 CE, during Hadrian's reign, so despite anchoring the same river-line frontier that Trajan began, it did not yet exist at the 117 CE snapshot.

A small, exact temple on a podium at the head of the forum of Nemausus: six Corinthian columns across the front, the rest engaged in the wall of the shrine behind. The dedication is to Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Augustus' grandsons and intended heirs, both dead young — the building is a memorial to a succession that never happened. Its proportions were copied from the Augustan temples of Rome and cut in local limestone by local masons, which is the colonial programme in a single object. In 117 CE it is a little over a century old and in daily use at the centre of a rich Gallic city.
properties.image_credit: Maison Carrée, Nîmes · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: CIL XII 3156
ancient_sources.quote: C. Caesari Augusti f. co(n)s.; L. Caesari Augusti f. co(n)s. designato; principibus iuventutis
ancient_sources.note: Dedicated to Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Augustus's grandsons and heirs. The bronze letters are long gone; the text was reconstructed from the nail-holes that once held them.

properties.notes: Agrippa's Pantheon of 27 BCE burned in 80 CE, and the temple rebuilt on the same ground burned again around 110 CE after a lightning strike. So nothing complete stands here in August 117 CE: the site holds scaffolding, stacked brick and the rising drum of the great domed rotunda begun under Trajan, which will not be dedicated for another decade. The circular building the name calls to mind belongs to Hadrian's reign rather than Trajan's, though it still carries Agrippa's name across the front.
properties.image_credit: Pantheon (later Hadrianic rebuild) · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: On Agrippa's building of 25 BCE and the argument over the name — either because it held images of many gods, or because its vault resembles the heavens.

properties.notes: The smaller of Heliopolis' two great temples is smaller only next to Jupiter's. It stands on its own podium behind a screen of Corinthian columns, forty-two of them, and almost every surface that can be carved has been: vines and poppies in the ceiling coffers, a doorway framed in grapes and wheat, lions' heads along the cornice. The god is usually taken to be Bacchus, though nothing on the building says so outright, and the imagery would suit the young god of the local triad just as well. In 117 CE the shell is well advanced and the carvers are still at work.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Bacchus, Baalbek · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Fifty-four columns ring this temple and each stands about twenty metres tall — the tallest in the Roman world. They rest on a podium built from limestone blocks so large that three of them, laid side by side in a single course, weigh several hundred tonnes apiece; the quarry is less than a kilometre away, and they were brought in on rollers by rope and muscle. The god is Jupiter Heliopolitanus, a Roman name laid over a much older local weather god who is still worshipped in the old way. In 117 CE the temple is finished and the vast forecourts in front of it are still being built.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Jupiter, Baalbek · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Macrobius
ancient_sources.note: Macrobius gives a detailed description of the cult of Jupiter Optimus Maximus Heliopolitanus at Heliopolis (Baalbek), including the gold cult statue said to have been brought from Egypt, its iconography, and the statue-borne oracle by which the god's will was divined, citing a 114 CE prediction to Trajan.

properties.notes: Palmyra's greatest sanctuary was dedicated on 6 April 32 CE and fills a walled precinct two hundred metres across, big enough to hold the whole civic body at festival. The temple inside quietly breaks the classical rules it borrows: the door is on the long side, and there are two shrines rather than one, at either end, the northern reached by a stair for carrying the god out in procession. Bel is worshipped here with the sun god Yarhibol and the moon god Aglibol. Ceiling beams show veiled Palmyrene women and a camel bearing a shrouded litter. In 117 CE the cult is at its height.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Bel, Palmyra (pre-2015) · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Palmyra set apart by its soil and its water in a great circuit of sand, and by a position that leaves it courted by Rome and Parthia both.

properties.notes: Two thousand years of building stand on this one site, and none of it is Roman. The hypostyle hall alone carries a hundred and thirty-four columns, the tallest of them twenty-one metres, set so densely that the roof slabs need almost no span. Obelisks of Hatshepsut and Thutmose rise beyond it, and a sacred lake lies to the south. Amun-Ra has been worshipped here since the Middle Kingdom, and under Roman rule the priesthood carries on, funded and supervised from Alexandria. Emperors' names go on being cut into these walls in cartouches. In 117 CE Karnak is old, working, and the largest temple complex in the world.
properties.image_credit: Great Hypostyle Hall, Karnak · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Thebes seen as a scatter of villages among enormous temples; Strabo measures the surviving avenues of sphinxes and the halls of columns.

properties.notes: The great temple of Hathor at Tentyra rises inside a mudbrick enclosure on the west bank, its hypostyle hall carried on twenty-four sandstone columns whose capitals all wear the goddess's face. Building began around 54 BCE and never really stopped: the hall was finished under Tiberius, and in 117 CE masons are still cutting reliefs that show Roman emperors dressed and titled as pharaohs, making offerings to Egyptian gods. A birth house for Hathor's son is going up at the front of the site. Crypts below hold the cult statues, and a sanatorium beside the sacred lake takes pilgrims hoping for a cure.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Hathor, Dendera · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo describes Tentyra (Dendera) and its people's ritual hostility toward crocodiles, unlike neighboring Egyptians, and notes that at Tentyra the goddess Aphrodite (Hathor) is worshipped, with a temple of Isis behind her shrine.

properties.notes: Egypt's most complete temple sits in the middle of Apollonopolis Magna, its pylon towers rising thirty-six metres over the town. Work ran from 237 to 57 BCE, and the walls carry the fullest surviving account anywhere of how an Egyptian temple was founded, consecrated and run. The falcon god Horus of Behdet lives here, in a polished granite shrine older than the building around it. Once a year his image travels downriver to meet Hathor of Dendera; priests stage the killing of Seth as a hippopotamus in front of the crowd. In 117 CE the rituals are still kept, in Egyptian, by Egyptian priests.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Horus, Edfu · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: Plutarch describes the custom at Apollonopolis (Edfu) of hunting and ritually killing crocodiles every year and casting the carcasses down opposite the temple, explained through the myth of Typhon (Set) escaping Horus in crocodile form.

properties.notes: The temple of Athena Parthenos has stood on the Acropolis rock for five and a half centuries by 117 CE, and Rome has left it very nearly as it found it. Inside is Pheidias' Athena, twelve metres of gold and ivory, the gold plates made removable so they can be weighed as a reserve of the city's treasure. Around the top of the shrine wall runs a continuous carved procession of horsemen, girls and cattle. The one Roman mark on the building was a line of bronze letters fixed to the east front honouring Nero, taken down again after his fall; the holes are still there.
properties.image_credit: The Parthenon · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Works through the pediments — Athena's birth, her contest with Poseidon — and the gold and ivory statue standing inside with a Victory in her hand.

properties.notes: Athens' best-preserved temple stands on the low hill of Kolonos Agoraios, looking down over the Agora. It went up from about 449 BCE in Pentelic marble, six columns across the front and thirteen down each side, and it honours Hephaestus alongside Athena Ergane — the right pair for a district packed with bronze foundries and potters' workshops on the slope below. Carved panels across the east front show the labours of Herakles and the deeds of Theseus. In 117 CE it is close to six centuries old and entirely intact, one of the few Greek temples Rome found no reason to touch.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Hephaestus, Athens · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The temple above the Kerameikos holding Hephaestus and, beside him, Athena — placed together, he says, because of the story of Erichthonius.

properties.notes: The largest temple in the Peloponnese, and everything about it is scaled to the statue inside. Pheidias' Zeus sits enthroned in gold and ivory, roughly twelve metres high and so close to the ceiling that visitors come away saying the god could not stand without lifting the roof off. Olive oil is poured on the floor in front of him to keep the ivory from cracking in the damp of the Alpheios valley. The east pediment shows Pelops readying the chariot race that gave the games their founding story. Every fourth summer the sanctuary fills; in 117 CE the festival is still running on its ancient count.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Olympia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Built from the spoils of Pisa, roofed in Pentelic marble cut to look like tiles, and holding Pheidias's seated Zeus — a god who, if he stood, would take the roof off.

properties.notes: Aphrodisias took its name from its goddess, and this Ionic temple is the reason the city mattered. Columns ring the shrine eight across and thirteen deep, many of them carrying the names of the citizens who paid for them. The Julian house claimed descent from Venus, so Augustus and his successors treated the sanctuary as family business: the city holds a grant of freedom and exemption from tax, carved up on a wall in public for anyone to read. White marble from quarries an hour's walk away feeds a school of sculptors whose signed work travels the empire. In 117 CE the cult is thriving.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Aphrodite, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Aphrodisias comes before the Senate in 22 CE to defend its temple's right of asylum, producing decrees going back to the dictator Caesar.

properties.notes: The largest temple the Greeks ever attempted, and after four centuries of work it is still not finished — many of its hundred and twenty-two columns stand unfluted and the pediment was never built. You do not so much enter it as pass through it: two vaulted tunnels lead down into a roofless court where laurel grows around a spring, and a small shrine there holds the bronze Apollo. A prophetess takes the water and answers the questions the priests put to her. The paved Sacred Way running the sixteen kilometres up from Miletus was rebuilt by Trajan in 101 CE. In 117 CE the oracle is busy.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Didyma · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The temple left without a roof because of the sheer size of it, with a sacred grove inside and out, and works of art the writer rated the finest in Asia.

properties.notes: A small temple to Isis stood in Pompeii's theatre quarter, rebuilt from its foundations after the earthquake of 62 CE at the expense of a freedman's six-year-old son — the boy was enrolled in the town council in return. Steps led up to a podium shrine; behind it a sunken basin held Nile water for purification, and a side room was painted with Egyptian scenes for initiates. The cult drew servants, freedmen and women in numbers no civic temple matched. Vesuvius buried the building in 79 CE. In 117 CE it lies under several metres of ash, its walls and paintings intact and unreachable.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Isis, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 846
ancient_sources.quote: N. Popidius N. f. Celsinus aedem Isidis terrae motu conlapsam a fundamento p(ecunia) s(ua) restituit
ancient_sources.note: Numerius Popidius Celsinus, a boy of six, rebuilt the temple from its foundations at his own expense after the earthquake of 62 CE, and the council enrolled him free of charge in thanks — the money, of course, was his father's.

properties.notes: The oldest sanctuary in Pompeii stood just west of the forum, a colonnade of forty-eight columns enclosing a raised temple reached by a broad flight of steps. Worship on the spot goes back to the sixth century BCE, when Greek and Etruscan traders were already dealing along this coast. A bronze Apollo drawing his bow faced a bronze Diana across the court, and a sundial on a column kept the sanctuary's hours. Vesuvius buried the whole city in 79 CE. In 117 CE the temple lies under several metres of ash and pumice, its roof gone and its columns snapped.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 787
ancient_sources.note: The magistrates Marcus Holconius Rufus and Gaius Egnatius Postumus paid 3,000 sesterces for precinct works, by decree of the council; the text names the town 'Colonia Veneria Cornelia'.

properties.notes: The Proserpina Dam held back a reservoir north of Emerita Augusta, an earthen embankment fronted by stone buttresses that still stretches 427 meters across the valley. Water released from its sluices fed the Aqueduct of the Miracles into the city below. Roman engineers built it in the first or second century CE alongside the nearby Cornalvo dam, and it has never stopped holding water since. Local swimmers still use its reservoir as a summer bathing spot today.
properties.image_credit: Embalse de Proserpina, Mérida · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: The Cornalvo Dam still backs a reservoir east of Merida behind packed earth and rubble faced with dressed stone, standing 194 meters long and up to 24 meters high. It formed a second water source for Emerita Augusta alongside Proserpina, feeding the city through its own aqueduct and a sluice tower that still works. Most scholarship dates it to the first or second century CE, though a few Spanish studies argue for a later Hadrianic date near 130 CE. Water still flows to Merida from it today.
properties.image_credit: Roman Cornalvo dam, Extremadura · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Nero dammed the Aniene river in three places above Subiaco, creating the Simbruina Stagna lakes that fronted his 75-hectare villa in the gorge. The tallest of the three dams reached roughly 50 meters, briefly the highest dam in the Roman world, and it kept holding its lake for over a millennium after Nero's death. Even after the emperor's fall in 68 CE, the lakes stayed intact in 117 CE. The largest dam finally failed in a 1305 flood; only Lago di San Benedetto survives today.
properties.image_credit: San Benedetto, Subiaco (site of Nero's dammed lakes) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Roman engineers raised this dam across the Aguasvivas river under Augustus or Tiberius, building it 34 meters tall, the tallest Roman dam known to survive anywhere. It stored water for irrigation across the dry Aragonese plain and remained Spain's tallest dam for over 1,500 years, only surpassed in 1590. Its rubble-and-mortar core, faced with cut stone, was already a century old by 117 CE and still holding back its reservoir, showing how far provincial engineers pushed dam technology.
properties.image_credit: Roman dam at Almonacid de la Cuba · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Nabataean engineers built this dam across the Siq's mouth around the mid-first century BCE, sealing Petra's main entrance from flash floods and diverting water through a tunnel cut nearly 90 meters through rock. Standing about 13 meters high, it protected the processional approach for centuries. Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom as Arabia in 106 CE, just eleven years before this map's snapshot, so by 117 CE the dam guarded a new Roman province rather than an independent kingdom.
properties.image_credit: Petra Dam at entrance to the Siq · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sixteen waterwheels arranged in two rows down a hillside at Barbegal drove what is considered the largest concentration of mechanical power in the ancient world, grinding flour for a small city. A dedicated aqueduct branch fed the wheels in sequence, each turning a pair of millstones before passing water on. Carbonate deposits point to that branch being built around 120 to 130 CE, just after Trajan's death, though a Trajanic coin found on site keeps the exact date genuinely debated.
properties.image_credit: Barbegal aqueduct and mill remains, Fontvieille · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Seventeen barrel-vaulted cisterns lie beneath a colonnaded plaza at Ptolemais known as the Square of the Cisterns, together holding some 7,000 cubic meters of water for a city with no spring of its own. Roman engineers carried water in from the surrounding hills to fill them, expanding what may have begun as a smaller Hellenistic reservoir. A 2025 excavation even found a human face carved into the plaster on one wall. The system was already old and in continuous use by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ptolemais archaeological site, Tolmeita · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: At least two dozen vaulted cisterns once stood in a line at La Malga, each roughly 130 Roman paces long, storing tens of thousands of cubic meters piped in from the Zaghouan aqueduct to supply Carthage and its baths. Hadrian ordered that aqueduct built starting around 128 CE, so these cisterns could not yet have held water at this map's 117 CE snapshot. Carthage instead relied on wells and smaller cisterns at Trajan's death. The ruins, later stables, are now overgrown with fig trees.
properties.image_credit: Roman cisterns of La Malga, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Carved into volcanic tuff above Misenum, the Piscina Mirabilis held up to 12,600 cubic meters of fresh water under a vaulted roof on 48 cross-shaped pillars in five aisles. Augustus had it built between 33 and 12 BCE as the final reservoir of the Aqua Augusta, giving the navy's fleet at Misenum water for its base and ships. Sailors nicknamed it the water cathedral, and by 117 CE it had supplied the fleet for over a century. It remains one of Rome's largest cisterns.
properties.image_credit: Piscina Mirabilis, Bacoli · photo by RaBoe, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

properties.notes: Gaius Julius Lacer built this granite bridge across the Tagus between 104 and 106 CE, financed by eleven nearby Lusitanian towns and dedicated to Trajan. Its six arches carry the roadway 194 meters across the gorge and rise 45 meters above the water, fitted from massive blocks without mortar. An inscription boasts its builder raised a bridge that would last forever, and in 117 CE it was barely a decade old, already carrying imperial traffic. It still carries traffic nineteen centuries later.
properties.image_credit: Alcántara Bridge over the Tagus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL II 759-760
ancient_sources.quote: Imp. Caesari divi Nervae f. Nervae Traiano Aug. Germ. Dacico pontif. max. trib. potes. VIII imp. V co(n)s. V p. p.
ancient_sources.note: Twin texts on both faces of the bridge's own arch name Trajan by his full titles. A separate verse inscription nearby (CIL II 761) names the architect, Gaius Julius Lacer.

properties.notes: Apollodorus of Damascus built this bridge across the Danube in just two years, finishing in 105 CE so Trajan's legions could cross freely during the Dacian conquest. Twenty stone piers over 40 meters tall carried wooden arches spanning 1,135 meters in total, the longest bridge built anywhere for a thousand years afterward. It still stood at full length in 117 CE. Hadrian later dismantled its wooden superstructure, but the stone piers endured, and several still break the Danube's surface today.
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Bridge over the Danube, 1907 reconstruction drawing by E. Duperrex · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Twenty piers of squared stone carrying arches across the Danube — the work Dio rates above everything else Trajan built, given the depth and the current.

properties.notes: Augustus's engineers tore this mountainside apart to reach its gold, channeling water for miles before releasing it in one collapsing torrent Pliny called ruina montium. Five tons of gold came out of these red cliffs over two centuries of mining. In 117 CE the works were still running at full capacity, decades before exhaustion finally closed them.
properties.image_credit: Panoramic view of the Las Medulas mining landscape · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: The ruina montium in detail — galleries driven in, the hill brought down by its own weight, and water run in from miles off to wash the gold out of the debris.

properties.notes: Roman engineers arrived within a year of Trajan's conquest of Dacia and drove galleries deep into these gold-bearing hills, importing Illyrian miners as an entire transplanted community. Waxed writing tablets left underground recorded contracts, wages, and burial-club dues from the settlement above the shafts. By 117 CE the mine was eleven years into what became a century and a half of continuous extraction.
properties.image_credit: Roman gallery at the Rosia Montana gold mines · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Copper had been smelted in this valley south of the Dead Sea since the Chalcolithic, but Rome turned Phaeno into an industrial-scale operation, damming wadis to cool furnace slag by the ton. Watchtowers of dressed stone still guard the approaches to the mines. The site's grim later reputation as an exile camp for condemned Christians was still two centuries away in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ruins at Khirbat Faynan, ancient Phaeno · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Roman engineers cut miles of leats across the Cothi valley to feed hydraulic mining at Britain's only known Roman gold mine, sluicing hillsides much as Las Medulas was worked in Spain. A fort called Luentinum stood guard nearby, its garrison overseeing convict labor in the shafts. Mining here had been underway for more than forty years by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Pithead gear at Dolaucothi Gold Mine · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0, Geograph)

properties.notes: Copper cementation tanks at Algares turned scrap iron and mine water into usable metal on an industrial scale at this Lusitanian mining district. Bronze tablets found here preserved the actual mining code Rome used to regulate leases, wages, and bathhouse fees at state-run mines. The workings had been active for decades by 117 CE, well before Hadrian's administration later formalized the regulations found inscribed on those tablets.
sources: Claude Domergue, La mine antique d'Aljustrel (Portugal) et les tables de bronze de Vipasca, 1983
properties.image_credit: Mining landscape of the Parque Mineiro de Aljustrel · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

properties.modern_location: Charterhouse, Mendip Hills, Somerset, England, United Kingdom
properties.notes: Roman lead ingots stamped from this Somerset hillside reached the legionary fortress at Chester within six years of the invasion of Britain, making Charterhouse one of the empire's fastest industrial start-ups. Silver skimmed from the ore helped pay soldiers' wages. A small amphitheatre built for the mining workforce is the only one of its kind linked to a Roman mine anywhere in southwest Britain.
properties.image_credit: Panorama of the Charterhouse lead mines, Mendip Hills · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Notes that in Britannia lead is found so near the surface, and in such quantity, that a law had to be passed limiting how much could be produced.

properties.notes: Lead pigs stamped DECEANGL after the local tribe left this Flintshire mountain and turned up at the legionary works in Chester, proof that Rome had the district under military control within two decades of conquest. A private smelter run by one C. Nipius Ascanius operated alongside the army's own works. Both lead and its telltale traces of silver kept the mountain in production through 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: View of Halkyn Mountain · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0, Geograph)

properties.notes: Pliny called this the empire's most valuable mine for the revenue it brought the treasury, and its cinnabar ore supplied nearly all the vermilion pigment used to redden Roman walls, cosmetics, and ceremonial togas. A leasing company called the societas sisaponensis ran the works on the state's behalf. The deposit here remains the largest mercury reserve ever found on Earth.
properties.image_credit: View of Almaden, site of the ancient mercury mines · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Cinnabar from Sisapo is a state monopoly: the ore is sealed at the mine, refined only at Rome, and the price is fixed by law to stop adulteration.

properties.notes: Augustan-era coins turned up alongside Roman wells and Archimedes-screw drainage systems at this pyrite-belt mine, the second-largest mining basin in Huelva province after Rio Tinto. Copper, iron, and silver came out of the same red-stained ground worked here for nineteen more centuries after Rome fell silent. Germanic invasions, not exhaustion, eventually shut the Roman works down.
properties.image_credit: Reservoir and slag heaps at the Tharsis mines · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.modern_location: Villanueva del Rio y Minas, Seville Province, Spain
properties.notes: Iron and copper drawn from the hills around this Baetican hill town paid for a hillside sanctuary to Fortuna and Hercules so grand it remains the largest terraced temple complex outside Italy. Rome granted Munigua municipal status under Vespasian in recognition of its wealth. Its mines kept supplying the empire with metal until a wave of closures swept Hispania's mining districts in the late second century.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Roman mining town of Munigua, Baetica · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

properties.notes: A bronze hydraulic pump recovered from these Huelva copper workings, now displayed in Madrid's national archaeological museum, shows Roman engineers draining shafts here with the same screw technology used at Rio Tinto. Tartessian miners had worked this ground centuries before Rome arrived. Roman-era slag heaps called teleras still mark the district today.
properties.image_credit: Roman bronze hydraulic pump from Sotiel Coronada, Museo Arqueologico Nacional · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.modern_location: Eastern Desert, Red Sea Governorate, Egypt
properties.notes: Named for the emperor Claudius who opened it, this Eastern Desert quarry supplied the gray granodiorite columns that still stand in the Pantheon and in Hadrian's villa at Tivoli. A fortified settlement housed the quarry workforce ninety miles from the Nile, supplied along a road guarded by watchtowers. Ostraca left by the garrison recorded rations, wages, and water deliveries in exacting detail.
properties.image_credit: View of the Mons Claudianus quarry site · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Numidian kings quarried this yellow marble a century before Julius Caesar's ally Lepidus first shipped blocks of it to Rome for his own doorsills. Augustus later paved his forum with giallo antico from these same Tunisian hills. By 117 CE, Simitthus had held colonial status for nearly a century and its quarries remained under direct imperial administration.
properties.image_credit: Ancient marble quarry at Chemtou (Simitthus) · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Pliny records that this Numidian yellow marble was first brought to Rome by the consular Lepidus, who used it for door-sills in his house — the earliest reference to the marble later called giallo antico that modern scholars trace to the Simitthus quarries.

properties.notes: Ships loaded at the nearby port of Luna carried this white and blue-grey marble to build the Pantheon, Trajan's Column, and dozens of other monuments across the capital. Large-scale quarrying began under Augustus and never really stopped for the next two centuries. More marble has come out of these Apuan Alps than any other quarry district on Earth.
properties.image_credit: Marble quarry (cave di marmo) at Carrara · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The quarries above Luna, worked in blocks and slabs of white and blue-grey marble, loaded straight onto ships in the harbour below for Rome.

properties.notes: A single abandoned obelisk still lies fused to its Aswan bedrock, cracked before workers could free it, and would have stood 137 feet tall had it ever been finished. Roman quarrymen reused these same pink granite pits, leaving wedge-and-water cracking marks unlike the hammer-dressed grooves of their pharaonic predecessors. Granite from here traveled the length of the Nile to build across the empire.
properties.image_credit: The Unfinished Obelisk in the Aswan granite quarries · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Marble cut from this coastal peninsula on Thasos loaded directly onto ships without ever touching a cart, a logistical advantage that kept the quarry in business for twelve straight centuries. Extraction here began in the Archaic period and only intensified as Roman demand grew. Much of the ancient quarry now lies underwater, submerged along the shoreline it once supplied by sea.
properties.image_credit: Ancient marble quarry on Thasos island · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Pliny names Thasian marble, alongside Cycladic and Lesbian marble, among the stones ancient sculptors worked — naming Thasos as a marble source, though not describing the Aliki quarry face itself.

properties.notes: Roman soldiers built watchtowers and a fortified well along this desert road to protect greywacke quarry convoys hauling bekhen-stone the ninety miles from the Nile to the Red Sea coast. Graffiti left by travelers here name emperors from Augustus to Antoninus Pius. Quarrying at Hammamat had already run for nearly three thousand years by the time Trajan died.
properties.image_credit: View of Wadi Hammamat in Egypt's Eastern Desert · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY, MediHAL)

properties.notes: A dozen salting workshops packed the shoreline of this Baetican port town, their stone vats still holding traces of the tuna-belly garum that made Baelo Claudia's fortune. Archaeologists working the site in 2015 found tuna skin fragments preserved intact in the bottom of a vat, the first such find anywhere in the empire. The Strait of Gibraltar's seasonal tuna runs kept the factories running for centuries.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Baelo Claudia, including the salting factories · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The port opposite Africa where the crossing to Tingis is made, on a stretch of coast whose towns live off tunny fishing and salting.

properties.notes: Salting tanks here could hold more than a million liters of fish at once, making Lixus the largest garum producer anywhere in the western Mediterranean. The factories sat inside the lower town gate, within sight of an amphitheatre and bathhouse the fish-salters' profits helped pay for. Production peaked under Claudius and was still running strong when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ruins at the Lixus archaeological site · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo describes Lixus as a Mauretanian town on the Atlantic coast opposite Gades, linking it to the legendary Garden of the Hesperides and the palace of Antaeus.

properties.notes: Twenty-five separate workshops packed the Troia peninsula with 182 salting tanks between them, an industrial concentration UNESCO calls unmatched anywhere else in the Roman world. Tuna and sardines came out of the Sado estuary and went into amphorae as garum bound for the length of the empire. Production here ran continuously from the 1st century into the 6th.
properties.image_credit: Fish-salting tanks (cetariae) at the Roman ruins of Troia · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Lists Caetobrix among the coastal towns of Lusitania south of the Tagus, the ancient name conventionally identified with the fish-salting settlement on the Troia peninsula opposite Cetobriga.

properties.notes: Strabo singled out this Baetican port for its salt, meat, and fish trade, and its very name comes from the Phoenician word for salt. Vats now sitting beneath the University of Malaga's rectorate building once cured anchovy and sardine into garum shipped across the Mediterranean. The industry had already defined the city's economy for centuries before Rome absorbed it.
properties.image_credit: Roman fish-salting pools beneath the University of Malaga rectorate · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Malaca, laid out in the Phoenician manner, with large works for salting fish serving the trade with the African coast.

properties.notes: A fishing settlement called Caetaria on the Strait of Gibraltar took its very name from the salting vats, or cetariae, that anchored its economy. The surviving tanks, now preserved in a public park, cured fish caught in the same strait that fed Baelo Claudia's factories just up the coast. Spain declared the site a protected cultural asset in 2002.
properties.image_credit: Salting vats (piletas) of the Roman fish factory, Parque Smith, Algeciras · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.name_english: Cerro da Vila Roman Villa and Fish Factory
properties.notes: A wealthy family from nearby Ossonoba built salting tanks and a garum warehouse into this Algarve coastal estate, curing tuna blood, roe, and liver into a delicacy prized across the empire. The estate had already stood for over a century by 117 CE and would keep expanding for two more, adding mausoleums for its owners. Purple-dye production ran alongside the fish trade on the same grounds.
properties.image_credit: Watercolour reconstruction of the fish-processing tanks at Cerro da Vila · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Garum from this Phoenician-founded port carried its own brand name, garum sociorum, and fetched a thousand sesterces for barely two liters according to Pliny, more than three years of a legionary's pay. Martial name-dropped the sauce in his poetry as a status gift for Saturnalia. Excavators uncovered the salting vats at El Majuelo park in 1970, nineteen centuries after they last cured a fish.
properties.image_credit: Fish-salting factory (Firmum Iulium Sexi) tanks at El Majuelo, Almunecar · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo names Sexi among the Phoenician-founded coastal towns of southern Iberia noted for large fish-salting establishments.

properties.notes: Salt pans on this Adriatic lagoon gave the town its very name, changed from Ficocle to Cervia after the acervi, or great heaps, of salt piled up in its evaporation ponds. Pliny catalogued Adriatic salinae like this one among the empire's standard methods of harvesting sea salt. Archaeologists date the excavated Roman-era saltern here to the second half of the 1st century CE.
properties.image_credit: Cervia salt pans, Emilia-Romagna · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Stone-lined evaporation tanks stretching over half a mile of the ancient Vigo coastline made this the most sophisticated salt-works excavated anywhere in Roman Galicia. Southern Galicia holds a denser concentration of confirmed Roman salinae than any other stretch of the empire's Atlantic coast. Production here ran through the first three centuries CE before the marsh reclaimed the site.
properties.image_credit: Excavated Roman salinae at O Areal, Vigo · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.modern_location: Ses Salines, Ibiza, Balearic Islands, Spain
properties.notes: Phoenician settlers first worked these salt flats on Ibiza's southern tip, and Rome kept the evaporation ponds running after making Ebusus a municipality under Vespasian in 70 CE. Ships from across the Mediterranean once queued to load salt harvested from these same pans, a trade that outlasted the empire itself by well over a thousand years. Flamingos now nest where Roman salt-rakers once worked.
properties.image_credit: Ses Salines salt flats, Ibiza · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Brick stamps bearing the name of Legio XIII Gemina turned up at this Dacian salt works, proof the Roman army itself ran production here to keep its garrisons supplied. Rome founded the site as Salinae within a decade of conquering Dacia in 106 CE, exploiting a salt dome nearly half a mile across. Wooden tools pulled from the old workings survive today in Alba Iulia's museum.
properties.image_credit: Roman wooden tools used for salt mining at Ocna Mures, National Museum of the Union, Alba Iulia · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Names a Dacian town called Salinae in his list of the province's settlements, conventionally identified with the salt-producing site at modern Ocna Mures.

properties.notes: A single kiln at this Gallic pottery town could fire forty thousand vessels at once, making Condatomagus the largest ceramics factory the Roman world ever built. Terra sigillata stamped here has turned up as far away as Britain and the Danube frontier. By 117 CE the workshops had passed their peak, with the rival center at Lezoux drawing away trade, but production continued for decades more.
properties.image_credit: The great kiln (Grand Four) and baths at La Graufesenque · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Fine red-gloss Arretine ware first made this Etruscan hill town famous across the Roman world, its potters' stamped molds still filling the local Maecenas museum. Emigrant potters had already carried the technique to Lyon and Pisa under Augustus, and by the Flavian dynasty the industry that made Arretium's name had largely moved on. In 117 CE the city's great pottery boom was history, not headline news.
properties.image_credit: Arretine ware potter's stamp (poincon) · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Arretium among the towns whose tableware is famous, in a passage arguing that earthenware still outranks silver at most Roman tables.

properties.notes: By the early 2nd century this Gallic town had overtaken La Graufesenque as the empire's leading source of fine red terra sigillata tableware, its sherds so distinctive they can date an archaeological layer to within a few decades. Pottery from Lezoux turned up as far as Roman Dacia, making up over half the fine ware at one excavated fort there. Production here was near its peak in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Lezoux plate, Musee departemental de la Ceramique · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Terra sigillata from this Rhineland town would eventually reach markets from Britain to Crimea, fired in kilns hot enough to reach a thousand degrees Celsius. The great pottery works that made Rheinzabern's name as Tabernae did not begin until roughly 150 CE, more than three decades after Trajan's death. In 117 CE this stretch of the Rhine frontier had not yet become an industrial center.
properties.image_credit: The Terra-Sigillata-Museum building in Rheinzabern · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Slave gangs on this Etruscan estate pressed wine and processed grain across workshops arranged around a terraced courtyard, following the model Roman agronomists Varro and Columella prescribed in their farming manuals almost to the letter. Built by the wealthy Sestii family in the mid-1st century BCE, it stood just three miles from the port town of Cosa that shipped its produce onward. Excavations here in the 1970s helped found modern Roman villa archaeology.
properties.image_credit: Lower terrace wall of the Roman villa of Settefinestre · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Eighteen wine vats filled this Campanian farmhouse's cella vinaria, the working heart of a busy wine-producing estate outside Pompeii. Mount Vesuvius buried the whole property under volcanic ash and pumice on 24 August 79 CE, entombing its dolia and its wine press mid-operation. By 117 CE the villa had lain sealed underground for thirty-eight years, its productive life already over.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Villa Regina at Boscoreale · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Colonnaded promenades stretched nearly a kilometer along this Istrian bay, linking a senatorial family's seaside villa to temples of Neptune, Venus, and the Capitoline Triad. The Laecanii family, who also ran a major amphora workshop nearby at Fazana, owned the estate before it passed into imperial hands under the Flavians. Its private beach still shows traces of the multicolored mosaics that once decorated it.
properties.image_credit: Brijuni National Park, site of the Verige Bay Roman villa · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Pliny names the Insulae Pullariae (the Brijuni islands) among the notable islands off the Istrian coast near the mouth of the Timavus river.

properties.notes: Highway construction crews accidentally uncovered this senatorial estate in 1962 while building a tollbooth outside Rome, revealing one of the most completely excavated great villas in Italy. The powerful Volusii Saturnini family ran productive farmland here alongside a lavish peristyle residence, next to the sanctuary town of Lucus Feroniae on the Via Tiberina. Its cryptoporticus and storage ranges still stand largely intact.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Villa dei Volusii Saturnini at Lucus Feroniae · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: A soaring drum-shaped tomb raised at the third milestone of the Appian Way for Caecilia Metella, daughter-in-law of the general who crushed Spartacus. Its 20-meter cylinder of travertine once carried a marble frieze of ox skulls and garlands, giving the road below the nickname Capo di Bove. Sitting on a square base of solid concrete, it was built to be seen from far down the road toward Rome. By 117 CE it had already loomed over Appian traffic for close to a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Tomb of Cecilia Metella, Via Appia Antica, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Cylindrical stone tomb of Cecilia Metella beside the Via Appia

properties.notes: A cylindrical mausoleum crowning Monte Orlando above the Gulf of Gaeta, built for Lucius Munatius Plancus, the consul and general who founded the colony of Lyon. Its drum spans nearly 30 meters and originally carried a stepped conical roof visible far out at sea. An inscription once ran the full circumference listing his offices as consul, censor, and triumphator. Ships rounding the cape had used it as a landmark for well over a century by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Mausoleum of Lucius Munatius Plancus, Monte Orlando, Gaeta, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Drum-shaped Roman tomb of Munatius Plancus on a hilltop above the sea

properties.notes: A wedge-shaped tomb built by a freed slave who made his fortune baking bread under state contract, standing where two busy roads met outside the city walls. Its frieze carved rows of round openings to mimic the mouths of dough-mixing machines, a boast in stone about the trade that made him rich. An inscription names him Marcus Vergilius Eurysaces, baker and contractor, beside his wife Atistia. Already close to two centuries old by 117 CE, it stood as a freedman's answer to senatorial tombs.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Tomb of Eurysaces the Baker, near Porta Maggiore, Rome, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Travertine tomb of the baker Eurysaces with rows of circular relief openings

properties.notes: A stepped tower tomb built for Lucius Poblicius, a discharged legionary who settled in the young colony of Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium. Rising close to 15 meters along the road south out of the city, it carried life-sized statues of the family in togas and ranked among the largest funerary monuments raised north of the Alps. By 117 CE it had watched over that approach road for decades, a landmark of Rome's veteran-settled Rhine frontier.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the reconstructed Tomb of Poblicius, Romano-Germanic Museum, Cologne, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Tall stepped Roman tower tomb with statues, reconstructed in a museum hall

properties.notes: An open-air cemetery running along the southern slope of the Vatican Hill, next to the ruins of Nero's circus and its Egyptian obelisk. Roman families had begun raising rows of small brick mausolea here by the start of the 2nd century CE, each fronted with a doorway naming the dead inside. A modest grave among these tombs is traditionally linked to the apostle Peter, two centuries before any basilica rose above it. In 117 CE it was still an ordinary pagan burial ground.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Vatican Necropolis beneath St. Peter's Basilica, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Row of small brick mausolea in the Vatican Necropolis

properties.notes: A mile-long avenue of tombs and carved stone sarcophagi lining the road just outside the walls of Roman Arelate. Wealthy citizens of the busy river port had lined the way with monuments since Julius Caesar planted a colony of veterans here, giving the cemetery its later name, the Elysian Fields. Rows of coffins stretched toward the horizon, a sight that centuries later drew painters like Van Gogh. By 117 CE it had already served as Arelate's main burial ground for well over a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Les Alyscamps necropolis, Arles, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Tree-lined avenue of ancient stone sarcophagi at the Alyscamps

properties.notes: An underground family tomb cut into volcanic rock beside the Via Appia, holding generations of the Cornelii Scipiones, the clan that produced the general who first fought Hannibal in Spain. Four square pillars left in the living rock divided the burial chamber, later enlarged with a brick gallery and its own facade on the road. Burials there had stopped roughly 150 years earlier, but the carved chamber remained intact. By 117 CE the once-famous tomb sat quiet beside the city's busiest road.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the entrance to the Tomb of the Scipios, Rome, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Entrance to the rock-cut underground Tomb of the Scipios

properties.notes: The largest tomb standing along the Appian Way, a drum of concrete and stone 27 meters across at the sixth milestone south of Rome. It originally rose in a cone ringed by stone seats and a carved frieze of weapons and garlands, long since built over by a small medieval farmhouse. Roman tradition connected it to the family of orator and general Valerius Messalla Corvinus, though the burial was never confirmed by inscription. By 117 CE it had watched over Appian traffic for over a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Casal Rotondo, Via Appia Antica, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Large circular Roman tomb mound topped by a small farmhouse

properties.notes: A steep marble-clad pyramid built as a tomb for Gaius Cestius, a magistrate on the priestly board that ran Rome's ritual feasts. Standing 37 meters tall and finished within 330 days by its own inscription, it borrowed the pyramid form from Rome's fascination with conquered Egypt. Its builders sealed the burial chamber with painted frescoes and left no visible door, so it stayed hidden for centuries. By 117 CE it had already stood beside the road to Ostia for over a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Pyramid of Cestius, Rome, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: White marble pyramid tomb of Gaius Cestius in Rome

properties.notes: A towering tomb facade cut into rose sandstone at the entrance to Petra, capital of the Nabataean kings. Its columned front rises some 40 meters, blending Hellenistic style with Nabataean tradition, carved for royalty rather than built from blocks. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom only eleven years before 117 CE, folding this tomb and its caravan city into the new province of Arabia. Legend later credited the stone urn on its facade with hidden treasure, giving the monument its modern name.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Al-Khazneh (the Treasury), Petra, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Rock-cut facade of Al-Khazneh at Petra, carved into pink sandstone cliffs

properties.notes: One of Petra's grandest royal tombs, cut into the cliff face of Jabal al-Khubtha above a broad forecourt on stone arches, with a facade rising some 17 meters. A large stone urn carved atop its pediment gave the tomb its name and may mark the resting place of a Nabataean king. Vaulted chambers built beneath the terrace served for storage or further burials. Only eleven years into Roman rule over Arabia Petraea by 117 CE, it remained one of the most striking monuments in the new province.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Urn Tomb, Petra, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Rock-cut Urn Tomb facade above a vaulted terrace at Petra

properties.notes: Sacred grove of Zeus at the heart of Olympia, enclosed by a wall on three sides and open to the Hill of Kronos on the north. Priests, athletes, and pilgrims packed the 200-yard precinct every four years for the Olympic Games, sacrificing oxen on the great ash altar of Zeus. By 117 CE the Altis held the temples of Zeus and Hera, dozens of treasuries, and centuries of victor statues. Trajan's own coins had circulated among the crowds here in the years before his death.
properties.image_credit: Plan of the Olympia sanctuary (Altis) · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The Altis itself: the great altar built up from the ash of burnt thighbones, the treasuries in their row, and the rule about who may climb to the top.

properties.notes: Built around 590 BCE, the Heraion is the oldest standing temple at Olympia and one of the earliest Doric temples in Greece. Its original wooden columns were replaced one by one with stone over centuries, so no two columns fully match. The temple held the discus used to light the Olympic flame and hosted the footrace of the Heraean Games for women. It still stood in active cult use when Trajan died in August 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Hera, Olympia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The oldest temple in the sanctuary, with one oak column still standing in the rear chamber in his day — the last of the originals, replaced in stone as each decayed.

properties.notes: Small Doric temple built around 400 BCE for Rhea, mother of the gods, and repurposed under Roman rule for the imperial cult. By 117 CE its cella held statues of Roman emperors rather than the old Anatolian goddess, including an oversized Augustus posed as Zeus with a thunderbolt. The switch turned a centuries-old temple into a showcase for Rome's living rulers. Six by eleven Doric columns still framed the small shrine at Trajan's death.
properties.image_credit: Metroon, Olympia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: A Doric temple of the Mother of the Gods that by Roman times held statues of emperors instead.

properties.notes: Doric temple built around 330 BCE to host the Nemean Games, one of the four Panhellenic 'crown' festivals. Argos moved the games permanently to its own stadium in 271 BCE, and Nemea's sanctuary slid into agricultural obscurity soon after. By 117 CE the temple's roof had already failed and its cult statue was gone, the ruin the traveler Pausanias later confirmed on his visit. Thirty-two Doric columns once ringed a shrine that a farming valley had long since stopped worshipping at.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Nemea · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Greece's oldest oracle, where priests read the rustle of a sacred oak's leaves and the clang of bronze cauldrons to hear the will of Zeus. Homer already knew the shrine by the 8th century BCE, long before Epirus's King Pyrrhus gave it a 17,000-seat theater and grander temple in the 3rd century BCE. Croesus of Lydia and generations of Greek states sent envoys here before major decisions. The oracle still answered questions in the mountains of Epirus when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Zeus, Dodona · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Two accounts of the founding side by side: the priestesses' black dove that spoke from an oak, and the Egyptian priests' woman carried off from Thebes.

properties.notes: Seat of the Pythia, the trance-speaking priestess whose cryptic verses steered Greek colonization, war, and politics for over a thousand years. The temple standing in 117 CE dated to about 330 BCE, the third rebuild after fire and earthquake destroyed its predecessors. The priest Plutarch served on staff here around this time, later writing candidly about the oracle's fading but still-real power. Pilgrims still climbed Parnassus to question Apollo the year Hadrian took the throne.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Delphi · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The maxims cut in the forecourt, the stone called the navel of the earth, and the inner room where the prophetess gave her answers.

ancient_sources.author: SIG³ 801d
ancient_sources.note: Marble fragments found by the temple preserve a rescript of the emperor Claudius naming 'Lucius Junius Gallio, proconsul of Achaia' — the same Gallio before whom the apostle Paul was brought at Corinth.

properties.notes: Circular marble shrine built around 380 BCE in the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, the goddess who guarded Delphi's approach. Twenty Doric columns ringed the outside and ten ornate Corinthian columns lined the inside of a building whose exact purpose no ancient source explains. Standing half a mile from the main oracle, it was already three centuries old and still admired for its craftsmanship in 117 CE. Fire would gut its roof only in the following century.
properties.image_credit: Tholos of Delphi, Marmaria · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Vitruvius
ancient_sources.note: Listed among buildings whose own architects wrote them up — Theodorus of Phocaea on the round temple at Delphi.

properties.notes: Ionia's rival to Delphi, where a priest, not a priestess, drank from a hidden spring and delivered verse oracles to pilgrims waiting outside. The marble Doric temple, begun in the late 4th century BCE, was still unfinished when Trajan died, completed only later under Hadrian. The oracle kept operating throughout construction, answering cities across Asia Minor from a crypt finished generations earlier. Colophon's harbor sent a steady stream of anxious questioners up this valley in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ionic temple ruins comparable to Claros's Doric sanctuary · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative)

properties.notes: Desert oracle so respected that Alexander the Great crossed 300 miles of Egyptian sand in 331 BCE just to ask Amun-Ra if he was a god's son. Built in the 6th century BCE atop an earlier shrine, the temple sat on Siwa's only natural hill, ringed by nothing but oasis palms and salt flats. Its priests answered by nodding or tilting a ceremonial barque rather than speaking outright. The oracle still drew travelers crossing the western desert when Rome ruled Egypt in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple of the Oracle of Amun, Siwa · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Arrian
ancient_sources.note: Alexander's march across the desert to the oracle, the rain and the guides, and a consultation whose answer he told no one.

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Places the sanctuary in its oasis and gives the Theban account that a priestess carried off from Egypt founded it.

properties.notes: One of Greece's five great oracles, consulted by rulers from Croesus to the Persian general Mardonius. Petitioners drank from two springs, Lethe and Mnemosyne, to forget their worries and remember the vision to come, before being lowered into a cave shaped like a bread-oven to meet the hero Trophonios. Visitors climbed out unable to laugh for weeks. Plutarch, writing a generation after Trajan's death, confirmed the oracle still spoke when other Boeotian oracles had gone silent.
properties.image_credit: Otto Magnus von Stackelberg, artist who documented the Trophonios oracle site in the 1830s · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative portrait, not a site view)
