properties.notes: Sanctuary of the seer-hero Amphiaraos, swallowed alive by the earth at Thebes and reborn as a healing and dream oracle on Attica's coast. Pilgrims slept in a 360-foot stoa hoping the hero would prescribe a cure or send an answer in a dream. Sulla had granted the shrine tax-free sacred status in 73 BCE, and its theater and baths still functioned under the empire. By 117 CE crowds had thinned from the sanctuary's 3rd-century-BCE peak, but its spring still drew the sick.
properties.image_credit: Amphiareion of Oropos · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The rite in full: purify yourself, sacrifice a ram, sleep on its skin on the ground, and wait for the answer to come in a dream.

properties.notes: The most famous healing sanctuary in the Greek world, where the sick slept in a colonnaded hall hoping Asklepios himself would appear in a dream and cure them. Its Doric temple, built around 375 BCE, stood beside inscribed stone tablets recording hundreds of claimed miracle cures, from blindness to tapeworms. Roman patrons and physicians alike sent gifts and visits to the sanctuary under the empire. In 117 CE pilgrims from across the Roman world still queued for a night in Asklepios's dormitory.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Asklepios, Epidaurus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The sacred grove with its boundary marks, the rule that no one may be born or die inside it, and the slabs recording who was healed and of what.

properties.notes: Enigmatic round building designed by Polykleitos the Younger around 360 BCE, its foundations concealing a spiral maze of six concentric walls that no surviving ancient text explains. Doric columns encircled the outside and Corinthian columns lined an inner ring, one of the earliest uses of that order anywhere in Greek architecture. Snakes, sacred to Asklepios, were kept in the maze below the floor. The Tholos still stood within the healing sanctuary when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Tholos of Epidaurus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: A round building of white marble by Polykleitos, worth going to see for the painting of Drunkenness drinking from a glass cup.

properties.notes: Older than the Asklepios cult it eventually shared a hilltop with, this sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas centers on a 6th-century-BCE archaic temple built over Mycenaean cult remains dating back to roughly 1500 BCE. Epidaurus's healers worshipped Apollo here for centuries before Asklepios, his mythological son, took the valley below. Excavated animal-bone deposits show near-continuous ritual use across two millennia. The temple still crowned the ridge above Epidaurus's crowded sanctuary in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas, Epidaurus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Healing sanctuary built around a spring where patients drank sacred water, bathed, and walked a tunnel meant to carry them symbolically toward the god. Founded near 400 BCE, its earliest buildings were a modest temple of Asklepios Soter, a treatment hall, and a fountain house. The sprawling complex with theater and library that visitors picture today did not exist in 117 CE; that rebuild began only under Hadrian. The sanctuary was respected but still generations from its greatest fame.
properties.image_credit: Asklepieion of Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Birthplace-by-legend of the physician Hippocrates and one of the ancient world's premier medical sanctuaries, built in stacked terraces on a pine-covered hillside. King Eumenes II of Pergamon funded its grand Doric temple in the 2nd century BCE, modeled on the sanctuary at Epidaurus. A fourth building phase was underway under Roman rule as Trajan's reign ended, adding terraces to a site already four centuries old. Physicians here used methods later cited by the doctor Galen.
properties.image_credit: Asklepieion of Kos · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: A famous sanctuary outside the town, hung with votive tablets recording cures — the same tablets Hippocrates was said to have learned from.

properties.notes: Healing sanctuary at the north edge of Corinth, built beside a spring that patients believed carried curative power. Excavators recovered hundreds of terracotta votives shaped like the body parts pilgrims hoped to heal, from hands to organs. Its four-columned temple, late 4th century BCE, was rebuilt after an earthquake and stood alongside dining rooms for patients. Corinth, refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BCE, still kept the Asklepieion running when Trajan died in 117.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Corinth near the Asklepieion · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Founded in 420/19 BCE on the Acropolis's south slope, after a priest smuggled the healing snake of Asklepios into Athens during a wartime plague. Its terrace held a temple, altar, sacred spring, and stoas where patients slept awaiting a healing dream, wedged between the Theatre of Dionysos and the Acropolis rock above. The sanctuary had run continuously for over five centuries by the time Trajan died in 117 CE. Its cure-tablets remain prime evidence for ancient medical practice.
properties.image_credit: Asklepieion of Athens, south slope of the Acropolis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The sanctuary on the south slope of the Acropolis, with its spring and the statues of the god and his children.

properties.notes: Gallo-Roman healing sanctuary built around a sacred pool fed by underground springs, dedicated to Apollo Grannus, a Gallic curative god Rome folded into its own Apollo. A processional road nearly 900 meters around encircled the precinct, drawing pilgrims from across Gaul to a site later tradition claims even emperors visited. The 1st-century sanctuary sat in the territory of the Leuci, in what is now the Vosges. By 117 CE Andesina's spring-fed shrine was an established stop for the sick.
properties.image_credit: Inscription to Apollo Grannus, Roman Grand (Andesina) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Healing shrine at the actual source of the Seine, dedicated to Sequana, the river's own goddess, whom pilgrims believed could cure whatever ailed them. Gauls built a wooden shrine here by the 2nd century BCE; Rome then raised masonry temples and a pool over the springs around 50 CE. Excavators recovered over a thousand votive offerings, carved eyes, limbs, and organs, left by pilgrims seeking cures. The sanctuary was still drawing the sick to Burgundy's source-country in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Bronze statuette of Sequana from Fontes Sequanae · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sanctuary of Diana on the volcanic crater lake the Romans called the 'Mirror of Diana,' guarded by a priest-king who won the post by killing his predecessor in single combat beside a sacred tree. Caligula would later sink two huge pleasure barges in the lake, raised again only in the 1930s, but in 117 CE the cult still ran on its old, violent rules. Slaves and freedwomen alike could serve as priestesses here. Pilgrims carried torches to the lakeshore each August for the Nemoralia.
properties.image_credit: Statue of Diana Nemorensis from her sanctuary at Nemi · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The priest of Diana at Aricia is a runaway slave who won the office by killing the last priest, and holds it with a drawn sword against the next.

properties.notes: Classical temple raised around 60-70 CE over Britain's only natural hot spring, merging the Celtic goddess Sulis with Rome's Minerva into a hybrid deity. Only one other truly classical temple existed anywhere else in Roman Britain, Claudius's shrine at Colchester. Visitors dropped curses etched on lead sheets into the sacred spring, some naming thieves who stole their bath towels. By 117 CE the temple had been drawing pilgrims to Aquae Sulis for roughly half a century.
properties.image_credit: Gorgon's Head pediment, Temple of Sulis Minerva, Bath · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Solinus
ancient_sources.note: Britain's hot springs, fitted out for bathing and set under the protection of Minerva, where the fire in the temple burns coal rather than wood.

properties.notes: Home of the Eleusinian Mysteries, secret initiation rites into the cult of Demeter and Persephone that even Roman emperors sought out. The Telesterion, a columned initiation hall built around 435 BCE under the architect Iktinos, could hold roughly 3,000 initiates under one roof each year. Hadrian would later fund the sanctuary's grand marble gateway, but that lay years ahead. In 117 CE Eleusis already had six centuries of secrecy behind it, its rites unrevealed to this day.
properties.image_credit: Telesterion, Sanctuary of Demeter, Eleusis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: He reaches the wall of the sanctuary and stops: a dream forbade him to write down what is inside, and the uninitiated may not ask.

properties.name_english: Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace
properties.notes: Mystery sanctuary on a remote Aegean island where sworn-to-secrecy initiates sought protection from shipwreck through rites Roman writers described only in riddles. Philip II of Macedon commissioned its earliest monumental building around 340 BCE; construction continued for centuries under the Ptolemies and Rome. The Winged Victory statue would later crown a fountain here, well after this snapshot. In 117 CE the altar court and theater already drew initiates from across the Greek world.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Diodorus Siculus
ancient_sources.note: The island's mysteries, open to anyone including slaves, and the belief that initiates come off better in storms at sea.

properties.notes: Largest round building ever raised in the Greek world, a gift from Ptolemaic queen Arsinoe II to the Samothracian mystery cult around 285 BCE. A ring of pilasters supported a marble roof spanning 20 meters, sheltering theoroi, sacred delegates sent from Greek cities to attend the mysteries. An early Roman-era earthquake forced repairs to its roofline, converting it to an octagonal tile pattern. The rotunda was still the sanctuary's grandest structure when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Rotunda of Arsinoe II, Samothrace · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Vast sandstone temple built by Amenhotep III around 1400 BCE for the annual Opet Festival, when statues of Amun, Mut, and Khonsu traveled by barge from Karnak to be reunited here. Ramesses II later added the towering entrance pylon and colossal statues that still guard the gate. Under Rome the forecourt held a shrine honoring the emperors, soldiers' graffiti scratched beside 3,000-year-old reliefs. In 117 CE the temple had stood in continuous ritual use for over 1,500 years.
properties.image_credit: Luxor Temple · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo, describing Thebes (Diospolis) which he visited under Roman rule, notes the city's ruins extended some eighty stadia and that several of its temples — damaged earlier by Cambyses — still stood alongside colossal statues and obelisks; a general eyewitness account of the great Theban temple precinct spanning the Luxor/Karnak area.

properties.notes: Isis's holiest shrine, built on a granite island in the Nile's First Cataract and finished under Ptolemy III after his father broke ground around 280 BCE. Pilgrims from as far as Meroe and Rome sailed here to petition the goddess, leaving Greek and Demotic graffiti across its walls. Roman emperors kept enlarging it; Trajan's own kiosk, with 14 unfinished columns, already stood on the island by 117. Philae's cult outlasted nearly every pagan temple, closing only under Justinian.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Isis, Philae · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The island above the First Cataract, shared by Egyptians and Ethiopians, with a temple of Isis reached by ferry from the rocks below.

ancient_sources.author: CIL III 14147
ancient_sources.note: A stele in hieroglyphic, Latin and Greek set up by Gaius Cornelius Gallus, the first Roman prefect of Egypt, recording his suppression of a revolt and an embassy received from the king of the Ethiopians.

properties.notes: Unique double temple sharing one roof between two gods, crocodile-headed Sobek on one side and falcon-headed Horus on the other, with mirrored sanctuaries and courts in parallel symmetry. Ptolemy VI began construction around 180 BCE on a Nile bend once thick with crocodiles kept as sacred animals. Later Ptolemies and Roman-era builders kept adding to the complex for two more centuries. By 117 CE the temple's twin cults still drew worshippers to this stretch of Upper Egypt.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Kom Ombo · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Juvenal
ancient_sources.note: Juvenal's Fifteenth Satire recounts a real, violent religious riot between the neighboring Egyptian towns of Ombos (crocodile-worshippers) and Tentyra (crocodile-hunters), including a notorious act of cannibalism during the clash — cited as an eyewitness-adjacent account of the crocodile cult centered on this temple.

properties.notes: Temple to the ram-headed creator god Khnum, believed by Egyptians to have shaped humanity on a potter's wheel from Nile clay. Its hypostyle hall, still visible today nine meters below the modern town, was raised under Roman rule beginning around the reign of Claudius. Decoration of its 24 columns continued for generations, running well into the 3rd century CE. In 117 CE the hall's columns were already carved and standing, part of a program that kept adding inscriptions for another 150 years.
properties.image_credit: Roman-period hypostyle hall, Egyptian Nile temple · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative)

properties.notes: Sandstone temple to Mandulis, a Lower Nubian sun god merged with Egyptian and Greek solar imagery, built around 30 BCE under Augustus near Egypt's southern frontier. Roman governors used its forecourt for imperial ceremonies, decorating the gateway with reliefs of Augustus offering to Mandulis. Its decoration was never entirely finished. It still marked Rome's Nubian border sanctuary in 117 CE, centuries before 1960s engineers dismantled it to save it from Lake Nasser's floodwaters.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Kalabsha (relocated to New Kalabsha) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Small sandstone temple that Augustus commissioned around 23 BCE for two deified Nubian brothers, Pedesi and Pihor, alongside the goddess Isis. Roman governor Petronius built it barely a generation after Actium, at Egypt's new southern frontier. Egyptian priests still tended its shrine when Trajan died in 117 CE, one of the smallest and most personal temples Rome ever funded. Egypt later gave the structure to the United States; it now stands reassembled in New York's Metropolitan Museum.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Dendur, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Nubian temple begun as a one-room chapel to Amun by the Kushite king Adikhalamani around 200 BCE, then expanded by Ptolemaic pharaohs and finished with Roman-era carvings under Augustus and Tiberius. Positioned near Philae on Egypt's southern frontier, it absorbed three dynasties' worth of religious patronage in under two centuries. By 117 CE its Roman decoration was complete. Egypt gifted the structure to Spain in 1968, and it now stands reassembled in a Madrid park.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Debod, now in Madrid · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Healing shrine built into the ruins of Queen Hatshepsut's 1,300-year-old mortuary temple, where Ptolemaic and Roman-era pilgrims sought cures from the deified sages Amenhotep son of Hapu and Imhotep. Sufferers slept inside hoping for a healing dream, exactly as at Epidaurus, a case of Greek and Egyptian medicine merging into one practice. Surviving graffiti record visitors thanking the gods for cures found nowhere else. By 117 CE the shrine had treated the sick for roughly four centuries.
properties.image_credit: Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sacred precinct where Carthaginians cremated and buried infants beneath stone markers dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit, in continuous use from the 8th century BCE until Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. Caesar's colonists, refounding the city a century later, built workshops, kilns, and housing directly over the sacred ground. By 117 CE the tophet's stelae lay buried under a Roman neighborhood, its rites gone, Baal Hammon's identity quietly folded into Rome's cult of Saturn.
properties.image_credit: Stelae at the Tophet of Salammbô, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Syria's grandest sanctuary to Atargatis, the fish-tailed mother goddess, its walls stretching over 600 feet according to the 2nd-century writer Lucian, who left the fullest surviving account of any pagan temple's daily rituals. A sacred lake inside the precinct, said to be bottomless, held fish so holy that only priests could touch them, some wearing gold rings. The sanctuary was already ancient, ruled by Commagenian and Seleucid kings before Rome, when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Coin of Atargatis, goddess of Hierapolis Bambyce · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Phoenicia's most sacred temple, built for the god-king Melqart under King Hiram in the 10th century BCE and known even to Herodotus, who described its two pillars, one gold and one of glowing emerald-green glass. Alexander besieged Tyre for seven months in 332 BCE partly because its priests refused him the right to sacrifice inside. Romans equated Melqart with Hercules and kept the cult running. In 117 CE the thousand-year-old sanctuary still anchored one of Rome's wealthiest Phoenician cities.
properties.image_credit: Melqart, god of Tyre · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Phoenician sanctuary to Melqart, worshipped by Romans as Hercules, founded by Tyrian colonists on the southern tip of Cadiz's island as early as the 8th century BCE. Ancient writers described bronze gate-columns engraved with the labors of Hercules and an eternal flame priests tended day and night. Julius Caesar wept before a statue of Alexander here, envying his youthful conquests. Roman coins from Gades still carried Melqart-Hercules's image when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Votive statuettes from the Temple of Hercules Gaditanus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Maltese hilltop sanctuary with four thousand years of sacred use, from a Neolithic megalithic temple through a Phoenician shrine to Astarte and finally a Roman-era temple of Juno. Cicero denounced governor Verres in 70 BCE for looting ivory tusks the sanctuary displayed as an offering, proof of its reach. Sailors and even pirates respected the shrine's sanctity passing Malta's coast. By 117 CE the temple had worshipped Juno, heir to Astarte's identity, for two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Punic votive stelae, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative Punic-Phoenician material culture, not Tas-Silġ itself)

properties.notes: Best-preserved freestanding temple in Petra, built around 30 BCE for Dushara, the Nabataean kingdom's chief god, standing over 75 feet tall at the end of the city's colonnaded street. Nabataean kings funded it in the same building boom that produced Petra's rock-cut Treasury facade. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom peacefully in 106 CE, turning Petra into the province of Arabia without a fight. In 117 CE the temple was barely a decade into Roman rule, still the city's religious heart.
properties.image_credit: Qasr al-Bint, Petra · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Petra reported at second hand from Athenodorus, who lived there: a rock plateau ringed by cliffs, with springs inside, and a people so orderly they barely go to law.

properties.notes: Palmyra's temple to Baalshamin, lord of the heavens and storms, traced to a small shrine of the late 2nd century BCE that gained a new altar in 115 CE, two years before Trajan died. The grand cella that later defined the site, funded by the Palmyrene Male 'Agrippa' to mark Hadrian's visit, was not dedicated until 131 CE. In 117 CE worshippers still used the older, smaller sanctuary, not the monument photographs later showed. Militants destroyed that later temple with explosives in 2015.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Baalshamin, Palmyra, before its 2015 destruction · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Palmyrene inscription
ancient_sources.note: A bilingual Greek and Palmyrene-Aramaic text by Malé son of Yarhai, a temple official. The Greek pairs Baalshamin with 'Zeus Oromasdes'; the Aramaic dedicates the building to Baalshamin alone.

properties.notes: Germanic tribes led by Arminius ambushed three Roman legions marching through the forest, wiping out roughly 20,000 men over three days. Governor Varus fell on his own sword rather than be captured. Rome never again pushed its permanent frontier east of the Rhine. Emperor Augustus reportedly banged his head on doors crying, 'Quintili Vare, legiones redde!'
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed defensive wall at the Kalkriese battlefield site, photo by Markus Schweiß · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Germanicus's men reach the field six years on and bury what is left: the half-ruined rampart, the bones lying where the ranks had stood, skulls nailed to trees.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: The fullest narrative of the ambush — the broken country, the rain, and three legions destroyed over several days of march.

properties.notes: Governor Agricola pushed deep into Caledonia and crushed a coalition of Caledonian tribes led by Calgacus, killing a claimed 10,000 warriors for only 360 Roman dead. It was the northernmost Roman battlefield victory in Britain. Rome still never permanently held the ground it won that day. The site itself remains unidentified among dozens of candidate hills.
properties.image_credit: Map of Agricola's campaigns, 80-84 CE · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Hannibal's double-envelopment trapped and annihilated a Roman army twice the size of his own, killing an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 men in a single day. It remains one of history's bloodiest one-day battles. Rome lost more citizens here than on any other day in its history, yet refused to negotiate and eventually won the war. Military academies still teach the maneuver.
properties.image_credit: John Trumbull, "The Death of Paulus Aemilius at the Battle of Cannae," 1773 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Polybius
ancient_sources.note: The line that bows forward and then folds in, the cavalry closing the back, and a casualty figure the author says he took from men who were there.

properties.notes: Scipio Africanus finally beat Hannibal on African soil, breaking Carthage's war elephants with disciplined gaps in the Roman line and finishing the fight with Numidian cavalry. The defeat ended the Second Punic War and Carthage's status as a great power for good. Hannibal survived and fled into exile. The battle is often staged as ancient history's classic general-versus-general showdown.
properties.image_credit: Cornelis Cort, "The Battle of Zama," 1567 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Polybius
ancient_sources.note: Scipio opens lanes through his maniples to let the elephants run through, then re-forms; the two commanders meet before the battle and neither gives ground.

properties.notes: Julius Caesar trapped Vercingetorix's Gallic army inside the hilltop fortress with a double ring of siege works, then held off a Gallic relief force of some 250,000 warriors from the outside at the same time. Vercingetorix surrendered in person, laying his weapons at Caesar's feet. The siege effectively ended organized Gallic resistance to Rome. It remains one of history's most studied feats of military engineering.
properties.image_credit: Lionel Royer, "Vercingetorix Throws Down His Arms at the Feet of Julius Caesar," 1899 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: His own account of the double ring of works — one facing the town, one facing the relief army — with the ditches, stakes and pits described piece by piece.

properties.notes: Julius Caesar, badly outnumbered, crushed Pompey the Great's larger army by anticipating a cavalry flanking move and countering it with hidden reserve troops. Pompey's forces suffered roughly 6,000 dead against Caesar's few hundred. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered on arrival. The battle effectively decided the Roman civil war and Caesar's path to dictatorship.
properties.image_credit: Apollonio di Giovanni, "The Battle of Pharsalus and the Death of Pompey," 15th century · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Mark Antony and Octavian fought Caesar's assassins Brutus and Cassius in two engagements three weeks apart on the plain west of Philippi. Cassius, wrongly believing the battle lost, took his own life; Brutus followed after the second defeat. The Liberators' cause died with them, clearing the way for the Second Triumvirate to carve up the Roman world. Tens of thousands of veterans were later resettled at the city as a reward.
properties.image_credit: Map of the first Battle of Philippi, 42 BCE · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Appian
ancient_sources.note: Two engagements three weeks apart on the marshy plain, and the deaths of Cassius and Brutus, each after mistaking how his own wing had fared.

properties.modern_location: Gulf of Ambracia, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: Octavian's admiral Agrippa outmaneuvered the combined fleet of Mark Antony and Cleopatra off the Ambracian Gulf, and Cleopatra's squadron broke and fled mid-battle with Antony following. The naval defeat ended their bid for power and left Octavian sole master of Rome. Within a year both Antony and Cleopatra were dead by suicide in Egypt. Octavian founded the victory city of Nicopolis on the spot and became Augustus four years later.
properties.image_credit: Lorenzo A. Castro, "The Battle of Actium," 1672, National Maritime Museum · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: The fleet undermanned and burning its surplus ships, and the moment Cleopatra's squadron turns for open water with Antony following.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: The line of battle off the promontory and the fighting at close quarters between heavy ships and light.

properties.notes: Parthian horse-archers and cataphracts under the general Surena wore down and destroyed seven legions under Marcus Licinius Crassus, killing roughly 20,000 Romans and capturing the legionary standards. Crassus himself died in the aftermath, reportedly with molten gold poured down his throat. It was Rome's worst defeat since Cannae and left the eastern frontier an open wound for a century. Trajan's ongoing Parthian War answers that old humiliation.
properties.image_credit: "Death of Crassus in the Battle of Carrhae," Cassell's Illustrated Universal History, 1882 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: The Parthian horse archers and the camel train that kept them supplied with arrows, and the retreat that ended with Crassus dead under a truce.

properties.notes: Roman legions under Titus Quinctius Flamininus caught Philip V of Macedon's phalanx on broken hilly ground where it could not hold formation, and flanked it with a detached maniple for a decisive win. Macedonian losses ran to roughly 8,000 dead against a few hundred Romans. The battle proved the flexible legion could beat the rigid Macedonian phalanx on uneven terrain. Flamininus later declared the Greek cities free at the Isthmian Games to wide applause.
properties.image_credit: Battle plan diagram, Battle of Cynoscephalae · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Polybius
ancient_sources.note: Two armies collide in fog on the ridge; Polybius uses the day to argue why a phalanx cannot hold formation on broken ground.

properties.notes: A Roman army under Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with his famous brother Africanus advising, smashed the huge Seleucid army of Antiochus III, including his scythed chariots and war elephants. Roman losses were light against tens of thousands of Seleucid dead and captured. The defeat broke Seleucid power west of the Taurus Mountains for good. Rome walked away the unrivaled power of the eastern Mediterranean.
properties.image_credit: Illustration of the Battle of Magnesia, 190 BCE · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Livy
ancient_sources.note: The Seleucid line with its elephants between the phalanx blocks, and the scythed chariots that break back into their own cavalry.

properties.notes: Consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus lured the Macedonian phalanx onto broken ground and picked it apart in gaps with sword-armed legionaries, killing an estimated 20,000 men in an afternoon. King Perseus fled and was later paraded in Paullus's triumph. The victory ended the four-century Antigonid dynasty and Macedon as an independent kingdom. Rome split the territory into four puppet republics rather than annex it outright.
properties.image_credit: Andrea del Verrocchio, "The Battle of Pydna," 15th century · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: The phalanx advances, the Roman line gives, and gaps open in the pike wall as the ground breaks up — the fighting decided in under an hour.

properties.notes: After a brutal multi-year siege, consul Scipio Aemilianus's legions stormed Carthage street by street in six days of house-to-house fighting. The survivors, some 50,000 people, were sold into slavery and the city was burned to the ground. Rome plowed the site and, by legend, salted the earth so nothing would grow. Augustus later refounded Carthage as a Roman colony, and by 117 CE it stands again as a thriving provincial capital.
properties.image_credit: Byrsa Hill, site of the citadel of ancient Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Appian
ancient_sources.note: Six days of street fighting from the harbour up to the citadel, house by house, and the surrender of the last defenders from the temple of Eshmun.

ancient_sources.author: Polybius
ancient_sources.note: Scipio watches the city burn and weeps, saying to Polybius beside him that one day the same will be said of Rome.

properties.notes: Consul Lucius Mummius crushed the Achaean League's army outside Corinth, then razed the wealthy city, killed its men, and sold its women and children into slavery. Its famous bronzes and artwork were shipped back to Rome as war trophies. The destruction, in the same year as Carthage's, marked Rome's brutal final word on Greek independence. Julius Caesar refounded Corinth as a colony a century later, and by 117 CE it is again a major provincial city.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo at Ancient Corinth, photo by George E. Koronaios · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Mummius kills the men, sells the rest, and ships the statues and paintings to Rome; the city stands empty until Caesar refounds it.

properties.notes: Lucius Cornelius Sulla, badly outnumbered, routed the army of Mithridates VI of Pontus on the same plain where Philip II had beaten the Greeks two and a half centuries earlier. Roman sources claimed only a few dozen Roman dead against tens of thousands of Pontic casualties. The win broke Mithridates's grip on mainland Greece during the First Mithridatic War. Sulla marched the victory straight into his own bid for dictatorship back in Rome.
properties.image_credit: Bust of Sulla, Glyptothek Munich · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: A local's own ground: Plutarch names the hills, has Sulla's men take the heights above the Pontic camp, and describes the scythed chariots failing on the level.

properties.notes: Julius Caesar fought his hardest battle here against Pompey's sons, at one point reportedly grabbing a shield and charging the front line himself to stop his men from breaking. Some 30,000 Pompeian troops were killed by the end, including Gnaeus Pompeius shortly after. It was the last pitched battle of Caesar's civil war and secured his uncontested rule. He returned to Rome to be declared dictator for life within the year.
properties.image_credit: Battle of Munda, initial troop deployment diagram · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Caesar's legions attacked before their general even gave the order, routing Metellus Scipio's Optimate army and its war elephants in a rout that turned into a massacre of surrendering troops. As many as 10,000 enemy soldiers died, many killed by Caesar's own men against his wishes. Cato the Younger, unwilling to live under Caesar's rule, took his own life at Utica soon after. The victory effectively finished organized Republican resistance in Africa.
properties.image_credit: Battle of Thapsus, reproduction of a 1619 copper engraving by Andrea Palladio · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.note: An eyewitness campaign diary: the elephants panicked by slingers on the left, and a slaughter carried on past the point where Caesar tried to stop it.

properties.notes: The Senate's consuls Hirtius and Pansa, backed by the 19-year-old Octavian, broke Mark Antony's siege of Decimus Brutus at Mutina, forcing Antony to retreat over the Alps. Both consuls died from wounds within days, leaving Octavian holding their armies. Cicero had just delivered his blistering Philippics against Antony in the Senate. Octavian used the resulting power vacuum to force his own march on Rome and a consulship at twenty.
properties.image_credit: Marble bust of Mark Antony, Vatican Museums · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Appian
ancient_sources.note: Two battles round the besieged town within a week, both consuls dead, and Antony withdrawing over the Alps with his army intact.

properties.notes: Octavian's admiral Agrippa destroyed the fleet of Sextus Pompeius off Sicily's northern coast, sinking or capturing all but seventeen of his roughly 300 ships. Sextus fled east and was hunted down and killed within a year. The victory ended the last serious naval threat to the Second Triumvirate and pushed the disgraced Lepidus out of power entirely. Octavian was left facing only Mark Antony for control of Rome.
properties.image_credit: Gold aureus of Sextus Pompeius, showing a warship prow, c. 42-40 BC · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Vercingetorix's Arverni handed Julius Caesar a rare defeat, holding their hilltop stronghold and killing as many as 700 Roman soldiers, including 46 centurions, when an assault got out of hand. Caesar himself admitted the loss in his own war commentaries. It was the only major setback of his Gallic campaign and forced him to lift the siege and retreat. Vercingetorix's momentum from Gergovia carried straight into the doomed stand at Alesia weeks later.
properties.image_credit: The Gergovie plateau, site of Vercingetorix's victory · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: The one clear defeat in the commentaries: the assault goes beyond its orders, and Caesar counts the centurions he lost.

properties.notes: Julius Caesar turned to face the pursuing Helvetii near the Aeduan capital of Bibracte and, after a long day of fighting, broke their army and forced their survivors back to their abandoned homeland in Switzerland. It was Caesar's opening battle of the Gallic Wars and set the pattern for the eight years of campaigning to follow. Roughly a quarter of the original 368,000 Helvetii migrants are said to have survived. Caesar dictated his own account of it in the Commentarii.
properties.image_credit: Site of Bibracte on Mont Beuvray · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: The Helvetii turn and fight on a hillside; the baggage laager behind them holds out until nightfall.

properties.notes: Julius Caesar's six legions broke the Suebian king Ariovistus's Germanic warband near the Rhine, driving the survivors into the river after a fierce close-quarters fight. Ariovistus himself escaped across the Rhine but died soon after, and his invasion of Gaul was over. It was Caesar's first battle against a Germanic force and set the Rhine as Gaul's eastern boundary for generations. The exact battlefield in modern Alsace is still debated by historians.

properties.modern_location: Iron Gates of Transylvania, Hunedoara County, Romania
properties.notes: Dacian king Decebalus ambushed a Roman invasion force at the mountain pass of Tapae, killing the praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus and destroying most of his army along with a legion's eagle standard. It was one of the worst Roman defeats of Domitian's reign and forced Rome onto the defensive on the Danube. Domitian ended up paying Decebalus an annual subsidy to keep the peace. The humiliation set the stage for Trajan's later wars of conquest.
properties.image_credit: Bust of Emperor Domitian, Musei Capitolini · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Iron Gates of Transylvania, Hunedoara County, Romania
properties.notes: Trajan personally led legions back through the same mountain pass where Fuscus had died fourteen years earlier, and this time broke Decebalus's Dacian army in a hard-fought win at the opening of the First Dacian War. Roman casualties were heavy enough that Trajan reportedly gave up his own clothing to bandage the wounded. The victory pushed the Dacians back toward their mountain capital. It set up the campaign that would end with Dacia's conquest five years later.
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Column relief depicting the Dacian Wars, plate XXXII, Conrad Cichorius · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Gradistea de Munte, Hunedoara County, Romania
properties.notes: Roman legions stormed the mountaintop Dacian capital after cutting off its water supply, ending the Second Dacian War in Trajan's favor. King Decebalus escaped the fall but took his own life soon after rather than be captured, a scene later carved on Trajan's Column in Rome. The Romans burned the six-citadel fortress and built a new provincial capital 40 kilometers away. Trajan's triumph back in Rome reportedly lasted 123 days of games and celebration.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Dacian sanctuaries at Sarmizegetusa Regia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: The Dacian capital falls, Decebalus takes his own life rather than be captured, and his head is sent to Rome.

properties.notes: Trajan raised this 40-meter drum-shaped monument to commemorate his hard-won Dacian War victories, ringed with 54 carved metopes of Roman soldiers battling Dacians and their allies. Unlike the battles it memorializes, the monument itself is a living structure still standing on its hilltop in 117 CE, dedicated to Mars the Avenger. It replaced an earlier altar honoring Roman dead from a costly battle fought nearby. Travelers on the road from Tomis could see it for miles.
properties.image_credit: Tropaeum Traiani monument at Adamclisi, photo by Munteanu Anca · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Vitellius's German legions broke Emperor Otho's army near this obscure Po Valley village, in the opening battle of the chaotic Year of the Four Emperors. Otho, unwilling to prolong a civil war, took his own life two days later rather than fight on. It was the first time in over a century that legion had openly fought legion for the throne. Three more emperors would rise and fall before the year was out.
properties.image_credit: Winged Victory of Calvatone, bronze statue found near the Bedriacum battle site, Archaeological Museum San Lorenzo, Cremona · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Otho's army is broken on the road between Bedriacum and Cremona while he waits at Brixellum; the survivors go over to Vitellius the next morning.

properties.notes: Vespasian's Danubian legions fought through the night and destroyed Vitellius's field army on the same ground where Otho had lost months earlier, then sacked and burned nearby Cremona in the aftermath. Vitellius was dragged through the streets of Rome and killed within weeks. The victory made Vespasian undisputed emperor and founder of the Flavian dynasty. It ended the bloodiest year of civil war Rome had seen since Actium.
properties.image_credit: Georges Rochegrosse, "Vitellius Dragged Through the Streets of Rome by the Mob," 1883 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: A night battle fought by moonlight in which a legion's soldiers salute the rising sun and are taken for the enemy's reinforcements by their own side.

properties.notes: Batavian rebel leader Julius Civilis, a former Roman auxiliary commander, besieged two full legions inside the fortress of Vetera for an entire autumn and winter until starvation forced their surrender. The garrison that marched out under truce was then ambushed and slaughtered anyway. It was the most dangerous native uprising Rome faced along the Rhine frontier. Roman forces crushed the revolt within a year and rebuilt Vetera as a stronger fortress.
properties.image_credit: LVR-Archaologischer Park Xanten, on the site of the Roman fortress of Vetera · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: The winter siege of the double fortress on the Rhine, the failed relief, and a surrender under terms that were broken as the column marched out.

properties.notes: Titus's legions surrounded rebel Jerusalem, breached its walls after months of starvation and infighting inside the city, and burned the Second Temple to the ground. Josephus put the dead in the hundreds of thousands, with tens of thousands more sold into slavery. It was the decisive blow of the First Jewish-Roman War and ended Temple-centered Jewish worship for good. Titus and his father Vespasian celebrated the victory with a triumph and the arch that still bears his name in Rome.
properties.image_credit: David Roberts, "The Siege and Destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans Under the Command of Titus, A.D. 70," 1850 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: The burning of the Temple, written by a man who watched it from the Roman lines and blamed the fire on a soldier acting without orders.

properties.notes: Vespasian and his son Titus battered the hilltop Galilean town for 47 days before storming it, killing most of its defenders and enslaving the survivors. The Jewish commander Josephus survived by hiding in a cistern and later became a Roman client, writing the war's most detailed surviving account. It was the opening major siege of the First Jewish-Roman War. The town was never meaningfully rebuilt after its destruction.
properties.image_credit: Memorial to the defenders of Yodfat at the site of ancient Jotapata · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: The forty-seven-day siege of the town Josephus himself commanded, ending with the suicide pact in the cistern that he alone walked out of.

properties.notes: Roman legion X Fretensis built a massive earthen assault ramp up the side of Herod's clifftop fortress to reach the last holdouts of the Jewish revolt. When the defenders breached the walls, they found nearly all 960 Jewish rebels inside had reportedly taken their own lives rather than be captured, according to Josephus. It was the last act of the First Jewish-Roman War, four years after Jerusalem fell. The Roman siege ramp still climbs the fortress's western face today.
properties.image_credit: Aerial view of Masada fortress above the Dead Sea, photo by Godot13 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: The Roman camps and the ramp up the western face, and the account of the last night given to him by two women who hid in a water channel.

properties.modern_location: Site disputed; candidate location near Mancetter, Warwickshire, England
properties.notes: Governor Suetonius Paulinus, with only about 10,000 legionaries against a far larger Britons force, chose a narrow defile that neutralized Queen Boudica's numbers and funneled her warriors onto Roman javelins. Tacitus claimed roughly 80,000 Britons died against fewer than 400 Romans. Boudica died soon after, ending her revolt following the burning of Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium. Historians still dispute the exact battlefield among several candidate sites.
properties.image_credit: Statue of Boudica and her daughters, Westminster Bridge, London (1905) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Roman commanders Lusius Quietus and Marcius Turbo cornered a Jewish rebel force under Julian and Pappus inside Lydda during the empire-wide Kitos War, then stormed the town and crucified many of its defenders. Rabbi Gamaliel II was reportedly trapped inside during the siege. It was one of the closing engagements of the diaspora-wide Jewish revolt that broke out while Trajan was fighting Parthia. The uprising was fully crushed within months, right as Trajan himself lay dying.
properties.image_credit: The Lod Mosaic, a Roman-period floor mosaic found in Lod (ancient Lydda), photo by Carole Raddato · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Jewish rebels under a leader named Artemion rose up during the Kitos War and razed Cyprus's provincial capital, with the historian Cassius Dio claiming a staggering 240,000 Greek and Roman dead on the island. Roman forces eventually crushed the uprising and rebuilt the city. Afterward Rome barred Jews from Cyprus entirely, even shipwreck survivors washed ashore, on penalty of death. It stands as the most destructive single episode of the empire-wide Jewish diaspora revolt of 115-117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman-period theatre at Salamis, Cyprus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Trajan's legions marched down the Tigris and took the Parthian capital, sending the Parthian king Osroes fleeing and seating a Roman puppet, Parthamaspates, on the throne. Trajan reportedly seized the king's golden throne as a trophy and pushed as far as the Persian Gulf, farther east than any Roman army before or after. He was hailed Parthicus by the Senate for the conquest. The gains proved impossible to hold and were largely abandoned within a year of his death.
properties.image_credit: The Arch of Ctesiphon at Taq Kisra (a later Sasanian-era structure marking the site of the Parthian capital Trajan captured in 116 CE), photo by David Stanley · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Trajan takes the Parthian capital, then rides down to the Persian Gulf and says he would sail for India if he were younger.

properties.notes: Trajan personally led the siege of this fortified desert city, but Hatra's archers and defenders rained down fire and arrows that reportedly wounded Trajan himself and forced a Roman withdrawal. It was the emperor's last major military operation before his death later that same year. Hatra's successful defense marked the practical limit of Rome's eastward expansion under Trajan. His successor Hadrian abandoned the eastern conquests entirely within months.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the fortified city of Hatra, Iraq · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: The desert city holds out against Trajan; the heat, the flies and the sudden storms do more damage to the besiegers than the defenders.

properties.modern_location: Weser river valley, between Minden and Hamelin, Germany
properties.notes: Germanicus led Roman legions in a punitive campaign against Arminius, the same chieftain who had destroyed Varus's legions at Teutoburg seven years earlier, and broke his army on this open plain by the Weser river. Germanic dead reportedly littered the field and river for miles as they tried to flee. It was Rome's clearest battlefield revenge for the Teutoburg disaster. Tiberius nonetheless recalled Germanicus and abandoned further conquest beyond the Rhine soon after.

properties.modern_location: Near Porta Westfalica, Lower Saxony, Germany
properties.notes: Days after Idistaviso, Arminius made a last stand behind an earthen tribal boundary wall between the Ems and Weser rivers, and Germanicus's legions stormed it in brutal close fighting. Roman accounts claimed a decisive win that scattered the remaining Germanic coalition for the season. It was the closing battle of Germanicus's three-year campaign of revenge for Teutoburg. Rome still chose to withdraw permanently to the Rhine frontier rather than hold the ground won that day.
properties.image_credit: View over the Porta Westfalica gorge on the Weser, near the presumed battle area, photo by Elya · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This merchant ship went down off Antikythera around 60 BCE carrying a plundered cargo of Greek art bound for Rome. Divers recovered 36 marble statues, bronze figures including the Antikythera Youth, and the corroded gears of the Antikythera Mechanism, an astronomical calculator centuries ahead of its time. The wreck lay at 55 meters and yielded finds still studied today.
properties.image_credit: Antikythera Ephebe bronze statue, National Archaeological Museum Athens · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: A geared bronze sphere brought back from Syracuse that reproduces the motions of sun, moon and planets on one turn of a handle — the closest thing in any surviving text to the mechanism found in this wreck.

properties.notes: This 40-meter Roman freighter sank off the Giens Peninsula around 65 BCE hauling roughly 6,000 Dressel 1B wine amphorae stamped by the potter Publius Veveius Papus. At 400 tons deadweight it ranks among the largest Roman shipwrecks ever excavated. French Navy divers found it in 1967, launching France's first scientific underwater excavation.
properties.image_credit: Madrague de Giens wreck display, Museum of Ancient Seafaring, Mainz · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A flat-bottomed river barge sank in the Po delta lagoon near Comacchio around 12 BCE, carrying 102 lead ingots weighing 3.1 tons, boxwood logs, and amphorae of wine and oil. Waterlogged mud preserved leather sandals, a soldier's kit, and a bronze statuette of Hercules and Nereus. Drainage workers struck the hull in 1980.
properties.image_credit: Bronze Hercules and Nereus statuette from the Comacchio wreck cargo, Museo Delta Antico · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Off Mazara del Vallo, Sicily, Italy
properties.notes: A spearfisherman mistook this Republican-era wreck for a rock three nautical miles off Mazara del Vallo, at 46 meters down. Hundreds of Dressel 1A amphorae, the standard Italian wine jar of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, litter the seabed around two lead anchor stocks. Italy's culture minister called it one of the most important underwater finds in years.

properties.modern_location: Off Ile du Levant near Hyeres, France
properties.notes: A flat-bottomed trader of 20 to 25 meters sank east of the Ile du Levant around 50 BCE with some 700 Dressel 12 amphorae of fish sauce from Baetica in its hold. A fisherman found it in 1952 while working a diving bell. Philippe Tailliez led France's second underwater archaeological excavation here in 1957, a 62-day campaign.

This 12 to 14 meter coastal trader went down south of Port-Vendres around 100 BCE loaded with Dressel 1B, Tarraconensis 1, and Pascual 1 wine amphorae. Its hold also held Roman bronze furniture, including couch fittings inlaid with silver and a bucket stamped with a Bacchic mask. The cargo captures the moment Spanish wine began challenging Italian imports.

Dramont A sank in the reef-strewn waters off Saint-Raphael around 50 BCE, one of more than ten wrecks charted in the Dramont anchorage alone. It carried Italian wine amphorae alongside fine Campanian black-glazed tableware bound for Roman Gaul. Archaeologists label the Dramont wrecks alphabetically from A through J for the density of losses here.

This 20-meter merchant ship sank at Dramont around 45 CE carrying a hold of Dressel 2-4 wine amphorae, the standard jar of the early Imperial wine trade. It rests among a cluster of wrecks piled on the same treacherous stretch of coast near Saint-Raphael. The Oxford Roman Economy Project catalogs it among thousands of wrecks charting Rome's seaborne wine trade.

properties.modern_location: Off Cap Camarat near Saint-Tropez, France
properties.notes: A small 10-meter coastal trader wrecked off Cap Camarat near Saint-Tropez around 110 BCE, its hold packed with Dressel 1C wine amphorae. Only a compact 6 by 2 meter patch of hull survived, lashed together in the mortise-and-tenon style typical of Republican-era shipbuilding. It represents the modest coastal traffic that fed wine along the Provencal coast.

This Roman transport sank near the mouth of the Thielle Canal on Lake Neuchatel sometime between 20 and 50 CE, likely supplying legions on the Rhine frontier. Drone photography spotted the site in 2024, and divers raised some 600 intact objects: Spanish olive oil amphorae, gladius swords, and a dismantled wagon with its wheels. Archaeologists nicknamed it the Eagles' Wreck.

Tiberius built Villa Jovis atop Monte Tiberio, 334 meters above the sea on Capri's eastern tip, completing it around 27 CE as the largest of his twelve villas on the island. He governed the entire Roman Empire from this clifftop retreat for the last decade of his reign, its cisterns storing over 2 million liters of rainwater for the isolated household. A sheer drop beside the emperor's private quarters fed rumors that disfavored courtiers were hurled into the sea below. The complex's massive vaulted substructures still stood in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Villa Jovis, Capri · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Tiberius withdraws to Capri and builds twelve villas there, drawn by an island with one small landing place and a sea that keeps visitors away.

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Names the Villa Jovis as the house Tiberius was in when he moved against Sejanus.

properties.notes: Tiberius raised this second grand villa directly above Capri's Blue Grotto sea cave, connecting the two with an internal passage cut through the rock. Excavations starting in 1937 uncovered marble floors and stuccoed walls, ranking Damecuta as the second-best-preserved of Tiberius's twelve island villas. Its scenic quarter let the emperor watch the sea from a shaded portico. The villa remained imperial property and still stood in 117 CE.

Augustus built this seaside palace on Capri's north shore after reputedly trading the larger island of Ischia to Naples for Capri around 29 BCE. Tiberius later enlarged it, and 20th-century excavations uncovered its scale along the harbor now called Marina Grande. Ancient writers called it simply the Palatium, "the palace by the sea." It remained imperial property through the Julio-Claudian, Flavian, and Nervan-Trajanic dynasties into 117 CE.

Domitian carved his retreat out of 14 square kilometers of the Alban Hills, terracing the slope in three tiers toward Lake Albano with a private hippodrome and a 300-meter cryptoporticus cut into the hillside. After his assassination in 96 CE his successors visited only occasionally, though Trajan and Hadrian both carried out modifications to the property in the early 2nd century. Its ruins now sit beneath the Apostolic Palace of Castel Gandolfo, the popes' summer residence.

A natural sea cave at Sperlonga became the centerpiece of a Late Republican villa that Tiberius transformed into an elaborate dining grotto, staging monumental marble sculptures of Scylla and the blinding of Polyphemus around a fish pool inside the cave. Tiberius used the retreat until 26 CE, when a rockfall during a banquet nearly killed him and pushed him to withdraw permanently to Capri. Archaeologists recovered thousands of sculpture fragments from the grotto floor starting in 1957.
properties.image_credit: The Grotto of Tiberius, Sperlonga · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: The roof of the dining grotto at Spelunca falls in during dinner; Sejanus crouches over Tiberius to shield him, and the rescuers find him doing it.

properties.notes: Pliny the Younger devoted an entire letter (Epistulae 2.17) to this seaside retreat 17 Roman miles from the city, close enough that he could work a full day in Rome and reach it by lamplight. He described a heated bath suite, a covered winter walkway, and a tower overlooking the shore, built for year-round rather than seasonal use. Excavations near Castel Fusano since the 1930s have been proposed as the site, though the exact match is scholarly-disputed. Pliny was almost certainly still using the property when Trajan died in 117 CE.

properties.modern_location: Colle Plinio, near Città di Castello, Italy (scholarly estimate)
properties.notes: Pliny the Younger described this hillside estate overlooking the Tiber valley in his letters, praising its amphitheater-shaped vineyard slopes and a temple he built at his own expense for the town of Tifernum Tiberinum after its citizens made him their patron. He credited the local climate with prolonging his health. A site called Colle Plinio ("Hill of Pliny") has yielded walls, mosaic floors, and marble fragments matching his description. Pliny died around 113 CE while governing Bithynia-Pontus, and the estate presumably passed to heirs and stood through 117 CE.

Livia Drusilla, Augustus's third wife, owned this villa 12 kilometers north of Rome, known in antiquity as Ad Gallinas Albas ("at the white hens") after a legendary omen. Its underground summer dining room was painted floor to ceiling with a single continuous garden fresco, one of the best-preserved illusionistic paintings to survive from antiquity. The marble Augustus of Prima Porta statue was unearthed here in 1863. The villa remained imperial property through the 2nd century CE.
properties.image_credit: Garden fresco from the Villa of Livia, Prima Porta (Palazzo Massimo alle Terme) · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: An eagle drops a white hen with a laurel sprig in its beak into Livia's lap at her villa on the Flaminia; the laurel grove grown from it supplied the crowns of every Julio-Claudian triumph.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Tells the same story and adds that the villa took its name from the hens — ad Gallinas Albas.

properties.notes: Villa San Marco sprawled across 11,000 square meters on the clifftop above Stabiae, built around a tetrastyle atrium in the Augustan age and enlarged with a colonnaded swimming pool under Claudius. Its owner has never been identified, though the scale of its peristyle gardens marks it as one of the largest villas on the Bay of Naples. Vesuvius buried it on 24 August 79 CE, ending its life as a residence 38 years before this map's snapshot — included, like Pompeii's Villa of the Mysteries, as part of the story the eruption erased.
properties.image_credit: Villa San Marco ruins, Stabiae · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Villa Arianna took its name from a large Ariadne fresco found on its walls and ranks among the oldest villas at Stabiae, its core dating to the 2nd century BCE. Its terrace commanded views across the Bay of Naples, and excavators uncovered frescoes of Flora and Artemis now in the Naples Archaeological Museum. Vesuvius buried the villa on 24 August 79 CE, 38 years before 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Villa Arianna, Stabiae · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This luxury residence at Oplontis, traditionally linked to Poppaea Sabina, Nero's second wife, covered its walls in some of the finest Second Style frescoes surviving from Roman antiquity. An earthquake in 62 CE damaged it badly enough that repair crews were still working when Vesuvius erupted on 24 August 79 CE, burying the site mid-reconstruction. Excavation uncovered an unfinished swimming pool 61 meters long, the largest known from any Roman villa. UNESCO listed Oplontis alongside Pompeii and Herculaneum in 1997.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Colonnade Villa Poppaea Oplontis Torre Annunziata Italy.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Peristyle colonnade, Villa Poppaea, Oplontis · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A few hundred meters from the Poppaea villa, this second Oplontis complex ran as a working wine business, its storerooms holding over 1,400 amphorae being readied for a new vintage when Vesuvius erupted. Excavators tied the property to a Lucius Crassius Tertius via a graffito naming him, though whether he owned or simply worked there remains debated. The complex combined cramped worker housing with a commercial packing and export operation for Vesuvian wine, ending on 24 August 79 CE.

Built outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate in the final decades of the Republic, this villa ranked among the largest private residences near Pompeii, its garden framed by a colonnaded portico on three sides. It took its modern name from Marcus Arrius Diomedes, whose tomb stood across the road, though nothing ties him to actual ownership. Bourbon excavators cleared it between 1771 and 1774, among the earliest large-scale digs at Pompeii. Vesuvius buried the villa on 24 August 79 CE, 38 years before this map's snapshot.
properties.image_credit: Villa of Diomedes, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Augustus built this villa above Boscotrecase for his grandson Agrippa Postumus, whose exile and execution around 14 CE left the estate confiscated by the imperial family. Its black-ground and red-ground bedroom frescoes, among the earliest examples of the Third Pompeian Style, rank as some of the finest Augustan-era wall paintings ever recovered, now held in New York's Metropolitan Museum. The original 79 CE eruption ended its life as a residence 38 years before 117 CE.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Fresco detail - villa at Boscotrecase - MET image.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Fresco from the Villa of Agrippa Postumus, Boscotrecase · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Workers laying Tiber embankments in 1879 struck the buried remains of a luxury villa on the river's west bank, its rooms covered floor to ceiling in Third Style frescoes and stucco reliefs from the height of the Augustan age. Scholars tie its ownership to Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa and, through him, to Augustus's daughter Julia. Its garden-room paintings and gilded stuccowork, now reassembled in Rome's Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, rank among the finest domestic decoration to survive from Augustus's reign. Note: the ancient find-site is unrelated to the 16th-century Renaissance building of the same modern name.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Fresco from the Villa Farnesina, 1st century CE; Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, Rome (29).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Augustan fresco from the ancient Villa della Farnesina, now Palazzo Massimo alle Terme · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Nero was born at his family's seaside villa in Antium on 15 December 37 CE and later razed the inherited property to rebuild it on an imperial scale, adding a private theater. The estate had passed down through generations of his family, the Octavii, before Augustus himself used it around 2 BCE. Nero also built an artificial harbor at Antium, remnants of which still shape the modern port of Anzio. The property remained in imperial hands after Nero's fall in 68 CE and stood through the Trajanic reign.

Villa Sora occupied a coastal terrace at what is now Torre del Greco, expanding through several phases after its mid-1st-century-BCE founding into a residence with frescoed capitals and reception halls. Recent excavations found evidence a construction site was still active on the property in 79 CE, work interrupted mid-stream when Vesuvius erupted. The villa lay largely forgotten for centuries beneath the modern town that grew over it.

properties.modern_location: Positano, Italy (beneath Santa Maria Assunta church)
properties.notes: A 2003 flood tore open the ground beneath Positano's Church of Santa Maria Assunta and revealed a buried Roman villa complete with painted walls and mosaic floors, hidden beneath the town's main piazza for nearly two thousand years. Its owners were mid-repair from 62 CE earthquake damage when Vesuvius erupted on 24 August 79 CE and entombed the property. The site opened as the Roman Archaeological Museum of Positano in 2018, reached by a stairway descending from the church.

This two-level villa sat at the mouth of the Reginna Minor river, built in the early 1st century CE around a garden courtyard with a central pool typical of wealthy Roman residences. Ash from the 79 CE Vesuvius eruption buried the site 11 meters deep, and it lay forgotten until the collapse of nearby houses exposed it in 1932. It stands as one of the few excavated standing Roman villa complexes on the Amalfi Coast's southern side.

properties.modern_location: Fishbourne, near Chichester, West Sussex, England
properties.notes: Fishbourne rose beside Chichester Harbour just thirty years after the Roman conquest of Britain, an extraordinarily early date for a palace of its scale, with four wings of formal rooms around a planted courtyard garden. Historians connect it to Tiberius Claudius Cogidubnus, a client king who ruled the Regni on Rome's behalf, though his ownership remains circumstantial. Excavations from 1960 uncovered more than 20 surviving mosaic floors, including the famous Cupid on a Dolphin design. It stands as the largest known Roman residence north of the Alps.
properties.image_credit: Fishbourne Roman Palace, West Sussex · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Certain territories are handed to king Cogidubnus, on the old Roman practice, Tacitus says, of using even kings as instruments of subjection. Whether this palace was his is argued over.

properties.notes: Gorhambury grew out of a late Iron Age farmstead north of Verulamium, passing through timber buildings in the early 1st century before a small but genuinely luxurious stone villa replaced them around 100 CE. Excavations from 1972 to 1982 traced its transformation across nine distinct building periods. An aisled barn and bathhouse eventually joined the main house, serving the working side of the estate. This early stone villa stood in 117 CE, decades before its late-2nd-century rebuild.

The first house at Lullingstone rose around 80-90 CE on the bank of the River Darent, a winged-corridor design linking two flanking wings that became one of the most common villa layouts in Roman Britain. That original building stood alone for roughly sixty years before a heated bath block was added around 150 CE, well after this map's snapshot. The site's famous 4th-century mosaics and early Christian house-church are centuries removed from this modest first-century structure — in 117 CE the villa was still in this earlier, simpler form.
properties.image_credit: Lullingstone Roman Villa site, Kent · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Eccles ranks among the earliest high-status stone buildings raised anywhere in Roman Britain, its first structure going up around 65 CE, barely two decades after the conquest. The original house held 12 rooms, five floored with tessellated pavement, plus a veranda and a probable second story. A large nearby bathhouse carried mosaic work reminiscent of Fishbourne Roman Palace, forty miles west. Archaeologist A.P. Detsicas excavated the site across thirteen seasons from 1963 to 1976.

Rockbourne began as an Iron Age roundhouse converted into a simple three-room house in the decades after the conquest, long before it grew into the 40-plus-room complex visitors see today. That first Roman house stood for roughly a century until around 150 CE, when a larger range called the West House replaced it. A farmer plowing his field in 1942 struck the first hint of the buried ruins, setting off excavations that revealed a well yielding a haul of Roman coins. In 117 CE the estate still consisted of this earlier, modest farmhouse.

Angmering was one of the earliest masonry villas built anywhere in Roman Britain, going up within a generation of the Claudian conquest and decorated with marble fittings imported from Italy alongside local Sussex stone. Its bathhouse featured painted wall plaster and hypocaust underfloor heating, evidence of a wealthy, thoroughly Romanized owner just decades after the invasion. First noted by antiquarians in 1819, the site was systematically excavated between 1936 and 1946. By 117 CE the villa had already stood for roughly half a century.

properties.modern_location: Southwick, West Sussex, England (site now built over)
properties.notes: Southwick ranked as the second-largest villa known in Sussex, a palatial residence built around 70-80 CE and decorated in a style closely comparable to nearby Fishbourne Roman Palace. Excavations in the 1930s found the villa had sprawled across an area now covered by a church and dozens of modern houses, and the site was largely lost to 20th-century development. Occupation there continued for nearly three centuries, from roughly 80 CE to the 340s CE — already an established estate by 117 CE.

Montmaurin grew from modest mid-1st-century-CE beginnings into one of the largest villas ever discovered in Gaul, its later footprint sprawling across 19 hectares with roughly 200 rooms fitted with marble, mosaics, glazed windows, and running water. Archaeologist Georges Fouet uncovered the site by chance in 1946. The estate's grandest phase developed gradually until about 350 CE, but its first-century core already stood as a working residence in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Atrium, Gallo-Roman villa of Montmaurin · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The first villa at Chiragan, on the Garonne along the road to Toulouse, rose modestly during Augustus's reign, centuries before the site became one of Gaul's grandest estates. By Trajan's reign the residence already included an atrium and two peristyle courtyards, expansion carried out as the property's wealth grew. Chiragan later yielded more than 700 sculpture fragments, including imperial portrait busts, now at the Saint-Raymond Museum in Toulouse — most of that famous sculpture collection dates generations after this snapshot.

Loupian's villa began as a modest farmstead near the Via Domitia and grew during the 1st and 2nd centuries into a large patrician residence overlooking the Bassin de Thau, with its own thermal baths. Viticulture drove the estate's wealth, its cellar holding a storehouse capable of 1,500 hectoliters of wine. The site remained continuously occupied for more than 600 years, an unusually long working life, before a 5th-century rebuild reduced the main house to a smaller mansion.

A Roman residence occupied this hilltop 12 kilometers from Tarraco from the 1st century CE onward, though the opulent villa whose mosaics and baths survive today was largely rebuilt starting in the mid-2nd century, a generation past this map's snapshot. Its later heyday belonged to Caius Valerius Avitus, a duumvir of Tarraco, and his wife Faustina. In 117 CE a working Roman residence stood on the site, but the grand aristocratic villa visitors see today was still a generation away.
properties.image_credit: Roman villa of Els Munts, Altafulla · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Vila Cardilio took shape in the 1st century CE as a working Lusitanian estate, its storerooms lined with large dolia jars for fermenting and storing wine and oil. Excavations begun in 1962 uncovered colored mosaics, coins, sculpture, and Latin inscriptions naming later owners Cardilio and Avita, the source of the modern name. The estate remained in continuous use for roughly 300 years, through a second major building phase in the 4th century. Its first-century core had already stood for decades by 117 CE.

Torre Llauder rose near Iluro, a Roman colony on Catalonia's coast, built around the time of Augustus with views over the Maresme shoreline. Local historian Maria Ribas discovered the buried villa in 1961, and study later connected its finest mosaic floors to a late-2nd-century refurbishment, well past this snapshot. Spain declared the site a monument of national historic-artistic interest, protecting its hypocaust and residential wings from Mataro's urban growth. By 117 CE the villa had already stood for over a century.
properties.image_credit: Hypocaust, Roman villa of Torre Llauder, Mataro · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: At the foot of the Penon de Ifach, Roman settlers built their first dwelling at Banos de la Reina toward the end of the 1st century CE, later adding baths and expanding into a coastal vicus under the jurisdiction of nearby Dianium. The site combined residential quarters with fish-salting basins cut directly into the coastal rock, exploiting Calpe's fishing grounds for garum production. Archaeologists have excavated only about a quarter of the roughly 5,000-square-meter site so far. In 117 CE this working coastal residence and fishery had operated for a generation.

properties.name_english: Royal Palace of Juba II, Caesarea
properties.notes: Juba II, the Numidian-born client king Augustus installed over Mauretania, refounded the Punic port of Iol as Caesarea around 25 BCE and built a royal palace modeled on the Hellenistic capitals of the eastern Mediterranean. He and his queen, Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony, filled the city with a lighthouse, theater, and amphitheater alongside their residence. After Rome annexed Mauretania as a province in 44 CE, Caesarea continued as the provincial capital, and the royal quarter remained a governing seat through 117 CE.

The House of Orpheus stood among the grandest private residences at Volubilis, Mauretania Tingitana's frontier city, built in the second half of the 1st century CE. It takes its modern name from a large floor mosaic of Orpheus charming animals with his lyre, one of the finest surviving figural mosaics from Roman North Africa. The house also included private baths, a mark of the wealth Volubilis's olive-oil trade brought its elite, an established residence when Trajan died in 117 CE.

A Roman villa at Anaploga, 750 meters from Corinth's Odeion, was excavated between 1962 and 1964 and yielded a striking still-life mosaic with elaborate geometric borders. Pottery beneath the mosaic's bedding dated its creation to the last quarter of the 1st century CE, decades after Corinth's refounding as a Roman colony. It illustrates the villa culture that took root even in this thoroughly Hellenic province by 117 CE.

Built at the northern tip of the Sirmione peninsula on Lake Garda around the turn of the millennium, this multi-story villa ranks as the most important Roman residence of its kind in northern Italy, with porticoes and terraces facing the water on every side. Its popular name, Grotte di Catullo, dates only to the 15th century, when locals linked the ruins to the poet Catullus, who died decades before the villa was actually built. The complex included its own lake-fed spa facility and remained in use until abandoned in the 3rd century CE.
properties.image_credit: Grotte di Catullo, Sirmione, Lake Garda · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Minas de Riotinto, Huelva Province, Spain
properties.notes: Rio Tinto's blood-red waters, stained by pyrite oxidation, marked one of the richest silver and copper districts Rome worked in Iberia. Engineers linked pairs of waterwheels to lift floodwater 30 meters from underground galleries, wooden fragments of which survive today. Two centuries of extraction had passed by 117 CE, the ore worked mostly by chained slave labor. Pliny the Elder named the mining settlement here Cotinae.
properties.image_credit: The Rio Tinto mining district, Huelva province, Spain · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Lead pigs stamped LVTVD or SOCIORVM LVTVDARES traveled from this Derbyshire mining district to ports across Roman Britain, one inscribed pig reading British lead worked from the silver mines. Matlock, Cromford, and Wirksworth together held the densest concentration of these finds anywhere in the province. By 117 CE the works had run for four decades under an organized company of lessees, the socii Lutudarenses.

Ovid himself praised the hardness of the steel dug from these Carinthian hills, and Roman legions armed themselves with weapons forged from Noricum's ore for four centuries. Six smelting furnaces and ten smithing hearths excavated at the Semlach Eisner site trace an industry running continuously since the province's annexation in 16 BCE. By 117 CE ferrum Noricum was the standard steel of the Roman military, prized above every rival source.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Sets out why iron differs from place to place — the ore, the water it is quenched in — in the passage behind the standing reputation of Noric steel.

properties.image_credit: Mining museum at Knappenberg, Hüttenberg, site of the Roman-era Ferrum Noricum iron works · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Two million tons of ancient slag still cover the ground around this copper mine in the Solea valley, half of everything Cyprus ever produced in antiquity. The Greek word for copper itself, kyprios, comes from this island's mines. Roman-period smelting here reached a scale never matched before or after, and by 117 CE the works had operated without interruption for well over a millennium.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons — the Skouriotissa copper mine site, Cyprus, worked since antiquity

properties.notes: Sanctuaries to Aphrodite stood beside the copper workshops of this inland city-kingdom, a pairing that put commerce and divinity under one roof. Homer already knew Tamassos by name for its ore. Rome kept the district's furnaces running alongside those at nearby Mavrovouli and Kokkinopezoula, and by 117 CE the site had supplied copper to Mediterranean markets for well over a thousand years.
properties.image_credit: Royal tomb at Tamassos, Cyprus, near the ancient copper-mining district · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Silver from the seventy-hectare hillfort of Castulo was rich enough that Hannibal married a local princess, Himilce, to secure access to it before ever marching on Rome. The Guadalquivir carried copper, lead, and silver out of these Sierra Morena workings for six centuries under Roman control. By 117 CE Castulo held municipal status and its mines remained central to the economy of the upper Guadalquivir valley.
properties.image_credit: Ángel M. Felicísimo, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons — the Mosaico de los Amores excavated at the Castulo archaeological site, Linares, Spain
