properties.notes: Philip II conquered this mountain range specifically to seize its gold, drawing roughly a thousand talents a year that later bankrolled Alexander's conquest of Persia. Roman-period archaeology shows the old workings intensified rather than abandoned once Macedonia became a province. Veterans of the Battle of Philippi settled in the plain below, and by 117 CE the mountain's gold still fed the Roman mint two centuries after Actium.

A Roman procurator named Marcus Ulpius Hermias ran the entire Dacian gold district from an office in this Carpathian town, backed by soldiers of the Thirteenth Legion and a staff of clerks and paymasters. Ampelum coordinated the mining settlements scattered through the Apuseni Mountains, including nearby Alburnus Maior. Founded in the years right after Trajan's conquest of Dacia in 106 CE, it was already the gold administration's headquarters by 117 CE.

properties.modern_location: Wadi Sikait, Red Sea Governorate, Egypt
properties.notes: This stretch of Egypt's Eastern Desert held the only emerald deposits known anywhere in the Roman world, and Cleopatra's own emeralds are traced to these hills. Eleven separate extraction galleries have been mapped around the valley, cut into stone still green-flecked today. Roman mining here began under Augustus around 30 BCE, and by 117 CE the gems had traveled the length of the empire as luxury stones for imperial jewelry.
properties.image_credit: Roland Unger, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons — rock-cut temple facade at Sikait, the ancient Roman emerald-mining settlement of Mons Smaragdus

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: On emeralds and the stones sold as them: Egyptian mines worked in the desert behind Coptos, and the trick of soaking poor stones in oil to deepen the colour.

properties.notes: Smoke from Elba's iron furnaces gave the island its ancient Greek name, Aithale, meaning sooty. Ore dug from Rio Marina's hillsides had crossed to the mainland smelters of Populonia for five centuries by the time Augustus made the Tyrrhenian a Roman lake. The furnace and the goat, a phrase modern researchers use for the island's fuelwood economy, captures how iron production here reshaped the landscape well into the early Empire, with 117 CE falling within its documented Roman-period operation.
properties.image_credit: Rio Marina, the historic center of Elba’s Roman-era iron mining district · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Vila Pouca de Aguiar, Vila Real District, Portugal
properties.notes: The largest open pit at this Portuguese gold complex runs 500 meters long and drops 100 meters deep, cut entirely by Roman hand tools and hydraulic sluicing. A full settlement grew up around the workings, complete with baths and an amphitheater for the miners. Gold, silver, and other ores came out of the Tres Minas, Gralheira, and Jales deposits together through the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, squarely spanning the year 117.
properties.image_credit: Corta da Ribeirinha open-pit at the Tres Minas Roman gold mines, Portugal · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Copper had been dug from this desert valley north of the Red Sea since the Chalcolithic era, but Roman engineers reopened the workings in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE with refined smelting techniques the earlier miners never had. A Roman fort at nearby Yotvata guarded the route. By 117 CE the renewed operation was feeding copper into the Roman economy of the province bordering the Gulf of Aqaba.
properties.image_credit: An ancient mine shaft in the Timna Valley copper district · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Purple-veined pavonazzetto marble from this Phrygian quarry framed the niches of Hadrian's Pantheon, cut on imperial account under a state bureau rather than sold on the open market. Columns of a size no other Anatolian quarry could match left Docimium for building projects across the Mediterranean. By 117 CE the Roman state had directly operated these workings for over a century, a monopoly documented in the quarry's own inscriptions.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The quarries near Synnada, once worked in small pieces, now sending blocks and columns to Rome big enough to make the haulage worth it.

properties.modern_location: Gebel Dokhan, Red Sea Governorate, Egypt
properties.notes: A soldier named Caius Cominius Leugas discovered this outcrop in 18 CE, and it turned out to be the only source of imperial purple porphyry anywhere in the Roman world. Stone hauled across the desert on the Via Porphyrites eventually clad the Pantheon and Constantinople's imperial palace. By 117 CE the quarry had operated under direct imperial control for nearly a century, its purple stone reserved exclusively for the emperor's own projects.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Egypt's red porphyry, quarried in unlimited blocks; Vitrasius Pollio brought the first statues of it to Rome under Claudius, to a cool reception.

properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/"Imperial Porphyry" - porphyritic metadacite to porphyritic meta-andesite (Dokhan Volcanics, Neoproterozoic, ~593-602 Ma; Mons Porphyrites, Red Sea Mountains, Egypt) 1 (25869817093).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Imperial porphyry stone sample from the Mons Porphyrites quarries, Egypt · Wikimedia Commons (photo: James St. John)

properties.notes: Marble cut from this Sea of Marmara island loaded straight onto ships at the harbor of Saraylar, sparing haulers a single mile of overland cartage. The quarries span more than 40 square kilometers, among the largest worked surfaces in the ancient marble trade. Extraction had run since the Archaic period, but demand from Rome pushed production to its Roman-era height, with 117 CE falling in the middle of that centuries-long boom.

Twenty-five separate quarries once scarred the southern slope of this mountain overlooking Athens, the same white stone that built the Parthenon centuries earlier. Roman builders began shipping Pentelic marble to Italy in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE for temple projects far from Greece. Pausanias later reported the veins running thin, but by 117 CE the mountain was still yielding stone for Flavian-era construction underway in Rome.
properties.image_credit: The Spilia marble quarry on Mount Pentelicus, source of Athens’s building stone · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Underground galleries called the Quarry of the Nymphs and the Quarry of Pan produced lychnites, a marble so translucent that quarrymen worked by lamplight even in daytime. This stone became the Venus de Milo and Praxiteles' Hermes, prized above every rival white marble in the ancient world. Extraction on Paros had continued for nearly three thousand years by 117 CE, still shipped from this small Cycladic island to buyers across the Roman Mediterranean.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons — ancient marble quarry remains near Marathi, Paros, Greece

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Parian marble, the sculptors' stone, and the seam called lychnites — quarried underground by lamplight, which is where the name came from.

properties.notes: Sculptors working forty kilometers from Aphrodisias found a rare two-toned black-and-white stone in this Carian plateau quarry, alongside a fine white marble that rivaled the city's own famous material. Aphrodisian workshops drew on Goktepe stone for statues that traveled as far as Rome and Gaul. Quarrying began in the early 1st century CE, and by 117 CE, just before its output peaked under Hadrian, the site was already an established alternate source for Aphrodisias.

Three stone blocks weighing roughly 800 tons each still sit in this Bekaa Valley quarry, cut for the podium of the Temple of Jupiter but never moved the final few hundred meters to the sanctuary. The largest uncarved stone recorded anywhere in antiquity lies here too, over 1,000 tons of solid limestone. Construction of Heliopolis's great sanctuary complex had been underway since the reign of Augustus, and by 117 CE the quarry had already supplied a century of monumental building.
properties.image_credit: The Stone of the Pregnant Woman, an unmoved ~1,000-tonne monolith still lying in the Baalbek quarry · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This Atlantic coastal town south of Cap Spartel existed almost entirely to make garum, its salting vats sitting alongside an olive press, temple, bathhouse, and villa. Founded early in the 1st century CE under Roman rule, Cotta shipped its fish sauce across the Strait of Gibraltar to markets on both continents. By 117 CE the factory had operated for roughly a century, drawing on tuna runs passing the Moroccan Atlantic coast.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: In his geographic catalog of Mauretania beyond the Pillars of Hercules, Pliny names Lixus and Cotte (Cotta) as two towns on the Atlantic coast.

properties.notes: Fish pools, warehouses, and wells lined the estuary shoreline at this old Phoenician trading post, declared a Roman municipality in 75 CE with its salted-fish industry already well established. Wealth from the sea here ran alongside silver drawn from the nearby Sierra Almagrera. By 117 CE Baria had spent decades as a working Roman town whose economy stood on salting vats as much as mining.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Lord of the Horses - Old Iberian god - Villaricos (Almeria) - Museu d'Arqueologia de Catalunya - Barcelona 2014.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Iberian sculpture from Villaricos (ancient Baria), Almería · Museu d'Arqueologia de Catalunya, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Pliny the Elder named this Gulf of Oristano port among Sardinia's most important towns, its lagoon setting ideal for salting the tuna and other fish that passed along the coast. A Roman road and aqueduct once served the settlement, whose ruins remain visible at the mouth of the Pabillonis river. By 117 CE Neapolis had operated for centuries as a commercial hub within the lagoon system now called Stagno di Marceddi.

Eight shallow stone vats sat clustered together at this Bosporan Kingdom town on the Kerch Strait, built wide enough to salt whole large fish rather than fillets. Fishing and wine production carried the town's economy through the first centuries CE, once Rome extended its protection over the Bosporan kingdom. By 117 CE Tyritake had processed Black Sea fish catches for the better part of six centuries.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons — excavated fish-salting vats at the ancient site of Tyritake, Crimea

properties.notes: Old salt beds still line the beach at the head of the Bay of Gibraltar where this Phoenician-founded city once layered imported tuna with salt for curing. Carteia became the first Latin colony founded outside Italy in 171 BCE, and its garum trade grew alongside wine exports shipped in amphorae fired in kilns on site. By 117 CE the industry had operated continuously through more than two centuries of Roman rule.
properties.image_credit: Forum ruins at Carteia, Roman Baetica, Spain · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Rows of cisterns for salting fish still line the ruins of this Greek colony on Crimea's southwestern tip, founded by settlers from Heraclea Pontica in the 5th century BCE. Winemaking and fishing anchored the city's economy for its entire ancient existence, trading grain, cattle, and salted fish with Scythian neighbors and Greek cities alike. Roman garrisons protected Chersonesus by the Flavian period, and its fish-salting industry was still active when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Chersonesus Taurica, Crimea · Wikimedia Commons (photo: Dmitry A. Mottl)

properties.notes: The largest urban center of southern Lusitania sat where modern Faro now stands, its harbor moving salted fish and garum out to Roman markets along with agricultural goods and minerals. Mosaics of fish and marine life turn up across the surrounding Algarve coast, a sign of how central the salting industry was to the region's identity. By 117 CE Ossonoba anchored a chain of fish-processing sites running the length of the Algarve shoreline.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Cemiterio romano de Faro - Estacio da Veiga.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Roman cemetery remains at Faro (ancient Ossonoba), Portugal · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This harbor town served as the port outlet for the inland colony of Ilici, its cetariae vats built specifically to render tuna and mackerel into garum for export. Warehouses, a necropolis, and a mosaic-floored villa grew up around the fish-salting works over the 1st century CE. By 117 CE Portus Ilicitanus had spent decades shipping preserved fish out through the same harbor that once brought colonists to Ilici.

This coastal town on the Opuntian Gulf took its very name from the Greek word for salt, halas, after the springs found in its immediate neighborhood. Strabo and Pausanias both placed Halae at the eastern edge of Boeotian territory in their accounts of the region. Salt production tied to these springs continued through the Roman period, and by 117 CE the town's name still advertised the industry that built it.

Founded as a Roman colony in 181 BCE, Aquileia grew into the northern Adriatic's leading trade hub, moving glass, wine, oil, wool, and salt out through the lagoon at its doorstep. The Grado lagoon's evaporation pans supplied salt to a city Cassiodorus later praised for its saltworks near Venice. By 117 CE Aquileia had operated as a major salt-producing and salt-trading center for nearly three centuries.

Legend credited king Ancus Marcius with founding these salt pans on the Tiber's north bank, close enough to Rome that barges moved the harvest upriver in a single day. State censors imposed a tax on the salt trade here as early as 204 BCE, and two named contractors managed the public pans under a formal lease by the 130s CE. By 117 CE the Campus Salinarum had supplied Rome's own table salt for the better part of six centuries.

Salting factories lined the channel banks at Eritheia, the island district of ancient Gades, feeding a fishing industry already flourishing before the 1st century BCE. Almadraba tuna caught in the strait went straight from these salt pans into the garum vats that made the city's fish sauce famous across the empire. By 117 CE Gades had built two centuries of Roman-era wealth on the salt harvested from its own tidal flats.

Scattered river-mouth settlements including the vicus of Habentia dotted this Po delta lagoon system, an area recognized as a salt supplier to northern Italy since antiquity. Roman-era reclamation turned the shallow stagnant waters of the delta into a working salt landscape alongside fishing grounds. By 117 CE the lagoon communities here had produced salt for the region for generations, part of the same Adriatic tradition as nearby Cervia.
properties.image_credit: The Comacchio salt pans (Saline di Comacchio), Italy · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Potters at this Tarn river workshop began stamping terra sigillata under Augustus and kept the kilns firing for two centuries, their wares reaching Britain, northern Spain, and the Rhineland. Clay-rich alluvial soil beside the river gave the workshop an easy raw-material supply that rivals like La Graufesenque lacked in the same abundance. By 117 CE Montans had been in continuous production for well over a century, one of three dominant South Gaulish sigillata centers.

Cups stamped at this Lozere workshop carried moulded drinking toasts and vine-scroll decoration, made for a Roman table culture that prized conviviality on its tableware. Banassac supplied around fifteen percent of all South Gaulish sigillata production, a smaller but steady share behind the dominant La Graufesenque. By 117 CE the workshop had been firing decorated Drag. 37 bowls for decades, distributed alongside its larger neighbors across the western provinces.

More than fifty craftsmen worked side by side at this Tiber valley manufactory, the earliest fully documented case in Italy of every stage of pottery production organized under one roof. Coral-red terra sigillata cups, plates, and bowls left Scoppieto by river barge bound for Rome and Mediterranean coastal markets. Active from Augustus through Trajan, the workshop was still producing when Trajan died in 117 CE, right at the end of its two-century run.
properties.image_credit: The Scoppieto archaeological site near Baschi, Umbria, Italy · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Terra sigillata hispanica fired at this Ebro valley town under Vespasian's municipal charter reached markets across Hispania and, in smaller quantities, as far as Gaul, Germany, and North Africa. Tricio and its sister complex at Los Villares de Andujar together dominated Spanish fine-ware production for two centuries. By 117 CE the Tricio kilns were roughly midway through their peak run, which lasted from the mid-1st to the mid-2nd century CE.

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's gazetteer of the Berones lists Tritium (Tricio) among their towns — a bare place-name entry, distinct from a similarly named Tritium of the Autrigones that Pliny separately mentions (Natural History 3.27).

properties.notes: A four-sided limestone marker inscribed at this Bagradas valley estate in 116-117 CE laid out exactly how tenant farmers, or coloni, could bring unused imperial land under cultivation and what share of wheat, wine, and olive oil they owed in rent. The text applied the lex Manciana, a tenure code Rome used across its North African estates. Dated to the very year of this map's snapshot, the Henchir Mettich tablet is the earliest known copy of that law in force.

properties.modern_location: near Bou Salem, Jendouba Governorate, Tunisia
properties.notes: Coloni working this imperial olive and grain estate northeast of Bulla Regia later petitioned the emperor Commodus directly, complaining that the procurator's soldiers had flogged tenants who resisted demands beyond their legal quota. Their appeal, engraved on stone found near Souk el-Khmis, cites the same Mancian tenure system already in force decades earlier under Trajan. By 117 CE the estate's coloni were already farming under that established sharecropping arrangement.

A freedman named Titus Flavius Abascantus built this cylindrical tomb on the Appian Way for his wife Priscilla, who died around 90 CE. The poet Statius devoted the closing poem of his Silvae to the burial, describing thirteen niches meant for statues above a travertine base. Abascantus rejected cremation and had Priscilla's body embalmed and wrapped in Tyrian purple instead. Medieval nobles later fortified the ruin into a small stronghold.

ancient_sources.author: Statius
ancient_sources.note: This epicedion (funeral poem), addressed to the freedman Abascantus, mourns his wife Priscilla and describes the tomb built for her on the Via Appia, including its construction and adornment.

properties.modern_location: Via Appia Antica, near mile 7, Rome, Italy
properties.notes: A massive concrete Roman tomb mound, faced with travertine and marble, rose at the seventh mile of the Appian Way. Local legend once claimed it as Pompey the Great's grave, though he was actually buried in his family's mausoleum in the Alban Hills. In the 12th century the Astalli family stacked a stone-and-flint watchtower directly on top of the ruin, giving the site its name. That medieval tower still crowns the ancient burial mound.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 3.0

properties.name_english: Tomb of the Horatii and Curiatii
properties.notes: Four truncated stone cones once rose from the corners of this massive tumulus outside ancient Alba Longa, built from huge blocks of local peperino stone in the early first century BCE. Roman legend tied it to the semi-mythical Horatii and Curiatii champions, though that duel was supposed to have happened six centuries earlier. Modern archaeology instead points to an Etruscan noble of the Arruntia family. Two of the four original corner cones still stand.

properties.modern_location: Parco degli Scipioni, near Porta Latina, Rome, Italy
properties.notes: This underground family tomb near Porta Latina was built between 14 and 54 CE for freedmen of the imperial household, its walls lined with niches for cremation urns. A mosaic panel over the entrance steps names Pomponius Hylas, who later bought the chamber for himself and his wife Pomponia Vitalinis. Excavators uncovering it in 1831 found the stucco and mosaic decoration almost perfectly preserved. It remains one of the best-preserved columbaria in Rome.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.modern_location: Between Via Appia and Via Latina, Rome, Italy
properties.notes: Three vast underground burial chambers stood between the Appian and Latin Ways, their brick vaults lined floor to ceiling with niches for cinerary urns. The oldest of the three belonged to freedmen and slaves of Marcus Claudius Marcellus, brother of Tiberius, and dates to the Augustan era. Excavated in the mid-19th century, the chambers held thousands of urns for imperial household staff who could never afford solo tombs. They remain among the largest columbaria found in Rome.

properties.modern_location: Via Labicana, near Porta Maggiore, Rome, Italy
properties.notes: A family of builders raised this tomb along the Via Labicana around 100-120 CE and covered it with marble reliefs advertising their own trade. One panel shows a giant treadwheel crane hoisting stone blocks, the clearest surviving depiction of Roman construction machinery. Another shows the funeral bier of Hateria, a freedwoman and priestess, lying in state inside a miniature temple. The reliefs, unearthed in 1848, now hang in the Vatican Museums.
properties.image_credit: 19th-century plate reproduction, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Dozens of tombs lined the Via dei Sepolcri just outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate, built between the colony's founding in 80 BCE and the eruption of 79 CE. Freedmen, magistrates, and merchants competed for plots visible to everyone entering the city, filling the road with altars, exedra benches, and aedicula shrines. Vesuvius buried the entire street under ash and pumice in 79 CE, sealing it exactly as it stood. Excavation from the 18th century onward has recovered it intact.
properties.image_credit: 19th-century watercolor by Luigi Bazzani, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A 250-meter stretch of road outside Pompeii's Nocera Gate held hundreds of tombs belonging to freedmen, local elites, and at least one military veteran. The priestess Eumachia received an exedra-shaped monument here, and nearby stood the high-podium tomb of magistrate Publius Vesonius Phileros. Founded when Pompeii became a Roman colony in 80 BCE, the cemetery was still filling with new burials the day Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. Volcanic ash sealed it in that instant.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

properties.notes: Pompeii's city council granted this prime plot to Mamia, a public priestess, so she could build her tomb in the form of a semicircular stone bench facing the road. Her inscription records that she paid for a temple to the emperor's Genius in the forum, generosity the decurions repaid with this burial site by public decree. Archaeologist Karl Weber uncovered it between 1758 and 1764. Vesuvius had buried it under ash in 79 CE, thirty-eight years before this map's date.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Metropolitan Museum of Art collection, via Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Pompeii's leading fish-sauce manufacturer got a public monument here, his father having spent it building on land the town councilors voted him. Scaurus's name appeared on roughly 29 percent of garum jars found across Pompeii and Herculaneum, making him the city's dominant exporter of the pungent condiment. The councilors also authorized 2,000 sesterces toward his funeral and a bronze equestrian statue in the forum. The 79 CE eruption sealed the tomb decades before this map's date.

A freedwoman named Naevoleia Tyche commissioned this monument for herself, her husband Gaius Munatius Faustus, and their own freed slaves while she was still living. One relief carved into the altar shows a full-sailed merchant ship with a woman at the helm, likely Tyche herself advertising the seaborne trade that made her fortune. The inscription spells out exactly who earned the right to be buried there. Vesuvius's ash sealed the tomb in 79 CE, before this map's snapshot date.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 4.0

properties.notes: Gaius Vestorius Priscus died in office as a Pompeian aedile at just 22 years old, and his mother paid for a tufa-stone tomb near the Vesuvius Gate to mark it. Painted walls inside show him entering through a doorway, a table stacked with writing tools and coin, and a pair of gladiators he had sponsored in the amphitheater. The city had voted two thousand sesterces toward his funeral. The 79 CE eruption buried the tomb, decades ahead of this map's 117 CE date.

Five walled burial enclosures belonging to Aquileian families lined a secondary road outside the city, used from the 1st century CE onward for both cremation and inhumation. Excavators recovered 87 tombs here, packed with glass balsam-jars, stamped oil lamps, and pottery imported from the eastern Mediterranean. Roman law barred burial inside the walls, so wealthy families competed for visibility along this road instead. It remains the only Aquileian necropolis still visible in situ.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: Fourteen barrel-vaulted columbaria lined the start of the consular road out of Puteoli toward Capua, most built in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. Niches inside held cremation urns for the dead, and some chambers still carry traces of their original stucco and mosaic decoration. One building has been read as the seat of a burial club, a collegium funeraticium, that pooled dues so ordinary members could afford a decent send-off. Rediscovered in the 1930s, it opened fully to the public only in 2022.

A local Gallo-Roman family called the Julii built this three-tiered tomb outside Glanum around 30-20 BCE to honor their father and grandfather. A square base carved with battle and hunt scenes supports a miniature triumphal arch, topped by a round temple sheltering two standing statues of the deceased. It stands roughly 18 meters tall and counts among the best-preserved Roman funerary monuments anywhere. Paired with a nearby arch, the site is still known locally as Les Antiques.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Carole Raddato, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

properties.notes: Numidian kings raised this circular royal tomb near Batna in the 3rd century BCE, ringing its drum with sixty engaged Doric columns beneath an Egyptian-style cornice. Its exact occupant is unknown, though historians link it to the Numidian king Massinissa or one of his Massylian predecessors — either way, its tumulus form and scale mark it as North Africa's oldest surviving royal mausoleum. It still stood as a recognizable landmark under Roman rule in the province of Africa two centuries later. Its diameter runs about 59 meters.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

properties.notes: King Juba II and Queen Cleopatra Selene II, daughter of Cleopatra and Mark Antony, were said to be entombed beneath this vast circular monument between Tipaza and Cherchell. Sixty engaged columns ring its drum, which rises in a stepped cone roughly 40 meters high on a base over 60 meters wide. No royal remains have ever been found inside, likely lost to ancient tomb raiders. Arabic tradition later renamed it Kbor er Roumia, the tomb of the Christian woman, for the cross-shaped lines on its false door.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

ancient_sources.author: Pomponius Mela
ancient_sources.note: Marks the common tomb of the royal house on the coast road west of Icosium.

properties.notes: A bilingual inscription in Punic and Libyan once crowned this 21-meter royal tomb, naming the Numidian prince Ateban, son of Lepmatath, as its occupant. Built in the 2nd century BCE, it blends Numidian and Hellenistic design across three stacked levels ringed with Ionic pilasters. The inscription was so prized that a British consul dismantled part of the monument in 1842 to carry it off to the British Museum. French archaeologists rebuilt the mausoleum between 1908 and 1910.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

properties.notes: A 30-meter tower rises on a square plan outside El Khroub, near ancient Cirta, built in the second half of the 2nd century BCE by Greek and Carthaginian masons working for the Numidian court. Tradition names it for King Massinissa, though the balance of evidence points to his son and successor Micipsa as the actual occupant. Its mixed Greco-Punic style reflects the cosmopolitan workforce Numidian kings employed at their capital. It still stood as a visible landmark under Roman rule.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

properties.notes: A three-tiered funerary tower rose beside the Via Augusta six kilometers from Tarraco, built in the early 1st century CE for a family that owned the surrounding land. Two carved figures on its face were mistaken for the Scipio brothers by writers from the 15th to 19th centuries, giving the tower its lasting name even though the real Scipios died a century earlier. Twentieth-century research settled the dating and cleared up the misidentification. It ranks among the best-preserved Roman funerary towers on the Iberian Peninsula.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: Wealthy families of Carmo lined this hillside along the Via Augusta toward Hispalis with rock-cut chamber tombs during the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. Cremation dominated the burial rite here, with ashes placed in holes cut directly into the bedrock beside elaborate underground chambers. Accidental discovery in 1830 led to full excavation from 1882 onward, uncovering one of the largest and best-preserved Roman burial grounds on the Iberian Peninsula. It opened to the public in 1885, the first Spanish site of its kind to do so.

The grandest tomb in the Carmona necropolis was built to resemble a complete Roman villa, with a colonnaded courtyard surrounded by family burial rooms. It takes its name from a statue pedestal found inside inscribed to Servilia, daughter of Lucius, marking it as the mausoleum of an aristocratic family in the 1st century CE. Excavators recovered several statues from its porticos, now displayed in Carmona's own archaeological museum. Its Hellenistic design set it apart from every other tomb on the site.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

properties.notes: A multi-chambered crypt cut deep into the rock at Carmona takes its popular name from a small stone elephant statue found inside, now kept in the site museum. A window aligned to the equinox sun points to an original use as a shrine to Mithras or to Cybele and Attis, before it was pressed into use for ordinary burials alongside the rest of the necropolis. Its dual life as sanctuary and tomb makes it one of Carmona's more unusual monuments.

Two Roman families, the Voconii and the Julii, built open-air cremation columbaria in this funerary district southeast of Emerita Augusta. Small above-ground chambers held rows of niches for cinerary urns, several of which survive today alongside a painted family portrait of the Voconii. The site grew up around the same time as a nearby luxury villa, the House of the Mithraeum, built for the colony's upper class in the late 1st or early 2nd century CE. It now forms part of Merida's UNESCO World Heritage listing.

Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism who moved her royal household to Jerusalem, was buried in this rock-cut funerary complex after her death around 50-56 CE. A monumental staircase and courtyard lead to a 28-meter facade that the historian Josephus said was once crowned by three pyramids. Underground chambers and passages inside could hold up to fifty burials, cut for her family from Assyria's Adiabene kingdom. A massive rolling stone still seals part of the original entrance.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Queen Helena of Adiabene is buried in the three pyramids she had built three stades outside Jerusalem.

properties.notes: A 20-meter monolithic tower rises from the floor of the Kidron Valley, its lower half carved from solid rock and its upper half built up in ashlar masonry to a concave conical roof. Tradition long linked it to Absalom, King David's rebellious son who died a thousand years earlier, but its Egyptian, Persian, and Hellenistic architectural blend points instead to the 1st century CE. Vaulted chambers cut into its square base held actual burials. It stands just meters from the tombs of Zechariah and the Bnei Hezir family.
properties.image_credit: Historic photograph, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Josephus records that Absalom built himself a marble pillar/monument in the King's Dale two stadia from Jerusalem, which by his own day (1st century CE) was popularly called 'Absalom's Hand' or monument, matching the traditional identification of this Kidron Valley tomb.

properties.notes: This solid, uncarved block of limestone stands cut directly into the cliff face of the Kidron Valley, facing the Temple Mount from across the ravine. Jewish tradition names it for the priest Zechariah ben Jehoiada, though the monument itself is a monolith carved from the rock rather than a hollow chamber, meaning it never actually held a burial. Architectural analysis points to construction sometime in the 1st century BCE or CE. It sits just six meters from the neighboring Tomb of Benei Hezir.

A Hebrew inscription carved above the entrance identifies this as the burial cave of the Benei Hezir, a family of priests who served in the Jerusalem Temple. Two rock-cut columns stand between pilasters below a Doric frieze, making it the oldest of the four monumental Second Temple-era tombs clustered in the Kidron Valley. Scholars date its excavation to the Hasmonean period, roughly the 2nd or early 1st century BCE. It remains a burial complex rather than a solid monument like its neighbors.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: King Herod built himself an elaborate three-story mausoleum on the slope of his hilltop fortress south of Jerusalem, its circular tholos ringed with an Ionic colonnade beneath a conical roof. Archaeologist Ehud Netzer identified its remains in 2007, along with fragments of a reddish limestone sarcophagus smashed into pieces. Jewish rebels who despised Herod's memory tore the tomb apart during the revolt of 66-72 CE, decades before this map's 117 CE date. No trace of Herod's actual remains has ever been found.

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: The funeral procession from Jericho: the bier of gold, the guard in arms, and eight miles' march to burial at Herodium.

properties.notes: Queen Artemisia II built this towering tomb for her husband and brother Mausolus around 350 BCE, stacking a colonnaded temple and stepped pyramid roof atop a massive podium roughly 45 meters tall. Ancient writers counted it among the Seven Wonders of the World, and its scale gave the world the word mausoleum. The monument still stood largely intact under Roman rule in 117 CE; only earthquakes centuries later, between the 11th and 15th centuries, brought it down. Crusader knights then quarried its stones to build a nearby castle.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction painting by Ferdinand Knab, 1886, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Gives the tomb its measurements and the four sculptors who each took a side, and says the fourth was still working when the queen who commissioned it died.

properties.notes: More than 1,200 tombs stretch across two kilometers on the slopes north and south of Hierapolis, making it the largest ancient burial ground in Asia Minor. Tumuli, house-shaped tombs, and elaborately carved sarcophagi span the late Hellenistic period through the early centuries of Roman rule. Visitors traveled here for the city's hot mineral springs, believed to have healing power, and many chose to be buried within sight of the sacred waters. The necropolis remains one of the best-preserved of its kind anywhere in the ancient world.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: West of Palmyra, a narrow valley filled with tower tombs rising four and five stories against the desert cliffs, the tallest funerary architecture anywhere in the Roman world. Wealthy Palmyrene families built these sandstone towers between roughly 9 BCE and 128 CE, packing each level with loculi for hundreds of family members across generations. Corinthian columns and painted coffered ceilings decorated the more elaborate interiors. Many of these towers stood until ISIL destroyed several with explosives in 2015.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.modern_location: Valley of the Tombs, Palmyra, Syria
properties.notes: Four Palmyrene brothers, Elahbel, Shagai, Mogimo, and Maani, finished building this four-story sandstone tower tomb in 103 CE, an exact date recorded in its dedicatory inscription. Corinthian pilasters and painted coffered ceilings decorated burial chambers that together held more than 300 bodies across the tower's levels. It stood as one of the tallest and best-preserved tower tombs in the Valley of the Tombs for nearly two thousand years. ISIL destroyed it with explosives in August 2015.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: Carved into Petra's eastern cliff face between 40 and 70 CE, this tomb takes its name from capitals loosely resembling the Corinthian order, though they're actually Nabataean floral horn designs. Its facade spans nearly 28 meters wide and 28 meters tall, modeled on the design of the famous Treasury nearby. The layout borrows heavily from Ptolemaic architecture that had developed in Alexandria. It stands directly beside the even larger Palace Tomb along the same royal cliff.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: The largest rock-cut facade in Petra spans 49 meters wide and 46 meters tall, carved into the eastern cliff toward the end of the 1st century CE. Its top story breaks with every other tomb in the city by extending beyond the cliff face as freestanding built masonry rather than carved rock. Four wide entrances on the ground floor lead into separate burial chambers behind the towering facade. Its scale and unusual construction mark it as one of Petra's grandest Nabataean monuments.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: Swirling bands of pink, purple, gold, and orange run across this tomb's sandstone facade, carved sometime in the first half of the 1st century CE. Iron and manganese oxides trapped in the rock, polished smooth by centuries of wind and water, produced the vivid marbled effect that gives the tomb its modern nickname. Compared with its grander neighbors along the Royal Tombs cliff, its facade is modest and unadorned by columns. The colors alone have made it one of Petra's most photographed monuments.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: Four elongated pyramids carved above this facade at Petra's entrance represent nefesh, Nabataean markers for the souls of the dead, with a worn figure of a cloaked man niched between them. Most scholars date it to the reign of Malichos II, between 40 and 70 CE, built directly above a separate dining hall known as the Bab as-Siq Triclinium. An inscription at the site records details connecting the two structures. Visitors today pass beneath it on the walk into Petra's main canyon.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 4.0

properties.notes: A carved figure wearing a muscled cuirass decorated with flowers stands at the center of this facade in the Wadi Farasa valley, its armor style so distinctly Roman that early visitors assumed it marked a soldier's grave. Archaeologists now date the complex to the third quarter of the 1st century CE, decades before Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE. A carved triclinium banquet hall sits directly across a courtyard from the tomb facade. The figure was almost certainly a Nabataean official, not a Roman legionary.

Rock-cut tombs spread across the hillsides ringing Cyrene, one of the largest burial landscapes to survive from the Greek and Roman world, with graves ranging from the 6th century BCE through the Roman period. The Western Necropolis holds the most monumental examples, its facades carved with Doric and Ionic porticoes along a dedicated funerary road. Temple-tombs and painted chamber tombs with rock-cut sarcophagi honeycomb the surrounding cliffs. Italian archaeologists continue to uncover previously unrecorded tombs here.
properties.image_credit: 19th-century illustration, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: An Ionic temple facade with columns carved straight out of the cliff, rather than built up in front of it, marks this rock-hewn tomb above ancient Telmessos. A Greek inscription beside the entrance names it for Amyntas, son of Hermagios, and dates the monument to around 350 BCE. It remains the grandest of a whole cliffside cluster of Lycian house-tombs overlooking the harbor. The city below, later renamed Fethiye, remained a landmark of Lycian territory throughout Roman rule.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 4.0

properties.notes: More than 100 rock-cut tombs honeycomb the cliffs above Myra, most carved in the 4th century BCE in the distinctive Lycian house-tomb style that mimics timber architecture in solid stone. Stonemasons reproduced beams, joists, and doors down to the smallest detail, and traces of the original red and blue paint still survive on several facades. The River Necropolis holds the famous Painted Tomb, decorated with life-sized carved figures on both its interior and exterior walls. Myra remained a major Lycian city throughout Roman rule of the province.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: Lycian ruler Arbinas built himself a Greek temple in miniature atop an 8-meter podium at Xanthos around 390-380 BCE, its columns framing statues of sea nymphs that gave the monument its modern name. Two carved friezes wrapped the podium with scenes of sieges and battles, part biography and part legend. The design later influenced the far larger Mausoleum at Halicarnassus. Only stone blocks of the podium remain in place today, the sculpted superstructure having been removed to the British Museum in the 19th century.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction drawing, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: An ordinary pagan cemetery grew up on the northern edge of Salona from the 2nd century BCE onward, filling with cremation and inhumation burials for the provincial capital's residents over the following centuries. By 117 CE it functioned as a typical extramural Roman burial ground outside Dalmatia's chief city, undistinguished from dozens of similar cemeteries across the empire. Its later fame as a Christian pilgrimage site, built around the martyred bishop Domnius, only began after his execution in 304 CE. Stone sarcophagi from the Roman-era burials still scatter the site today.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: The largest of Rome's four imperial gladiator schools, built by Domitian directly east of the Colosseum and linked to it by an underground tunnel so fighters could reach the arena unseen. Its own small oval training ground, ringed by barracks and cells, could hold roughly 2,000 gladiators at full capacity. Excavated remains are still visible today just off the Via Labicana. In 117 CE it was Rome's premier gladiatorial training ground, fully staffed and in daily use.
properties.image_credit: Ludus Magnus, Rome, photographed 2006 by Jastrow - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodian
ancient_sources.note: Recounts that the emperor Commodus, in his obsession with gladiatorial combat, wanted to abandon the imperial palace and live instead in the gladiators' barracks (the Ludus Magnus) next to the Colosseum.

properties.modern_location: Rome, Italy, near the Caelian Hill
properties.notes: Founded under Domitian and completed under Trajan to train gladiators drawn from Dacian prisoners, its fighters specialized in the falx, the curved blade that had cut through Roman shields on the Danube frontier. It stood on the slope of the Caelian Hill east of the Colosseum, alongside Rome's three other imperial schools, though its exact footprint has never been pinned down by excavation. Trajan's Dacian triumph of 106 CE kept it freshly supplied with captives in the years just before 117 CE.

One of Domitian's four imperial gladiator schools, training fighters in the heavy-armored style associated with Gallic warriors, whose bulky equipment was prized for spectacle even as it slowed a fighter's footwork in the arena. Ancient sources place it in Rome's Regio II near the Colosseum alongside the Ludus Magnus, Dacicus, and Matutinus, but unlike the Ludus Magnus its precise site has never been excavated. It was still functioning as one of the four state-run schools in 117 CE.

The fourth of Domitian's imperial schools, training bestiarii, the men who fought and hunted wild animals in the morning program before the afternoon's gladiator bouts, hence its name. Topographers have placed it between the Claudianum and the Vicus Caput Africae, but like the Gallicus and Dacicus, no excavated structure has been firmly identified as this school. It was one of four functioning state schools supplying the Colosseum's beast hunts in 117 CE.

The most famous gladiator school outside Rome, and the oldest one on record: a lanista named Aurelius Scaurus was training state gladiators here around 105 BCE. It became infamous in 73 BCE when roughly 70 gladiators, led by the Thracian fighter Spartacus, broke out and touched off the Third Servile War. Its ruins lie beside Capua's amphitheater, second in size only to the Colosseum. The school was still operating, and the amphitheater still hosting games, in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Santa Maria Capua Vetere, adjacent to the gladiator school site - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: Describes the gladiatorial school at Capua run by Lentulus Batiatus, where about 70-78 gladiators including Spartacus broke out with kitchen implements in 73 BCE, sparking the Third Servile War.

properties.notes: Ravenna hosted one of the handful of gladiator schools outside Rome brought under direct state administration by the early empire, alongside Praeneste, Alexandria, and Pergamon. Its exact site within the ancient city has not been located archaeologically, and its history survives mainly through epigraphic and literary mentions rather than excavated remains. Ravenna's standing as home port of Rome's Adriatic war fleet made it a natural garrison town for a state-run school of this kind.

Alexandria's gladiator school was one of a small group of provincial ludi absorbed into direct imperial administration by the late 1st century CE, training fighters for Egypt's amphitheaters. Its physical location within the ancient city is not archaeologically fixed, and it is known chiefly through literary references grouping it with the state schools at Pergamon, Praeneste, and Capua. Alexandria's rank as the empire's second city made it a natural site for imperial investment in the games.

Pergamon's gladiator school was another of the provincial ludi brought under state control in the early empire, training fighters in a city also renowned for a great school of medicine. Its exact location has not been excavated or identified, and it is attested mainly alongside the other named state schools at Alexandria, Praeneste, and Capua. Pergamon sat in a province where Greek athletics, not gladiatorial games, remained the dominant public spectacle.

Begun under Caligula on his family's estate on the Vatican Hill and finished under Claudius, this circus is separate from the Circus Maximus across the river, best known as the site of Nero's persecution of Christians after the fire of 64 CE. Its spina carried an Egyptian obelisk from Heliopolis, the same one standing today in St Peter's Square since 1586. Still active in 117 CE, it later gave its ground to the basilica of St Peter's.
properties.image_credit: Vatican Obelisk, originally the spina obelisk of the Circus of Nero - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes Nero's persecution of Christians after the Great Fire of 64 CE, including executions staged as spectacles in the circus on the Vatican hill where Nero's family had an estate (Pliny the Elder, Natural History 36.74, separately describes the obelisk erected there by Gaius and Nero).

properties.notes: Built over a former necropolis at the end of the 1st century CE, Carthage's circus stretched more than 470 meters, about a third the length of the Circus Maximus, and could seat roughly 45,000 spectators for chariot races. It ranked among the largest circuses anywhere outside Rome and Antioch, reflecting Carthage's status as Africa's leading city. In use and hosting races by 117 CE, it remained active for centuries afterward, with further building work added in the early 3rd century.

ancient_sources.author: Salvian
ancient_sources.note: Describes Carthage's citizens still packing the circus and shouting for the races as the Vandal army closed in on the city in 439 CE, calling it a mark of how far the city's morals had fallen even in its last hours.

properties.notes: Carthage's amphitheater went up west of the Byrsa hill at the end of the 1st or start of the 2nd century CE, with an inscription confirming it was already in service by 133-139 CE, just after this map's snapshot. It seated around 30,000, one of the largest arenas in Roman Africa. Christian tradition later placed the martyrdoms of Perpetua and Felicity here in 203 CE. Under construction or newly finished as Trajan's reign closed in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Carthage, interior view - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous (redactor, incorporating Perpetua's own prison diary)
ancient_sources.note: Early-3rd-century (c. 203 CE) martyrdom account that narrates in detail the execution of Perpetua, Felicity, and companions by beasts and sword in the amphitheatre of Carthage.

properties.notes: Long before the massive amphitheater that made El Djem famous, Thysdrus already had a much smaller arena, an earthen structure excavated in 1973 with a capacity of around 6,000, dated by specialists to the 1st century CE. A second, intermediate amphitheater followed on the same site before the great stone amphitheater seen today rose around 238 CE, over a century after Trajan's death. In 117 CE it was this small first-generation arena serving Thysdrus, not the monumental one tourists visit now.

Built under the Flavian emperors in the closing decade of the 1st century CE, Nimes's amphitheater could seat around 24,000 spectators and remains one of the best-preserved Roman arenas anywhere, still hosting events today nearly two thousand years later. Its two tiers of arcades in dressed limestone reflect the wealth Nemausus drew from its position on the road linking Italy to Spain. Fully operational and hosting games in 117 CE, a generation or so after its completion.
properties.image_credit: Arena of Nimes - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL XII 3316
ancient_sources.note: A text on the podium wall reserves places for the guilds of Rhône and Saône boatmen, by decree of the town council of Nîmes.

properties.notes: Raised around 90 CE under Domitian, not long after the Colosseum in Rome, Arles's amphitheater measures 136 by 107 meters across two levels of arcades, 60 arches below and 34 above, and could hold roughly 20,000 spectators for gladiatorial combat, beast hunts, and public executions. Arelate's wealth as a Roman colony and river port on the Rhone funded a building program on a scale that rivaled cities twice its size. Fully active and staging games in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Arenes d'Arles (Arles Amphitheatre) - Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Raised outside Verona's walls in the early 1st century CE, most likely around 30 CE, in pink and white limestone, the Verona Arena could seat around 30,000, one of the largest amphitheaters in Roman Italy after the Colosseum and Capua's arena. Its outer ring mostly collapsed in a 12th-century earthquake, but the inner structure survives intact enough to still host opera today. In full use for games nearly a century before Trajan's reign closed in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Verona Arena - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Pliny writes to Maximus praising him for giving a gladiatorial spectacle to the people of Verona as a memorial to his late wife, a Veronese woman; the letter does not name the amphitheater building itself but is about games staged at Verona.

properties.notes: Begun under Augustus as a smaller structure, then enlarged for gladiatorial games under Vespasian from 79 CE and finished under Titus around 81 CE, the amphitheater at Pula in Istria could hold about 23,000 spectators. Its full limestone outer wall survives intact, unlike most Roman amphitheaters, making it one of the six largest and best-preserved arenas from the ancient world. Actively hosting games as a fully finished, mature amphitheater in 117 CE, roughly one generation after completion.
properties.image_credit: Pula Arena, Croatia - Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Docimium's quarries had been worked on imperial account since the 1st century BCE for their prized purple-veined marble, and would go on to become one of the empire's great sarcophagus-carving centers, exporting garland- and column-decorated coffins as far as Rome and Africa. In 117 CE that specialty hadn't started yet: the earliest dated garland sarcophagi belong to the Hadrianic period beginning in the 130s CE. Docimium was already a mature imperial marble exporter, just not yet a sarcophagus workshop.

Athens became one of the Roman world's three major sarcophagus-exporting centers, its workshops carving Pentelic marble coffins shipped across the eastern Mediterranean. But the dating is unambiguous: surviving Attic sarcophagi run from roughly 130 to 260 CE, with output really taking off only after 200 CE. In 117 CE this industry had not yet started. Athens under Trajan still cremated its dead, a full generation before its famous sarcophagus workshops carved their first pieces.

Aphrodisias already had a thriving marble-sculpture export trade by 117 CE, with signed work by its sculptors turning up in Rome, Greece, and Africa on the strength of local quarries and a renowned sculpture school. Its columnar sarcophagi, an architectural facade with figures between the columns, are a later specialty documented from the 2nd century, with nearby Goktepe marble spreading Mediterranean-wide only from the mid-2nd century. In 117 CE it stood on the edge of its own sarcophagus boom.

properties.notes: Aquileia's forum anchored the colony's public life at the junction of the Via Iulia Augusta and the Via Sacra. Workers paved the square with pale Aurisina limestone slabs quarried from the nearby Karst hills, replacing the timber-and-rubble forum that had served the colony since its founding in 181 BCE. A civil basilica closed the square's south side, housing courts and the city council, while merchants kept shops along its east and west flanks. A canal ran beneath the pavement, channeling river water toward the port. By 117 CE the forum had stood at the heart of Aquileia for over a century, hosting markets, trials, and the colony's public assemblies beneath the Alpine sky.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum, Aquileia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: AE 1996, 685
ancient_sources.note: An honorific elogium for one of the colony's founding triumvirs recorded the powers granted him to draft Aquileia's laws, enroll its senate, and dedicate a temple during the colony's 169 BCE reinforcement.

properties.notes: Marcus Agrippa financed the theatre for the new colony of Augusta Emerita, and builders finished it in 16 BCE. A two-story colonnaded stage backdrop rose behind the orchestra, its columns and marble statuary framing performances for an audience of six thousand. Veterans of the Roman legions who settled the colony filled its semicircular tiers for comedies, tragedies, and public ceremonies alike. Under Trajan, workers refaced the stage building's facade in marble and fenced a sacred precinct into the front seating rows with a marble railing. Cut into a hillside above the Guadiana River, the theatre stood 132 years old in 117 CE, still the beating heart of the colony's cultural life.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre, Merida · Hakan Svensson (Xauxa), Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL II 474
ancient_sources.note: A lintel inscription over the theatre's side passages named Marcus Agrippa, three times consul, as its builder, opening with the same 'M AGRIPPA L F COS' formula he later used on Rome's Pantheon.

properties.notes: Trajan founded Timgad in 100 CE as a colony for army veterans, laying the city out as a nearly perfect grid centered on its forum. Porticoes and rows of shops framed the paved square, with the curia and a basilica standing at its heart and a small temple to Victory tucked into one corner. Retired soldiers of the Third Augustan Legion walked its colonnades to conduct civic business and hear public announcements. A dedicatory tablet found near the forum commemorated the emperor's foundation of the colony and the legionary legate who oversaw the work. Seventeen years old in 117 CE, the forum still smelled of new-cut stone from a city built at Trajan's order in the empty steppe.
properties.image_credit: Forum of Timgad · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII 2355
ancient_sources.note: A fragmentary tabula found near the forum and west gate commemorated Trajan's founding of the colony of Thamugadi, carried out through his legate and the Third Augustan Legion; scholarship places it tentatively in this area rather than on any specific standing arch.
